On WNBA players supplementing their salaries overseas

Prior to the collective bargaining agreement that was instituted during the 2026 offseason, the average salary for a WNBA player was a little over $100,000 ... and that necessitated a lot of players to play overseas during their WNBA offseasons. ... And that means that players are competing year-round, not giving them a lot of time to rest, recover their bodies, work on their games even, or spend time with their families and loved ones during their break from their WNBA season.

For the majority of the WNBA's history, players made more money on their overseas contracts, whether that was playing in Russia or Turkey or France or Italy or Australia, compared to their WNBA contracts. I mean, it got so ridiculous at points that a player like Diana Taurasi, after winning a WNBA title in 2014, goes to play in Russia during that offseason and then her team says, we're going to pay you a million dollars not to play on the WNBA this year, just so you can rest and be ready for our next season. And so she sits out instead of defending her title and makes ten times as much money as she would for not playing as she would by playing.

Sponsor Message

The new collective bargaining agreement has created an average salary of about $600,000 now for WNBA players. ... And there is a revenue-sharing component in the CBA such that as the WNBAs revenue rises, whether that's more media money, more ticket money, any sort of revenue that the league brings in, that would create a corresponding change in the WNBA salaries.

Monique Nazareth and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

World.title: Barbara Keating died in the 9/11 attack. She's finally being laid to rest
World.content:
Barbara Keating died in the 9/11 attack. She's finally being laid to rest

toggle caption Family of Barbara Keating, used with permission/Keating family

As communities across the U.S. commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, the family of Barbara Keating will gather privately in Framingham, Mass., to finally lay her to rest.

Keating was flying home to California after visiting her family when terrorists linked to al-Qaida crashed American Airlines Flight 11 into the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. A team of forensic researchers identified Keating's remains last year.

Her son, Paul Keating, told NPR that the family is gathering to celebrate her life. "We carved the headstone 25 years ago, but she wasn't there, and now she will be," he says. "This feels like, at least to some degree, some closure."

Sponsor Message

According to Keating, on the day of the attack in 2001, he was traveling in New Jersey on business and saw the twin towers burn and fall.

"Basically everyone stopped what they were doing, we were like across the water from it, watching it," he recalls. "At some point, I got a call and found out that that was my mother's plane."

Barbara Keating was 72 years old, with five children and 12 grandchildren, and had retired from a career leading a chapter of the children's advocacy group Big Brothers Big Sisters near Boston. She'll be laid to rest next to her husband. "She was tough, funny, very smart, she was fabulous," Keating says.

New York officials say 40% of the 2,753 people who died on 9/11 in New York City still have not been recovered or positively identified. But teams continue to search through rubble and debris collected from the World Trade Center site.

Keating praised the ongoing effort to reconnect grieving families with the remains of their loved ones: "It just means a lot to comb over miles and miles of city blocks of debris for every day, 60 hours a week for 24 years."

Efforts continue to find roughly 1,100 victims of 9/11 still unaccounted for in New York City. In a statement, the city's chief medical examiner, Dr. Jason Graham, described the effort as a "sacred commitment."

Sponsor Message

"A quarter century after the day that forever changed our world, we are keeping the promise to identify those who died at the World Trade Center in 2001 and return them to their loved ones," Graham said.

Using increasingly sophisticated forensic DNA techniques, researchers identified one more previously unknown woman last month. Her name is being withheld at the request of her family.

World.title: Elon Musk threatens to sue over Gibney documentary's "space lasers" claim
World.content:
Elon Musk threatens to sue over Gibney documentary's "space lasers" claim

toggle caption Evan Vucci/AP

Elon Musk has in recent days been targeting his ire at filmmaker Alex Gibney, whose forthcoming documentary, Musk, offers a scathing look at the tech mogul's rise. Now, a lawyer for Musk is threatening to file a defamation lawsuit ahead of the film's release next month.

In a letter sent to Gibney's Jigsaw Productions, the company behind the film, Musk attorney Alex Spiro homes in on an exchange between Gibney and Ashley St. Clair, a former MAGA influencer who dated Musk and had a child with the billionaire.

St. Clair described text messages Musk sent her before the November 2024 presidential election in which he said he was "feeling more optimistic" about Donald Trump winning because "tomorrow we unleash the anomaly in the matrix." When St. Clair asked for clarity, Musk said he planned on tapping "'Lasers' from space," adding that "I have over 10 thousand lasers in space right now."

Sponsor Message

In the film, Gibney asked St. Clair if she believed Musk's texts referred to satellites owned by his rocket company, SpaceX. She responded, "I don't know where else he has lasers."

NPR has obtained and authenticated the texts between Musk and St. Clair, which were sent on Oct. 6, 2024.

In Spiro's letter, which NPR has also reviewed, he described a debunked conspiracy theory that SpaceX's Starlink satellites somehow uploaded votes for Trump in swing states. Spiro argued that Gibney promoted that refuted claim in his film.

"Starlink was not connected to vote tabulation. Election officials in multiple states, independent cybersecurity researchers, and fact-checkers publicly refuted the Starlink vote-rigging claim in November 2024, and nothing since has revived it," Spiro wrote. "Starlink's satellites communicate by laser inter-satellite link; that is what 'lasers in space' describes," he wrote. "You are therefore on notice, before release, that the insinuation is false, that the material refuting it is public, and that you chose not to be told the rest."

Jigsaw Productions said in a statement that its "right to engage in open debate and fact-based examinations of powerful public figures" is protected by the First Amendment, adding that it is "something that should be recognized and defended by all Americans, including the associates of Elon Musk, who has proclaimed himself to be a 'free speech absolutist.'"

Sponsor Message

St. Clair said Musk's legal threats are "a joke" in a statement to NPR.

"They are more likely to colonize Mars than win a defamation case against Alex Gibney," she said. "Alex Spiro is sending fairy dust letters with obtuse legalese."

Spiro wrote in the letter that Gibney and the production "refused" to hear from Musk's team, which Spiro described as a "conscious decision to disregard the truth." But Gibney has said Musk declined to be interviewed for the film. To substitute for the real Musk, Gibney featured a deepfake version of Musk made with AI, who speaks directly to the camera using Musk's words from public appearances.

Neither Spiro nor Musk has seen Gibney's documentary, which runs nearly four hours and features interviews with Musk's first ex-wife, Justine Musk, his father, Errol Musk, the co-founder of Tesla, and a host of former business partners, journalists and other critics of the tech titan.

NPR attended a screening of the sprawling film this week. It covers everything from how Musk was bullied as a child in South Africa and his early fortunes in the dot-com era to his acquisition of Twitter, his stint in the White House and his ever-growing wealth and influence. Gibney's organizing thesis is that Musk is a self-mythologizer and "stock pumper" who became the richest man in the world by selling the public, investors and the federal government on exaggerated promises.

Musk has taken to X in recent days to attack Gibney's film as a "hit piece," writing that the Oscar-winning director's goal was "fabricating a false film."

Proving that Gibney's film is defamatory under the law, however, is another matter entirely.

For Musk to win a defamation case, his lawyers must show Gibney engaged in "actual malice." In other words, they must prove that he knew an assertion was false and still decided to include it in the documentary, or had "reckless disregard" for whether something was true or not, according to Genevieve Lakier, a professor at the University of Chicago Law School.

Sponsor Message

"It's a very demanding standard, and even if the documentary included a statement that turns out to be wrong, that is not actual malice," Lakier said.

Otherwise, Lakier said, filmmakers like Gibney have quite far-reaching free expression rights under the First Amendment, especially when it comes to applying scrutiny to public figures like Musk.

"The threat of initiating a lawsuit is used all the time to try to chill and suppress speech," Lakier said. "It sounds like Musk doesn't like the documentary, so he wants to do whatever he can to shut it down and intimidate distributors. It would be a much more impoverished democracy if we weren't allowed to make documentaries about public figures that were critical of them."

World.title: 'I've never seen anything like this' -- A U.S. doctor treats Ebola's youngest victims
World.content:
'I've never seen anything like this' — A U.S. doctor treats Ebola's youngest victims

toggle caption Courtesy of Dr. Rupa Narra. Diptych by NPR.

An Ebola treatment unit in the city of Butembo, in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, has 30 beds. Tonight, they're all full.

"I don't know how this is going to slow down," says Dr. Rupa Narra, a U.S. pediatrician who arrived in August to work for Doctors Without Borders. "It's the most devastating thing I've ever seen in my life."

With at least 6,800 confirmed cases and more than 3,310 deaths since May, the latest outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is on track to be the worst on record. Last week, Narra's unit lost eight patients — all under the age of 5.

Sponsor Message

The outbreak is being driven by the Bundibugyo strain of ebolavirus; which has no approved antiviral medication or vaccine. Without these medical options, about 30% of adults who are diagnosed with the virus die within two weeks. The death rate is even higher for children, whose immune systems are less developed. For newborns, the virus is almost always fatal.

While children have made up 1 in 4 confirmed cases in this outbreak, they represent 1 in overall 3 deaths.

Narra and her colleagues spend their days providing supportive care: running fluids through an IV, giving oxygen or blood transfusions. Treating hypothermia, fever or secondary infections as their patients' bodies try to fight the virus. Part of her role is helping train about a dozen doctors and nurses in Butembo on how to adjust this care for pediatric and newborn patients.

"I had to change my mindset, that we were going to save kids," Narra says. "Now, it's — we're going to minimize suffering, and we're going to let the Congolese staff know that they did everything they could to save that baby's life."

The Bundibugyo strain can often begin with symptoms similar to malaria, so 15 of the beds in the unit are for sick patients who are waiting on test results. The other 15 beds are for confirmed Ebola patients. But in recent days, Narra says, there are so many people coming to the clinic that they have begun using quarantine beds for confirmed cases.

Sponsor Message

"It's still not enough," Narra says. "I know everyone is trying to scale up as fast as possible, but it's moving at a rapidity that never was the case."

There's a tricky thing about taking care of kids in an Ebola unit. Because there's no approved vaccine — it's hard to find someone already immune to the virus, from a prior infection, who can watch over the smallest patients. Narra and her colleagues are limited to about an hour at a time due to the difficulty and risks of working in protective gear.

Shortly after she arrived in Butembo, Narra says, a young mother died in the Ebola unit soon after giving birth. Her newborn daughter was entirely alone.

"I didn't know what we were going to do with this baby, because there were no other family members who had been exposed, and there was a high likelihood for this child to have Ebola," Narra says.

But when she entered the baby's room — there was a woman there, holding her in her arms.

"Actually, she was an Ebola survivor," Narra says. "She did not know the family and agreed to take care of this baby."

The baby lived for 10 days — but eventually succumbed to the virus. Her caregiver never left her side.

Narra is no stranger to crisis. She worked as an epidemiologist in 2014, responding to the West Africa Ebola outbreak that killed 11,310 people. She was a pediatrician in an emergency department in Brooklyn when COVID-19 hit the United States. She worked for Doctors Without Borders in Haiti.

"I've never seen anything like this," she says. "The speed of transmission, along with other aspects of a fragile healthcare system."

The latest Ebola outbreak is concentrated in the eastern border region between the DRC, Rwanda and Uganda, where fierce clashes between the Congolese army and Rwandan-backed paramilitary forces have forced families to find refuge in cities like Butembo. Meanwhile, the region's healthcare system is already stretched thin, treating children with malnutrition and outbreaks of malaria or measles on a regular basis. The conflict, and cuts to foreign aid have disrupted routine vaccinations and other assistance.

Sponsor Message

As a pediatrician, there's little Narra can do to help a kid feel a little less scared.

Every day, before she sees her patients, she puts on a fully disinfected hazmat suit. Only her eyes are visible.

"You're 5 years old, and these people walk in with what looks like a spacesuit. Of course you're going to scream!" she says.

She can't bring in a toy to distract them, wear a funny hat. Pick them up and show them around the clinic, bouncing them on her hip. She can't hold their hand through the night, when they get really sick.

"That's been the very difficult part for me — is I can't be at the bedside of this critical child," she says.

She remembers one 5-year-old patient in quarantine, waiting on test results, whose father would sit with her, letting her watch Bollywood movies on his smartphone. Narra, whose family is from southern India, recognized one of the songs — a number from the romantic comedy, Desi Boyz.

After her shift that day, Narra took off her gear and ran outside to her patient's window. She knocked, this time looking like herself –- and did her best Bollywood dance moves from the film.

"And then, she was smiling, laughing and clapping," Narra laughs. "I was like –- I don't even know these moves but I will make them up for you!"

A few days later, the test results came back for the little girl: negative. One bright spot, in Narra's painful summer.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: How did 9/11 reshape national security?
World.content:
How did 9/11 reshape national security?

It's been 25 years since al-Qaida terrorists attacked the United States by hijacking four commercial airplanes and crashing them into the World Trade Center towers and the Pentagon.

A fourth plane crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pa..

Sept. 11, 2001 represented a new kind of national security threat, and a new national security architecture was created to confront it.

Before a live audience at NPR's headquarters in Washington, D.C., Sources and Methods host Mary Louise Kelly discussed how that day changed the country and its spy agencies, with people who worked on the frontlines of government and intelligence.

That panel included Stephen Hadley, Jane Harman, John Mclaughlin and Michael Morell. At the time of the attacks, Hadley was serving as deputy national security adviser in the Bush White House. Jane Harman was a Democratic member of Congress representing California. John McLaughlin was deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency. Michael Morell was also at the CIA and was President Bush's CIA briefer that very day.

The following highlights from their conversation have been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

On their memories of the day:

John McLaughlin: I was running a staff meeting. We were talking about the budget, including the budget for counterterrorism. We were talking about the Balkans and some other problems we were struggling with at that moment. And the first plane hit. And like everyone else, my thought was, 'Could be terrorism. But let's see what is going on here.'

Sponsor Message

And of course, the second plane left no doubt in our minds. I thought, and I think everyone there thought, 'We are under attack.' The other thought was in my mind and the mind of many people would say, 'OK, that's it,' because we had been anticipating a major attack. We did not know time, target or method. But we had been receiving that summer, a giant spike in reporting about terrorism, something that the director subsequently characterized as the lights were blinking red all summer. But at the end of the day, I did write on my computer, 'Nothing will ever be the same.'

Stephen Hadley: I was in the Situation Room. Dick [Richard] Clarke, the White House counterterrorism chief at the time, had a group in the back room, trying to figure out what we knew, what happened, whether this might be the first of successive attacks, more coming.And then the White House evacuated, and we saw these people running down West Executive Avenue. So I asked the group in the Situation Room, 'Do you want to leave? Or do you want to stay?' Everybody said: 'We've got to stay and help the president manage this crisis,' so we did.I think one of the things I remember most was Norm [Norman] Mineta, then secretary of transportation, getting thousands of airplanes in the air over this country down onto the ground, because we did not know how many might have been taken over by terrorists and become a weapon against this country.

Sponsor Message

Jane Harman: If I could back it up just one day, on September 10th, I had lunch with Ambassador Paul Bremer.At the time, he had chaired something called the National Commission on Terrorism. I was a member of that commission, which was one of three commissions predicting, based on studies we had made, that there could be a major terror attack on U.S. soil. And Jerry [Paul Bremer] and I were having lunch near the Capitol, bemoaning the fact that no one was paying attention to us. So, 20 hours later, guess what?

[That morning] I was going to my office, and then I was going to the intel rooms, which were in the dome of the Capitol at the time. And later, most of us thought that the target of that plane that went down in Pennsylvania was the U.S. Capitol. So my office called and said the office buildings are evacuated, a plane has hit the World Trade Tower and we're not sure what it is, but the office buildings are closed. The Capitol just closed. And so a lot of us I mean, I would say hundreds of members were milling around outside the Capitol. We would have had a continuity of government crisis if that plane had hit the Capitol. And what I heard, I'm not sure this is true, is that it left late, that United plane 93, and had it not left late, it would have been in flight before we got real news of what happened to the Trade Towers, and it might have hit when the rest of us were around.

Mary Louise Kelly: Michael, I've saved you for last because you were traveling with President Bush on his plane that day as his CIA briefer. Did the briefing that morning, the president's daily brief, that you delivered to President Bush mention al-Qaida, mention terrorism?

Michael Morell: Contrary to what you read on the internet. It did not. I remember distinctly that it focused on the second intifada, which was then raging in the West Bank, which the president was very much focused on. No mention of terrorism, no mention of al-Qaida outside the intifada.There was a piece in the PDB (president's daily briefing) that caught the president's attention, and he called Condi Rice [Condoleezza Rice] to ask her to follow up on something. I think the briefing lasted about 20 to 25 minutes, started at eight. And then we left the briefing and got in the motorcade to go to Booker T. elementary school.

Sponsor Message

The president did say to me that he wanted me to call Director Tenet [George Tenet] and tell him that if he got any information as to the perpetrator, that he, the president, wanted to be the first to know.

I remember distinctly the head of the Secret Service telling the president that he needed to stay away from Washington. And I remember the president saying, 'The American people want to know where their president is. I'm coming home now.'

How the government viewed the terrorist threat in the wake of the attacks:

Hadley: I think it's hard to understand the actions that were taken without a sense of the mood at the time we had been attacked. We were surprised. We did not really know from whence it came. We did not know as much about al-Qaida as we needed to. And the intelligence community was saying at the time, that they thought it was likely or at least highly probable that this was a first of a wave of mass casualty attacks, some of which might involve weapons of mass destruction from this enemy that we felt we did not know well enough. So it was an all- hands-on-deck moment to get the country in a position so that that reality would not happen. And all the steps we were taking to change missions, organizations and the like, you can criticize individual pieces of them but the country pulled together and that prophecy did not come true. And that's a great tribute to what this country did in that moment of crisis.

Morell: It is really hard to overstate how worried we all were in the immediate aftermath of 9/11 that we were going to be hit again. There were many days when George Tenet and I walked from the old executive office building across the West Executive Avenue to the West Wing, where we said to each other, 'I wonder if we're going to get hit today.' And these weapons of mass destruction that Steve talked about, we learned an awful lot about al-Qaida's efforts in that arena in the immediate aftermath of 9/11. We knew they were talking to Pakistani nuclear scientists, trying to get their hands on a nuclear weapon. We had reporting that maybe they were going to sneak one into New York City. It is really hard to overstate the threat that we all felt. So I think it's easy to criticize sometime, that we may have overreached here or overreached there. But that context is everything.

Sponsor Message

Kelly: I just want to quote you, John, because you and I have talked about this over the years in various interviews. I was pushing you on some of the actions that the CIA took after 9/11, (like waterboarding). You told me in 2018, 'If you were a CIA officer back in 2002, you were torn. On the one hand by the sense you might be doing something in conflict with basic values that you hold dear. On the other hand, failure to get that information might put the blood of Americans on your hands.'

McLaughlin: Listen, difficult decisions were taken in those days, and we often say we hope that no one has to make those decisions again. And what I can tell you is they weren't perfectly executed. But on the other hand, the United States was not attacked by al-Qaida again. The gloves did come off.

Hadley: [There were measures] kept secret because if they disclosed to the enemy, their purpose and usefulness would be lost. We knew at the time that we were going to authorize and do things and establish programs that when the crisis of the moment and the concern of the moment had died down, The American people might be at the safe space, after we'd gotten after al-Qaida, after we reduced the threat. The American people may be uncomfortable with them. We knew that was a possibility, but we thought these were measures we had to do to get on top of the threat to prevent the country from being attacked again. And I think that was the right trade-off.

Harman: I certainly respect the fact that the CIA and our whole intelligence community was worried about a second wave of attacks. But I would say as someone who was in the chairs in Congress, I became the ranking member on the House Intelligence Committee during that time and who struggled to get information, that the information was not adequate at the time.

Sponsor Message

I remember asking someone, 'Why did we open Guantanamo Bay prison in a piece of Cuba that is U.S. soil?'

Answer: To be beyond the reach of U.S. law. Now, I'm a trained lawyer and I knew that made no sense. But I thought maybe there's something I don't understand. Well, guess what? The Supreme Court agreed with me. And now Guantanamo Bay has to employ the protections under our Constitution. So my bottom line is, there were others who were trying to get on top of this story who really cared, as everyone did, about doing this the right way. And I'm not sure we got there fast enough.

On the legacy of the post-9/11 tactics :

Kelly: Should we still risk privacy for the sake of security? I understand that hindsight is 2020, but the trade-offs that America made – I take the point. We didn't know what was coming next. And we didn't know where bin Laden was. The enhanced interrogation techniques, the torture, whatever intelligence they produced of value, how do you weigh that against the damage to America's reputation as a country that believes in the rule of law?

Morell: Steve mentioned earlier our concern about how the American public would react at the end of the day. You know what? They supported everything that we did, the American public in every poll that's ever been taken. It was the elite who grabbed this as an issue. The American people thought that we did the right thing to protect the country.

I think we're talking about a whole bunch of issues here that result in us losing the big picture. The big picture is that despite intentions, plans, plots to attack America again after 9/11, it didn't happen. We're talking to the people in the room here. We're talking to your audience. Your government and your intelligence community protected you after 9/11 and deserve a tremendous amount of credit for that.

Sponsor Message

Kelly: I appreciate that point and I appreciate you making it. And I'm raising questions in the interest of asking what are the trade-offs that were made in terms of America's moral standing?

Laughlin: I would go back to something I said at the very beginning, which is in one sentence, difficult decisions were made. They were not perfectly executed. America has not been attacked again.

World.title: Carney says he's regularly speaking with Trump and still believes there's a deal to be had
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's still in regular contact with U.S. President Donald Trump despite the ongoing trade rift and some unsavoury remarks from administration officials.

The prime minister suggested that his recent conversations with Trump have been focused on global events, including how the wars in Ukraine and Iran are impacting international energy and grain markets.

"In terms of playing that [international] role, we continue to work with the United States. We can compartmentalize," he said during a news conference alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Calgary on Thursday.

"I spoke to [Trump] recently in the last few days, a couple of times, related to issues [in Ukraine], related to issues in Iran, other global developments. Because that's part of our responsibility."

WATCH | Carney gives examples of topics of discussion with Trump: Canada ready to support Russia-Ukraine ceasefire where U.S. can play 'decisive role': Carney | Duration 2:17 Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said a cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine offers a possible 'shorter-term solution' to global issues around access to energy and agricultural goods.

Tariff negotiations between Canada and the U.S. fell apart last month, with both sides hurling blame at the other.

The U.S. immediately slapped 50 per cent levies on hundreds of Canadian goods, and Canada countered with new tariffs on roughly an equivalent value of U.S. imports on Monday. The Trump administration responded on Wednesday by announcing it would place further tariffs on some Canadian imports and outright ban others later this month.

Carney didn't say whether his government would respond with more counter-tariffs on U.S. goods.

"We're looking closely at the measures the Americans just recently announced," he told reporters later on Thursday.

Carney said that even though talks have stalled, he believes there's still a deal to be had with the U.S.

"Canada's always ready to strike a fair deal. We believe there's still a mutually beneficial deal for Canada and the United States," he said at the news conference with Zelenskyy.

WATCH | Carney says government is reviewing Trump's latest trade actions: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

Trump and some of his key cabinet members have disparaged Canada in the media and online in recent weeks.

The president notably decided his government would refer to Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have both derided the Canadian Armed Forces. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told the Financial Times that it's "unhinged" for Canadian leaders to characterize the administration's tariffs as a trade war.

Carney has pushed back when asked about some of the Trump administration's more unsavoury remarks, saying they're "beneath their office."

WATCH | More about the trade war: Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war? | Duration 2:28 U.S. President Donald Trump dropped tariffs on certain Canadian products, including toilet paper, cement and salt. In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million worth of the product, making it the largest international provider of toilet paper to the U.S.

When asked about why he thinks Trump has continued to disparage Canada since talks fell apart, Carney wouldn't speculate.

"I can't look deeply into the souls of other people and see their emotions. This isn't a question of emotion, it's a question of sovereignty for Canada," he said.

World.title: Man accused in Mexican condo scheme claims he was a victim, too
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

CBC's Mexico team traveled to Harry Robinson's real estate office to discuss the accusations he faces in a Mexican court, including arrest warrants issued for him and his former business partner, Jacqueline Herrera Herrera. Robinson is a suspect in a fraud case involving an Ontario couple, Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown, who invested $280,000 in a plan to flip condos in Playa del Carmen, but never received the property or their money back. Robinson and his lawyer, Blanca Figueroa Ornelas, agreed to an interview for this report.

Accused in Mexican scam of Canadian couple tells his side of the story

A U.K. man facing accusations he took part in a scheme that wiped out a Canadian couple's retirement savings says he's provided proof to Mexican authorities probing the case that he never touched a dime of the vanished funds, and that he's also a victim of his co-accused.

Harry Robinson, 66, is accused of working with a Mexican national named Jacqueline Herrera Herrera to defraud Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., of $280,000 by offering them a fake deal to buy and flip seven condos.

Robinson provided CBC News with a memo and HSBC bank records, both filed with the state attorney general's office of Quintana Roo, that he says proves Herrera redirected Thompson and Brown's money — sent over three installments — through cashier's cheques and transfers to other, unknown accounts.

The memo, filed Aug. 24, alleges that Herrera had total control over the account which was under the name of Xen Investments, their former joint venture. It claims Herrera put the account under a "lock" to prevent Robinson from accessing or moving funds.

CBC News was not provided with any documented proof outlining the alleged lock on the account.

The memo asks state investigators to seek a judicial order to obtain the names linked to the cashier's cheques and other bank accounts to trace the final destination of the funds.

"If you watch any criminal show on TV, the one statement that is made all the time: Follow the money," Robinson told CBC News in his real-estate office in Puerto Morelos, a small port town between the tourist hotspots Playa del Carmen and Cancun.

Cindy Thompson, right, and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., sent $280,000 to a company co-owned by Robinson and his co-accused Jacqueline Herrera Herrera. (Submitted by Cindy Thompson)

"And yet, here we are in a fraud case with missing money and no one has made any attempt to follow the money."

However, state authorities are not focusing their case against Robinson and Herrera on what happened to the money, according to other court records. There have been no applications yet before the courts to trace the movement of Thompson and Brown's funds after they landed in Xen Investments's account.

The investigation is simply focused on proving there was fraud by deceit — that Herrera and Robinson did not have any access or control over the seven condos they offered Thompson and Brown as part of a deal, which promised the couple 100 per cent profit.

"This operation evolved as more resources were collected, without the existence … availability or actual allocation of the promised units being documentally proven," says a state prosecutor's filing seeking arrest warrants against Herrera and Robinson, which was obtained by CBC News.

"For months [Thompson and Brown] were kept in a narrative of extensions, new fund requests … and imminent refunds that never materialized."

Herrera was co-owner of a company called Xen Investments, which is registered in Mexico. She pitched the sale of a condo to Thompson. (Jacqueline Herrera Herrera/Facebook)

A state judge issued those warrants on July 24. Herrera and Robinson both obtained stays in Mexican federal court against the warrants, but their state-level criminal proceedings are waiting on a judge to set a date to commence.

"I don't think I'm being fairly treated … by the prosecutor's office. I think they're not going after the true criminal in this case," said Robinson.

"I've lived my whole life honest, no problems, no criminal record, nothing … and all of a sudden I'm now some sort of master criminal? Nobody makes that transition like that."

Publicly available records show Robinson was born in Liverpool and that he worked in Australia and the U.S. before moving to Mexico. CBC News could find no evidence of any sanctions against Robinson or court cases involving him or his businesses.

Robinson says he moved to Mexico around 2020 and also has Australian citizenship.

A fraud by deceit conviction could lead to a prison sentence ranging between three to 12 years.

Robinson says he's asked the U.K. Embassy for help.

The 'middleman'

Thompson said that Robinson was the "middleman" throughout the months of attempted dealmaking, which started in 2024.

"I had 100 per cent faith in [Robinson]," she said.

"He was very convincing … anytime we had any questions or concerns, he always had an answer … I would get: ‘relax, calm down, everything's going to be fine, it's just taking a long time. It's Mexico, right?'"

Robinson says he was also duped by Herrera and believed the deal was real — though he put none of his own money into the pot, despite telling Thompson he would also go in as an investor.

"The deal was that all my time and effort, everything else, was going to be paid in commission. That commission was set aside and put toward the deal," he said.

This condo building in Playa del Carmen was part of the alleged scheme that is now under investigation by Mexican authorities. (Gustavo Huerta/CBC)

"And I would see it one day. So I didn't even get anything upfront."

Robinson said he met Herrera around three or four years ago and attended several private events with her and that she seemed to be well connected and respected as a Cancun realtor with 30 years of experience.

"Everybody seemed to now have gone out of their way to tell me how good a person Jacqueline was, how trustworthy she was, how I couldn't have found a better business partner," said Robinson. "I was a mark in exactly the same way [Thompson] was."

Seeking settlement

Herrera claims Robinson also took some of Thompson and Brown's money. She is seeking to avoid criminal proceedings by offering to repay part of the missing money through an alternative justice channel that is part of the Mexican system.

Herrera is offering to repay $2.4 million pesos — roughly $196,000 — in two installments to Thompson and Brown under a court-authorized settlement. Herrera has claimed — through her lawyer, according to Thompson — that Robinson is responsible for the rest.

Herrera declined an interview request, but told CBC News it was "never" her intention to defraud Thompson and Brown.

Thompson and Brown say they are facing a tough decision on whether to proceed with Herrera's settlement offer.

"Our biggest worry is, if we accept that, do we get the rest of the money?" said Brown.

World.title: Orange Shirt Day founder says her truth is being 'pushed aside' by controversial shirts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The founder of Orange Shirt Day says she was sick to her stomach when she learned orange shirts with slogans like "Dig deeper" and "Still no proof" were being sold online.

Holding back tears and speaking from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc in B.C., which announced a discovery of potential unmarked graves near a former residential school site in 2021, Phyllis Webstad said her campaign was being used in a "hateful way."

"I've been trying to understand why they believe that it's OK to hurt people," she said.

In 1976, Webstad wore a present from her grandmother, an orange shirt, on her first day at a residential school at St. Joseph's Mission, in Williams Lake, B.C. The shirt was taken from her by school officials and never returned.

Webstad founded Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30, 13 years ago, to honour Indigenous children who were forced to attend residential schools.

In late August, Rebel News announced it was selling orange T-shirts on its website for the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and that the shirts are about "challenging the identity politics that Canadians are increasingly pressured to accept and standing up for the whole truth in our complex Canadian history."

Statements printed on the shirts include "Still no proof," "You can't handle the truth," "Buried Truth" and "Dig Deeper," as well as "Canada was built not stolen."

Webstad called the sales a direct attack on her work with the Orange Shirt Society.

"It's my truth and what I know is the truth," Webstad said.

"It seems like this truth is not being respected. It's not being understood. It's being pushed aside."

Orange T-shirts with various slogans were posted to the Rebel News store at the end of August. (Rebel News Store)

In an emailed statement, Ezra Levant, founder and owner of Rebel News, pointed CBC News to a video on its website launching the sale of the shirts, saying their reporter "approaches these issues with compassion."

"The stated purpose of the National Truth and Reconciliation Day is noble – to honour residential school survivors and their communities by recognizing the lasting impacts of Canada's residential school system, so Canadians can better understand its legacy as part of our ongoing journey toward truth, healing, and reconciliation," Levant quoted what was said in the video.

In the video, the Rebel News reporter goes on to say "But five years later, Canadians are still being told that there are some truths they're not allowed to question."

Levant added in the statement that Rebel News staff are "dedicated to freedom of expression including the right to seek the truth" and "these orange shirts are a response for people who are forced to wear orange shirts at school or at work, as part of an 'official' political narrative."

"No Canadians should be compelled to support any political view, including Orange Shirt Day’s politics."

In the video promoting the shirts, the Rebel News reporter says "what's more than likely underneath the apple orchard soil at the Kamloops site is probably an old septic plot."

Webstad pointed to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, which has so far documented more than 4,000 deaths of Indigenous children in Canada's residential school system.

WATCH | B.C. regional chief speaks on residential school denialism: ‘Denialism is not an academic debate. It’s hate speech,' says regional chief | Duration 1:32 Regional Chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations Terry Teegee said violence, anti-Indigenous rhetoric and hate speech are linked to residential school denialism and that, if left unaddressed, denialism ‘undermines truth and reconciliation.'

She said her own auntie, Agness Jack, shared a personal story about what it was like living in the Kamloops Indian Residential School in a book published in 2001, Behind Closed Doors: Stories from the Kamloops Indian Residential School.

Webstad also said her grandmother and her grandmother's 10 children including Webstad's mom were all forced to attend residential school.

"My mother was so traumatized that she could not take care of me; thank God my Granny was there, thank God my auntie was there," said Webstad.

"I want to say that we aren't liars. Indian Residential School survivors are not liars. Have some respect and give us the space and time to do what we need to do as individuals, as family, as a community, as a nation."

The orange shirts available on the Rebel News website are listed in youth sizes as well as adult.

"That is a whole new level of every word in the book: disgusting, unbelievable, sickening. Where are their minds?" said Webstad about the youth sizes.

MPs and ministers condemn shirts

Last week, the Liberal Indigenous Caucus published a statement that said merchandise "that mocks survivors' experiences and dismisses their truths is reprehensible and beneath any organization."

A request for comment from Conservative MP Billy Morin, the party's shadow minister of Indigenous Services, was not returned by time of publishing.

Morin told APTN News last week, “I find it racist and I find it absolutely disgusting that they’re attempting to make a profit off the pain and suffering of residential schools."

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, who is a member of the Waswanipi Cree Nation in northern Quebec, said people across the country have raised concerns about the shirts to her.

"Not just people living in my riding but also from Canadians who are appalled about this really disgraceful and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering for financial gain," said Gull-Masty.

Gull-Masty's mother and grandmother were both forced to attend the La Tuque Indian Residential School in Quebec.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, a member of Waswanipi Cree Nation in northern Quebec, says she heard concerns from people all over Canada about the shirts being sold online. (Marie-Laure Josselin/Radio-Canada)

Gull-Masty said she expressed her concerns to Justice Minister Sean Fraser, but didn't say what avenues the government would explore. She said she felt Fraser understood how serious the matter is.

"I think this is one of the areas where we are seeing behaviour that is not only being perpetuated more commonly but it is reaching a level that is unacceptable," said Gull-Masty.

In a statement to CBC Indigenous, a spokesperson for Fraser said, "Seeking to profit from Indian residential school denialism is deeply disgraceful and represents a cruel and grotesque attempt to exploit human suffering."

"Residential school denialism is a serious and distinct issue, and our government has said this issue warrants dedicated further parliamentary study," the statement said.

"Any legal response should be developed carefully in consultation and co-operation with Indigenous Peoples and the communities most affected."

Earlier this year, Canada's Senate voted down an amendment to Bill C-9 that would have criminalized residential school denialism, by making it illegal to wilfully promote "hatred against Indigenous Peoples by condoning, denying or downplaying the Indian Residential Schools System."

Webstad said she supports the idea that residential school denialism should be added as hate speech to Canada's Criminal Code.

"I believe what Rebel News is doing right now is what is needed to convince our Canadian government that yes, a law needs to be passed," said Webstad.

Shirts designed to provoke conflicts in schools, says academic

Sean Carleton, an associate professor in history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba, said he feels the shirts monetize anti-Indigenous racism and deliberately profit off of pain and suffering.

"Thousands of Indigenous children died, we know that," said Carleton.

"So what [Rebel News] is trying to do is cast doubt, shake public confidence and are trying to convince Canadians that maybe we shouldn't care about Indigenous people and reconciliation anymore."

Carleton said the easiest way to understand denialism is to look at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's simple formula.

Sean Carleton, an associate professor in history and Indigenous studies at the University of Manitoba, says the shirts monetize anti-Indigenous racism, and deliberately profit off of pain and suffering. (Submitted by Sean Carleton)

"We've got to have truth first," he said.

"Truth will lead to healing and justice. Healing and justice will lead to reconciliation. Denialists know that and what they're trying to do is keep us stuck in the truth part."

Carleton said he believes the inclusion of youth sizing is a tactic designed to provoke conflicts within schools where parents may be influenced by denialist rhetoric and use their children to challenge school policies.

He said the slogans on the shirts not only defend the colonial status quo but promote colonization as a compassion project, and said they question survivors' lived experiences.

NDP MP Leah Gazan tabled a private member's bill in Parliament last fall to criminalize residential school denialism.

In a letter to the Indigenous Liberal Caucus on Tuesday, Gazan said anti-Indigenous racism and denialism are growing and have now resulted in "the production of merchandise denying genocide and mocking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. We must respond to this as what it is – the incitement, monetization and promotion of hate."

Gazan called on the Indigenous Liberal Caucus to table her bill as a government bill.

A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.

World.title: First phase of Army restructuring creates division focused on defending Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's Army formally made one of the biggest changes to its structure in decades Thursday by shifting from divisions based on geography to ones built around specific purposes.

Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Edmonton held a signing ceremony and parade to stand up the 1st Canadian Division, which will serve as the main force responsible for deploying on large-scale combat operations and responding to crises.

Headquartered in Edmonton, the "manoeuvre division" will bring multiple capabilities together under one roof, including tanks and other armour, artillery, light infantry, paratroopers and engineers.

The idea is to prepare the army to rapidly deploy a large force and sustain prolonged operations.

The change is meant to improve the army's responsiveness, said Brig.-Gen. Wade Rutland, shown here speaking in Calgary in June 2025. (Dave Chidley/The Canadian Press)

"This is a big change," Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the new 1st Canadian Division, said in an interview.

"This is not an exercise in restructuring the deck chairs. We're doing this in order to be more agile, more lethal, more relevant to defend Canada."

Rutland said the threat environment has changed and the world is returning to large-scale combat operations with hundreds of thousands of soldiers, like the ones in Ukraine.

"We realized that we needed to stand up what we call a war fighting division, which will bring together thousands of troops able to integrate air, cyber, space effects and actually contribute as a really trusted ally into that likely future fight," he said.

It's part of a series of structural changes ordered by Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright, who laid out his plan to modernize the army in a 2025 document titled Inflection Point.

Alongside the manoeuvre division, the army is setting up a support division, which will be run out of Kingston, Ont.

The army also is standing up a "defence of Canada" division based out of Montreal, to be known as the 2nd Canadian Division. It's made up largely of part-time soldiers and will focus on national emergencies and domestic defence.

The 3rd Canadian Division — which traces its history to the First World War and took part in the 1944 D-Day landing at Juno Beach — is being retired to the supplementary Order of Battle.

This retirement happens when a regiment is powered down but continues to exist administratively in case it needs to be returned to duty.

The 3rd's regular force troops will go into the 1st Division, its reserves and rangers will go into the 2nd division and its support troops will join the support division.

Under the changes, the 1st Canadian Division — a division that dates back to 1915 and helped to capture Vimy Ridge — will command three Canadian Mechanized Brigade Groups, located in Edmonton, Petawawa, Ont., and at CFB Valcartier in Quebec.

It also will oversee the 3rd Light Infantry Regiment, the Canadian Artillery Brigade, 6 Canadian Combat Support Brigade and 1 Canadian Sustainment Brigade.

"It means a lot to us," Rutland said. "You know, the 1st Division was the first one into the fight in the Second World War. They were the first ones in major combat in Italy, Sicily, in the Second World War."

World.title: Cat in the Hat suspect who chased a teen girl in B.C. appears to be a trend copycat
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A disturbing incident in which someone dressed in a Cat in the Hat costume chased a teenager in West Kelowna, B.C., occurred amid an online trend that twists the popular children's character into something sinister, leading police in some jurisdictions to warn of offline consequences.

While the incident in the Okanagan region last month happened in real life and has triggered an RCMP investigation, the Cat in the Hat social media trend typically involves generative AI depictions of the character and his distinctive red-and-white striped hat standing outside schools, homes or other locations.

Posts include TikTok videos with thousands of views showing the character in front of B.C. secondary schools or malls.

Other posts have included the names of individuals and their schools along with onscreen text such as "see you soon" or "bye bye."

With captions like "watch out," and "you're next," the unsettling images are leading police to warn the posts may have real world consequences if taken too far.

This week the Nechako Lakes school district in B.C.'s central Interior said it was aware of the social media trend and asked community members to report the posts to police.

B.C. RCMP spokesman Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said police were aware of the trend, including a case in Fort St. James in the Nechako Lakes school district, as well as the West Kelowna incident on Aug. 24 that was described by police on Tuesday.

Clark said he was "not aware of any other events in B.C. RCMP jurisdictions."

The criminality

Regarding criminality, "it would depend on the totality of the circumstances and whether sufficient evidence existed before an assessment for charge approval could be made," he said.

"Generally speaking, based on what I have seen, some potential offences could be uttering threats or criminal harassment; however, there are any number of others that may be considered depending on the available evidence."

West Kelowna RCMP had said last month's "concerning prank" may constitute criminal harassment, and other charges such as assault, uttering threats or intimidation could be considered if the evidence supported them.

"Regardless of whether the individual intended the behaviour as a joke, following a young person and causing them to fear for their safety is extremely concerning," Cpl. Devon Gerrits said in a statement, which included a photo of the character taken at night.

“People should understand that behaviour intended as a prank can have serious consequences when it causes another person to reasonably fear for their safety.”

Police in Tennessee, meanwhile, have said a student was arrested for making threats against school property with an AI-generated Cat in the Hat post and a teenager in Colorado was charged with harassment for a similar post that implied the character would appear outside a middle school and homes.

The Cat in the Hat character first appeared in the book of the same name by Theodor "Dr. Seuss" Geisel in 1957, but the costumed version from the videos is seemingly inspired by the 2003 live-action movie starring Canadian actor Mike Myers.

A viral post about the costume from the movie going up for auction may have sparked the horror-inspired trend, with some commenters describing it as uncanny and "nightmare fuel."

World.title: Poilievre tells U.S. TV Canadians are 'wounded' and 'confused' to be in America's crosshairs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is telling Americans their northern neighbours are feeling "wounded" and "confused" over how Canada and its economy became a key target for U.S. President Donald Trump.

"I think we feel a little bit wounded," Poilievre told reporters on the U.S. network CNBC on Thursday during a trip to New York where he is advocating for a return to normal trade relations.

"We're kind of confused as to how it is, suddenly, that Canada ended up in the crosshair."

The Conservative leader said Canada and the U.S. have a deeply interconnected economic relationship that has delivered peace and prosperity for decades and the only way forward should be tariff-free trade.

"Both countries are going to have their grievances," he said. "America had buy-America policies that prevented us from selling into subnational procurement markets and tariffs on our softwood lumber.… But the bottom line is: let's sit down and work them out for the mutual benefit of our people."

WATCH | Poilievre appears on CNBC:

In a statement Poilievre said he went to New York to fight against tariffs and for jobs on both sides of the border.

He said he will be meeting with investors and business leaders but his "main audience is the American people" to which he is making the case "that both our countries can be safer, richer and more affordable if we trade freely."

Poilievre also said he will stay in New York for the 25th anniversary of 9/11 on Friday, to honour the victims and highlight "how Canadians and Americans stood together after the terrorist attacks."

'Politics ends at the border': Poilievre

That national spirit was on display during Poilievre's CNBC interview, when he refused to be goaded into answering a question about whether he believed Prime Minister Mark Carney was acting in good faith during the recent round of trade negotiations.

"I'm not going to attack my prime minister on foreign soil. It's just not something I'm going to do," he said. "My mission here is to fight for my country, not to score political points domestically. Politics ends at the border."

Poilievre said Canada needs to leverage the "single biggest asset Canada has in the U.S., which is our friendship with the American people who overwhelmingly love Canada."

Co-host Joe Kernen said he respected Poilievre for refusing to criticize Carney while abroad, noting that politicians in opposition in the U.S. do not maintain that standard.

"You actually have a little bit of class," Kernen said.

When Kernen pressed Poilievre on Canada's economic performance over the last decade, the Conservative leader also avoided criticizing the country, saying Canada has had "a lot of good public policy successes by different levels of government."

Going forward Poilievre said rivals and risks to the U.S. are "slowly mounting" and rather than combat them on their own, the U.S. should rebuild the Western alliance that won the Cold War rather than fighting with friends.

"I think the United States would be better off if it united with those countries that believe in free speech, free markets, free trade and free people," he said.

"We could build an incredible North American fortress with the resources that we have on this continent, but it's going to take a collaborative relationship to do it."

World.title: These tiny endangered raccoons make their own toys out of trash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with biologist Nessie O'Neil: As It Happens 6:22 Endangered Mexican pygmy raccoons make their own toys out of trash

The first time Nessie O’Neil witnessed a pygmy raccoon making a toy ball out of trash, she didn't realize that she'd just made a major scientific discovery.

"My first thought was, oh my gosh, this is adorable," O’Neil, a biologist at Miami University in Ohio, told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.

Then she showed the footage to her advisor.

"She was like, 'Nessie, this is very important. Do not post this on social media because we need to write a paper about this.'"

That paper, now published in the journal Wild , documents the itty bitty Mexican critters rummaging through bins for paper and other materials, crafting those scraps into balls to play with, and teaching their family members how to do the same.

The authors say this is first documented evidence of “material culture” — socially shared cultural information about objects — in the Procyonidae family, which includes raccoons, ringtails and other similar creatures.

"We know that raccoons are very playful animals. If you give them a cat toy, they will bat it around or chew on it and chase it," O'Neil said. "But up until now, we have not seen anything like this."

Pygmy raccoons are a critically endangered species found only on Cozumel Island off the coast of the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico.

Weighing about three to four kilograms, they are much smaller than the chunky mainland raccoons who dwell in Canadian and American cities. They have long limbs, which they use to navigate their native mangrove forests and forage for crabs and other shoreline prey.

But as their natural habitat is increasingly razed for development, O'Neil says they've turned to tourist scraps and to garbage bins for sustenance.

In fact, O'Neil was observing a family of raccoons at a beach club when she first witnessed the toy-making behaviour.

"I actually saw one of the juveniles go into a trash can and dig through and pull out a rather long receipt. And she brought the receipt back to a stainless steel water bowl that one of the staff members had put out for her and began to dunk it in the water," she said.

"She started to roll it between her hands and shape it into a ball. And then she would roll it in the sand and maybe dump it back in the water a little bit and then go back to the sand and work on shaping it. And after she got it how she wanted it, she began to play with it like a cat with a little mouse toy."

WATCH | Pygmy raccoon crafts her own toy: Watch this pygmy racoon make a toy ball out of trash | Duration 0:28 Pygmy raccoons in Mexico have been documented fishing scraps of paper out of trash bins, then using water and sand to form them into little balls to play with. Credit: Nessie O'Neil/Miami University.

Then, O'Neil says, she shared her skills.

"Her sister learned how to do this behaviour, too. She would watch and practise alongside her," O'Neil said.

The mother raccoon also tried to make a ball, the study noted, but gave up when was unable to retrieve her paper towel from the water dish.

"The success of the mother during this attempt might have been influenced by her earlier consumption of one ounce of a margarita, which appeared to lower her dexterity," the study reads.

Novel behaviour

Benjamin Beck, a retired scientist from the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute and co-author of the book Animal Tool Behavior, says he's seen many instances of animals playing using random objects as toys.

But he says he's never heard of an animal making its own toy.

"I think it's a distinct category to say that you made your play toy as well as used your play toy," he said. "What that distinction means, I'm not absolutely sure. Maybe it suggests a higher level of foresight and creativity."

What's even more interesting, he says, is that the raccoons were seen batting the ball back and forth between each other.

"That's social object play," he said. "And that I have no record of."

The researchers observed at least six instances of the raccoons playing with the balls they'd made. (Submitted by Nessie O'Neil)

Still, he says, he'd be hesitant to label the behaviour as an example of culture, given the small sample size.

"You're going to have to look at a sequence of generations to make sure that the behaviour persists, it is being learned intergenerationally, before you can make the leap to any sort of culture," he said

The plight of the pygmy

There are only 200 pygmy raccoons alive today in Cozumel, and O'Neil says those numbers are shrinking as tourist developments destroy their habitat and cut them off from their natural food supply.

In fact, the pygmy raccoon O'Neil first filmed making a paper ball has since died.

"She was so malnourished due to eating almost nothing but tortilla chips," she said.

A pigmy racoon grabs some tortilla from a trash bin on a Mexican beach club. Researcher Nessie O'Neil says the creatures have become reliant on human scraps, and it's leading to malnourishment. (Submitted by Nessie O'Neil)

O'Neil says she hopes this research will shed light on the plight of pygmy raccoons, and inspire people to change their behaviour — especially tourists.

"People need to stop feeding them. Stop feeding them tortilla chips. Stop offering them margaritas. Stop supporting resorts and beach clubs that are destroying their homes," O'Neil said.

"Every animal has an intrinsic value. Even if humans can't see it, they have a right to be there. This is their home."

World.title: Edmonton Oilers facing online backlash after signing Alex Formenton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Edmonton Oilers decision to sign a hockey player who was acquitted last year of sexual assault has sparked a wave of disappointment and calls for the team to "do better."

The intensely negative reaction started rolling in Wednesday after the team announced it had signed Alex Formenton to a one-year contract worth $850,000 US.

Formenton was one of five players from Canada's 2018 world junior team accused of sexual assault, charges that stemmed from an encounter with a woman after a Hockey Canada gala in London, Ont.

"The initial reaction from the fan base has been really, from what I’ve seen on social media, pretty overwhelmingly negative," Daily Hive sports journalist Preston Hodgkinson told CBC News on Thursday.

"I remember the pushback for Corey Perry was one; Mike Babcock just happened this summer, even Stan Bowman. There was a lot of pushback for all that. This one seems more intense."

On an Oilers Instagram post about the signing, commenters said they were "embarrassed," "disgusted" and "disappointment." While some defended the Oilers' signing, many said they would not support the team as long as Formenton was on it.

"T o the Oilers organization: you need to do better for your female fans," said a comment posted by @ireland1102 that had received more than 4,200 likes as of Thursday morning.

"This isn’t just about hockey, it’s about the message you are sending to the women and girls who wear your jersey, buy your tickets and have supported this team their entire lives. "

A screen capture of the Edmonton Oiler Instagram post about Alex Formenton's signing, along with some reaction. (Edmonton Oilers/Instagram)

One of the team's most high-profile fans echoed the sentiment in her own social media post.

"Although he was acquitted in court, I cannot ignore my conscience or what this decision represents to me," wrote Mary Loewen, who dresses up during NHL playoffs as a sequined Stanley Cup known as "Mama Stanley."

Loewen wrote on her Instagram page that she was a sexual assault survivor, adding, "For that reason, as long as Formenton remains an Oiler, I CANNOT AND WILL NOT support or cheer for this team."

On Thursday, she launched an online petition calling for the Oilers to end Formenton's affiliation with the team. Loewen did not immediately respond to a request from The Canadian Press for an interview.

Acquitted in July 2025

The five accused hockey players — Formenton, Cal Foote, Carter Hart, Dillon Dube and Michael McLeod — were acquitted in July 2025. The NHL later reinstated all five players.

Last month, a n independent appeal board ruled that all five breached the Hockey Canada code of conduct, and recommended continued suspensions from any Hockey Canada-sanctioned program for four of the players.

Only Formenton was named eligible for immediate reinstatement.

Formenton has said he is grateful to join the Oilers after what he called a "difficult road."

The 26-year-old native of Barrie, Ont., spent three of the past four seasons playing in Switzerland for HC Ambri-Piotta and the other not in hockey at all. He recorded 33 goals and 19 assists for 52 points over 88 games with HC Ambri-Piotta. He last played in the NHL during the 2021–22 season with the Ottawa Senators.

Hodgkinson said he is baffled why Oilers management would take on the "baggage" of signing Formenton given his on-ice performance in recent years.

"It’s not like you’re bringing in a star player," he said. "You’re bringing in a bottom lineup guy and you have to deal with all this. It doesn’t really feel worth it to me."

While the outcry has been fierce, Hodgkinson noted that there are some people who have expressed support for giving Formenton a chance in light of the acquittal.

He also pointed out that among those vocally criticizing the signing are people, like Loewen, who have identified themselves as being survivors of sexual assault "and this is a blatant 'eff you.'"

Late Wednesday, the Sexual Assault Centre of Edmonton (SACE) issued a statement that noted Oilers announcement " may be difficult for many survivors and members of our community.

"If this news is bringing up hard feelings or emotions, please know that you don’t have to carry them alone. SACE is here. We hear you, we believe you, and we stand with you."
