World.title: Rubio doubles down on claims that cartels control large areas of Mexico, hinting at unilateral US action
World.content:
Listen to this article

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Mexico isn’t doing enough to combat drug cartels and suggested that the United States could act unilaterally against such criminal organizations in Mexican territory.

In remarks to reporters outside the U.S. Embassy in Quito, Ecuador, Rubio also asserted that narco-terrorist organizations — i.e. drug cartels that the U.S. government has designated as foreign terrorist organizations — control large parts of Mexico.

SECRETARY RUBIO: There are territories, vast territories in Mexico, that are not governed by the state. They are controlled by these narco-terrorist organizations. pic.twitter.com/udRGZXv0xU — Department of State (@StateDept) September 9, 2026

The secretary of state, who traveled to Quito to speak with President Daniel Noboa about security cooperation between the United States and Ecuador, had been speaking about criminal threats in the Western Hemisphere when a reporter put it to him that if he was “talking about groups that are stronger than the state and fracturing the states, it sounds like a pretty similar situation to Mexico.”

“Mexico’s bad. It’s a bad situation,” Rubio responded.

The reporter then asked the secretary of state what the U.S. government’s plan was for combating organized crime in Mexico “given the fact that the Mexican government isn’t welcoming, or draws a pretty bright line about what it will accept in terms of U.S. military involvement.”

“How can you overcome that and have this kind of more tough approach that you’re describing?” she asked Rubio.

“The case of Mexico … [is] an even graver challenge because of the size of the country, because of the power of the cartels that are there,” he said.

“I don’t think it’s any mystery to anybody that there are territories, vast territories in Mexico, that are not governed by the state; they are controlled by these narco-terrorist organizations,” Rubio said.

He added that, “in fairness, the Mexicans have done more than they’ve ever done before to go after these groups.”

Indeed, the current Mexican government has captured or killed significant numbers of alleged cartel members and leaders, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) kingpin Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera, sent scores of prisoners to the United States to face justice and seized more than 500 tonnes of drugs and over 34,000 firearms.

However, in Rubio’s view, what the Mexican government has done is “still not nearly enough.”

“They know that, we’ve expressed that to them,” he said.

“And we hope to work cooperatively with them to do more because … the head of the snake are these cartels in Mexico,” Rubio said.

“And they are a threat to the Mexican state, and the people of Mexico will tell you that. The number one issue in Mexico, poll after poll shows, is security. Political candidates are routinely assassinated in Mexico; judges — routinely assassinated; journalists who report on the cartels — routinely assassinated by these groups. So these groups pose an enormous threat right on our border. They have drones now. They’re using drones to try to traffic drugs and people across the border,” he said.

“These groups are very dangerous, they’re very well financed, they need to be confronted,” Rubio said, referring to criminal organizations such as the CJNG and the Sinaloa Cartel.

“Our hope and our intent is to do it in partnership with Mexico. That’s the ideal. But eventually, that threat will have to be confronted, one way or the other. But our hope is to do it cooperatively with Mexican authorities,” he said.

Rubio’s “one way or the other” remark alluded to the possibility of the United States taking unilateral action against cartels in Mexico. Asked about his comments at her Thursday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum characterized them as electorally motivated given that the U.S. midterms are coming up in November.

The secretary of state is by no means the first Trump administration official to suggest that the United States could act on its own against cartels in Mexico. U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance said in June that the United States “would take military action” in Mexico “if we feel like we have to to protect our people.”

Like Rubio, Vance said that the United States wants “to work with the Mexican government,” but he asserted that the U.S. has to “reserve the right” to take unilateral action against cartel threats.

For his part, U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson told U.S. senators in March 2025, shortly before he took up his post, that on “any decision to take action against a cartel inside Mexico, our first desire would be that it be done in partnership with our Mexican partners.”

However, he added that, “should there be a case where the lives of U.S. citizens are at risk, I think all cards are on the table.”

In January, U.S. President Donald Trump said himself that the United States — whose military has targeted suspected drug boats at sea — was going to start “hitting” cartels on land. No confirmed U.S. attacks on Mexican criminal groups in Mexico have occurred since then, although CNN reported in May that the CIA facilitated a “targeted assassination” of an alleged Sinaloa Cartel member in México state in March.

Is Rubio’s cartel control claim true?

In asserting that cartels control “vast territories in Mexico,” Rubio echoed claims made by Trump and other current U.S. government officials, such as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. In 2021, General Glen D. VanHerck, commander of the United States Northern Command at the time, asserted that criminal organizations operate in “ungoverned areas” of Mexico that account for 30% to 35% of national territory. President Andrés Manuel López Obrador promptly rejected his claim.

Sheinbaum has also rejected claims about cartel control in Mexico. However, there is, according to Ioan Grillo, a Mexico-based British journalist who specializes in organized crime, a “duopoly of power” in parts of the country.

A 2024 article published on Grillo’s site CrashOut is headlined “How Much of Mexico is Governed by Cartels?”

The subheading reads, “A: None 100%. But there is a duopoly of power in chunks of the country.”

“Cartels certainly exert an amount of control in chunks of Mexico. This can be seen in squads of gunmen operating openly, running checkpoints, ordering curfews, dictating what journalists can report, charging quotas on sales of avocados, moving votes for candidates, and controlling (or assassinating) mayors,” Grillo wrote.

“Yet unlike with the Islamic State caliphate, the Mexican government still operates in those turfs. It provides electricity, sends teachers and collects garbage. And the army can still go in (while the cartel gunmen hide) and then leave (and they come out again),” he wrote.

Later in his article, Grillo wrote that in his “subjective judgement,” about “a third of Mexican states have a severe cartel presence and high levels of violence; another third have a medium (but still important) level of cartel problems and bloodshed; and a last third have levels of violence compared with regular U.S. cities, and less serious problems from gangsters.”

Since that article was published in late January 2024 — around nine months before Sheinbaum took office — homicides and other high-impact crimes have declined, according to official statistics, suggesting that Mexico’s overall security situation has improved. Nevertheless, cartels continue to operate, fight turf wars and pose major challenges to authorities in various parts of the country.

World.title: Mexico gears up for Independence Day with a military parade, concerts and of course the Grito — all set for Sept. 15-16
World.content:
More than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are preparing to march, fly and roll out new equipment in Mexico City next week as the country marks the 216th anniversary of its independence.

On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo reviewed the logistics for the capital’s Sept. 16 Independence Day parade.

In Mexico, Día de la Independencia commemorates the start of the rebellion against Spanish rule in 1810, although the nation’s War of Independence didn’t end until 1821.

The parade will include Army, Navy, Air Force and National Guard personnel, cadets, pilots, military engineers, medical workers, communications specialists, military police and special forces. It also will include horses, dogs and even eagles, according to El Heraldo de México.

Contingents will be designated “Justice and Peace,” “Sentinels of the Nation,” “Crucible of Patriots” and “Roots of Honor,” among other names, Trevilla Trejo said during his briefing on a military base in Naucalpan, México state.

The roughly 5-kilometer parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Sept. 16 with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central plaza — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes, continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

The capital’s celebrations begin the night before, when President Claudia Sheinbaum leads the traditional Grito de Independencia (“Shout” or “Cry” of Independence) from the National Palace balcony.

In conjunction, the Grammy-winning Texas-based band Intocable, whose Norteño-Tejano sound has landed them 21 No. 1 songs on Billboard’s Regional Mexican Airplay chart, will headline a free concert in the Zócalo.

Free concerts, food fairs and municipal Grito ceremonies are also planned across Mexico City’s 16 boroughs. The musical lineup includes norteño-banda group Calibre 50 (a record 27 No. 1 hits on Billboard’s regional Mexican chart) and Sinaloan balladeer Pancho Barraza (a headliner since the 1990s).

The observances will reach beyond the capital, as well, as the Grito tradition is replicated by governors and mayors nationwide.

In present-day Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato — then known simply as Dolores, where priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla called on residents to rise against Spanish rule in the early hours of Sept. 16, 1810 — Independence Day festivities are running nearly all month.

In nearby San Miguel de Allende, Sept. 16 observances include a reenactment of the start of the independence movement in 1810.

This year, the Sept. 16 national holiday falls on a Wednesday, meaning there will be no three-day weekend. Public schools and banks will close, as will many government offices and private workplaces, as it is a mandatory day of rest under federal labor law. Employees required to work are entitled to premium holiday pay. Sept. 15 remains a regular work and school day.

With reports from Milenio, Infobae, El Informador, El Heraldo de México, N+, El Sol de Bajío and ADN Noticias

World.title: Education Ministry blames screen use for Mexican students’ falling scores
World.content:
Education Minister Mario Delgado on Wednesday addressed the low scores earned by Mexican students in the latest international PISA evaluation test by blaming “the excessive use of cell phones and computer screens.”

Speaking in Mexico City during the opening of National Days of Traditional Games, Delgado expressed doubt that the results amount to a comprehensive evaluation of the Mexican educational system, though he did concede that the sample was “statistically representative.”

“The low reading comprehension scores can be explained by the fact that screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images, and teenagers find it difficult to read more complex and longer texts,” he said.

Mexico ranked 64th out of 91 countries evaluated, with a drop in math and reading scores to the lowest levels since 2009.

Before promoting team games as a partial remedy, Delgado defended the New Mexican School — the official public education model implemented under the previous presidential administration — though without providing specific pedagogical strategies.

Delgado said the Education Ministry (SEP) simultaneously implemented formative assessment programs under the New Mexican School scheme, including 7 million integrative learning exercises during the past year.

Still, officials sought to put Mexico’s poor scores in a global perspective, insisting that international reading and math scores declined by 27 points and 22 points, respectively. Such emphasis ignores the fact that the lower scores are equivalent to losing a year of learning.

Although President Claudia Sheinbaum has often criticized what she calls “the structural limitations of the PISA test (saying “it applies the same exam across countries with vastly different local characteristics”), she initiated a public debate about the excessive use of screens and the early access of children and adolescents to digital platforms. This led to new national guidelines restricting cell phone use in schools.

Delgado said that with cell phone regulation in place, new activities — such as team games — can be used to effectively get the attention of students and build cooperative learning skills.

Unlike mobile phones, which promote isolation and limit social skills, Delgado said games like yo-yo, marbles, spinning top, and cup-and-ball encourage teamwork, shared fun and the formation of new friendships.

The aim is to encourage students to spend more time playing and socializing, Delgado said, insisting that being in front of a phone limits opportunities to connect with other people.

With reports from Vanguardia, Animal Político and El Universal

World.title: Mexico’s inflation rate rises to 3.26% in August, ending 4-month decline
World.content:
Mexico’s annual inflation rate rose slightly in August compared to July, ending a four-month streak of declines.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported Wednesday that the annual headline inflation rate was 3.26% in August, up from 3.12% in July.

Month-over-month inflation was 0.20% in August, while the annual core rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was 3.88%, down from 3.95% in July.

Both the annual headline rate and the core rate came in just below the median estimates of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg.

The increase in Mexico’s annual headline rate came after inflation slowed on a month-over-month basis in each of April, May, June and July. The headline rate thus fell from 4.59% in March to 3.12% in July, a decline of 1.47 percentage points. During the same period, the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) cut its key interest rate by 25 basis points on two occasions, lowering it to 6.75% in March and 6.50% in May.

The central bank, which targets 3% inflation, appears unlikely to make any additional cuts to its key rate this year. Banxico is currently forecasting that inflation will be 3.5% at the end of 2026. It anticipates that the headline rate will gradually decline in 2027 to converge to its 3% target in the final quarter of next year.

Services inflation remains above 4%

Of the four broad categories monitored by INEGI, services recorded the largest year-over-year increase in prices in August. Annual services inflation was 4.33%, down slightly from a 4.36% reading in July. Education fees, one of the services sub-categories, rose 6.04% annually in August, the month in which students across Mexico returned to school.

Annual inflation for goods was 3.41% in August. Within that category, inflation was 4.68% for processed food, beverages and tobacco, and 2.32% for non-food goods.

Energy prices, including those for electricity and gasoline, rose 3.33% annually in August, while prices for agricultural products fell 1.53% year-over-year. The overall deflation for the agricultural products category was the product of a 5.22% decrease in meat prices and a 4.1% increase in fruit and vegetable prices.

World.title: While Mexico’s northern border states deal with a heat alert, monsoon conditions drench the Pacific Coast
World.content:
Low-pressure troughs and Tropical Wave 37 were baking large swaths of Mexico on Thursday, even as the Mexican monsoon was dumping heavy amounts of rain over much of the rest of the country.

The Pacific Coast states received the brunt of the storm system, although the Gulf-side municipality of Coatzacoalcos suffered extensive flooding after being pounded by an intense storm on Wednesday.

Cooler temperatures are expected on Friday, but for Thursday the National Meteorological Service (SMN) issued a heat alert for residents in north and northwestern Mexico. Temperatures above 45 C (113 F) were forecast for parts of Baja California and Sonora, with temperatures between 40-45 C (104-113 F) in parts of Sinaloa, Coahuila, Tamaulipas and Nuevo León.

“Stay hydrated, avoid prolonged exposure to the sun and take precautions against the heat,” the SMN advised in a social media post.

The heat wave extended south to Guanajuato and Guerrero, while some regions along the Gulf Coast saw temperatures hitting 38 C (100 F) on Wednesday.

At the same time, the rainfall map showed persistent heavy rains across the length and breadth of the country, accompanied by lightning and hail in some instances.

While Sinaloa was projected to get the most rainfall through Friday, the SMN said Guanajuato could expect to see the most intense midweek rains.

The SMN said rainfall produced by the Mexican monsoon could reach 150 millimeters in Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco and Colima through Thursday. Very heavy and locally intense downpours were also forecast for Baja California Sur, Sonora and Sinaloa.

The Friday forecast also calls for continued heavy rain storms in central Sinaloa, with heavy to very heavy rainfall in Baja California Sur, Sonora, Durango and Nayarit.

The SMN said Tropical Wave 37 has been met by the arrival of Tropical Wave 38, which has crossed into the Yucatán Peninsula and southeastern Mexico from the east, increasing the likelihood of heavy rain in those regions through Sunday.

The SMN said the states of Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo will register heavy to very heavy rainfall with electrical activity during the initial approach of the new weather system.

Veracruz, Tabasco, Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero will also experience an increased probability of heavy rains with electrical discharges as the system moves west, while Michoacán, Jalisco, Colima and Nayarit will be affected by the passage of the phenomenon throughout the weekend.

With reports from El País, El Financiero, Milenio, Diario del Istmo and El Sol del Chilpancingo

World.title: Cancún airport’s international traffic drops 15% in August
World.content:
In August, Cancún International Airport (CUN) recorded a 15% year-over-year drop in international passenger traffic, handling 1.19 million international passengers.

The drop doesn’t come as a surprise.

In July, an analysis by the Center for Advanced Research in Sustainable Tourism (STARC) of the Anáhuac University of Cancún, anticipated that U.S. airlines would offer nearly a million fewer seats to Mexican beach destinations in July and August, a trend industry experts attributed to rising jet fuel prices, sargassum-covered beaches and safety concerns, among other issues. Cancún, Cozumel and Tulum alone were expected to lose over half a million seats.

A more recent report by STARC revealed that CUN’s decline began early this year after losing 845,714 international passengers between January and August, falling from 13.7 million to 12.9 million passengers — down 6.1% compared to the same period last year.

Although the decline was greater in the international market, the domestic market also fell 4.8% in the same period, from 6.6 million passengers to 6.3 million.

In total, Cancún International Airport served 19.2 million domestic and international passengers so far this year — 5.7% less than the 20.4 million passengers CUN mobilized during the same period last year.

STARC’s figures show that Cancún has now seen six consecutive months of decline, with the steepest drops being registered in May (down 11.1% compared to 2025), June (down 13%), July (down 12.7%) and August (down 15%).

Including national and international travelers, CUN handled 2.1 million passengers in August, compared to 2.3 million the previous year — a 9.3% total drop.

CUN’s Director Carlos Trueba Coll told El Economista that the drop in international traffic is partly due to the bankruptcy of U.S. airline Spirit.

However, he noted that the lost seat capacity has been gradually recovered through airlines such as JetBlue, and expressed confidence that the resumption of seasonal flights in December would help reverse the negative figures recorded between May and August.

Other airports across Mexico saw more moderate declines: Southeast Airport Group (ASUR), which operates Cancún’s airport, said in a statement that on average, its airports in Mexico reported a 13.6% year-on-year decrease in international traffic. One exception to the trend: Mérida, ASUR’s second-busiest airport in Mexico, reported a 4.5% increase in international traffic, serving just over 280,000 international travelers so far this year.

World.title: MND Local: Earthquake drills, K-pop and El Grito in CDMX
World.content:
Mexico News Daily is officially launching MND Local CDMX, a weekly roundup of the news, events and cultural moments that capture the beating heart of the nation’s capital.

Coming up: South Korean culture takes over the capital, the city pauses for a national earthquake drill, coveted tickets for the NFL Mexico City Series 2026 go on sale, and President Claudia Sheinbaum leads the country in its annual Independence Day celebration.

K-EXPO takes over Mexico City, Sept. 25-27

From bibimbap to gamja hot dogs, and BTS to “Squid Game,” South Korean culture shows no sign of slowing its march across Mexico. Now, the South Korean government and one of the country’s leading creative-content agencies are bringing K-mania to Mexico City with K-EXPO 2026, a three-day celebration of Korean food, music, entertainment and lifestyle.

The free public events run Sept. 25-27 at the Centro Internacional de Exposiciones y Convenciones (CIEC) WTC in Colonia Nápoles, roughly 15 minutes driving from Chapultepec Park. Visitors can meet some of Korea’s leading tastemakers in food, content creation and lifestyle, while taking in a K-Pop All-Star cover-dance performance, a live cooking show and an idol makeup workshop.

Then comes the main event — and this one isn’t free. On Sept. 26, K-Pop acts Winner, Dayoung, Soyou, Touched and Alpha Drive One will perform at Pepsi Center WTC. Ticket details are expected to be announced soon.

For the latest updates, check K-EXPO Mexico City’s official website or Instagram page.

What: K-EXPO Exhibition and Events

Where: CIEC WTC, Filadelfia s/n, Nápoles, Benito Juárez, CDMX

When: Sept. 25-27

Price: Free

What: K-EXPO Concert

Where: Pepsi Center WTC, Dakota s/n, Nápoles, Benito Juárez, CDMX

When: Sept. 26

Price: To be announced

Don’t be alarmed — this is only a test

It may not be the most exciting item on the calendar, but anyone in Mexico City on Sept. 19 — especially visitors — should know what’s coming.

At noon, the city’s loudspeakers, cellphones, radio and television broadcasts will erupt with an earthquake alarm, marking the start of Mexico’s second national earthquake drill of the year. The simulated scenario: a magnitude 7.7 quake.

According to the National Coordinator of Civil Protection, the exercise is designed to strengthen government preparedness and coordination while encouraging the public to play an active role in reducing disaster risk.

If you live here, consider it a good excuse to finally put together that go-bag. If you’re visiting, take a deep breath, remember it’s a drill and don’t freak out.

The date itself carries some serious significance. Several of Mexico City’s most devastating earthquakes have struck on Sept. 19, including the disasters of 1985 and 2017. To mark the solemn occasion, President Claudia Sheinbaum will raise the national flag in the Zócalo at 7:19 a.m. in honor of the victims.

NFL tickets are coming. Good luck.

Football fans, get your clicking fingers ready.

The NFL is bringing the 2026 Mexico City Series to Estadio Banorte on Nov. 22, when the Minnesota Vikings face off against the San Francisco 49ers.

The game is still more than two months away, but if previous NFL games in Mexico City are any indication, waiting until the last minute for tickets is probably not the move. When the league last played here, in 2022, presale tickets reportedly disappeared within an hour, while general-sale tickets are also said to have sold out almost immediately.

Here’s the schedule for the 2026 ticket rush, with sales taking place through Ticketmaster:

American Express Presale: Sept. 14 at 10 a.m. CST — limit of 6 tickets per person

Banorte Presale: Sept. 17 at 10 a.m. CST — limit of 4 tickets per person

General Sale: Sept. 22 at 10 a.m. CST — limit of 4 tickets per person

And, of course, El Grito

MND Local CDMX will always aim to point you toward the things happening below the radar. But considering our inaugural edition lands just ahead of El Grito, we’d be remiss not to give you the quick-and-dirty guide to one of the biggest nights on Mexico’s calendar.

The official celebration of Mexican Independence is held Sept. 15 and draws enormous crowds to Mexico City’s Plaza de la Constitución — better known as the Zócalo — in the historic center.

The festivities begin well before the main event, with people arriving hours in advance to stake out a spot with a view of the Palacio Nacional. Then, at 11 p.m., President Claudia Sheinbaum steps onto the main balcony and delivers the iconic Grito de Dolores, or Grito de la Independencia, officially kicking off the celebrations.

What follows is exactly what you’d expect from Mexico City on one of its biggest nights: street food, music, fireworks, flags, an abundance of green, white and red, and a whole lot of people. This year’s musical lineup is headlined by Tejano superstars Grupo Intocable.

If you don’t shy away from crowds, we highly recommend experiencing the spectacle at least once. It’s loud, chaotic, deeply patriotic and very, very Mexico City.

If, on the other hand, the prospect of being packed into a square with millions of people sounds less than appealing, fear not. Hundreds of smaller celebrations will be happening across the city, offering plenty of Grito energy, with plenty more breathing room.

Welcome to MND Local CDMX. We’ll see you next week.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

Five Brazilian clubs are still alive in the quarterfinals, the champion banks around US$25 million, and a place in the 2029 Club World Cup is on the line. This guide covers the date, the venue, the favorites, tickets and travel.

Copa Libertadores final 2026: date, venue and kickoff

CONMEBOL has set the final for Saturday 28 November 2026 at the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo. As in every edition since 2019, it is one match at a neutral venue; if level after 90 minutes, the trophy is decided by extra time and, if needed, penalties.

The Centenario is the sport’s most historic ground: it hosted the first World Cup final in 1930 and holds roughly 60,000 fans for football. CONMEBOL confirms the exact kickoff time after the semifinals, usually a late-afternoon start suited to the European television window.

Montevideo is a deliberate choice. The city staged memorable recent finals and offers compact logistics: the stadium sits inside the Parque Batlle district, about 15 minutes by road from the city center and the port where many Argentine and Brazilian fans arrive.

The road to Montevideo: who is still alive

The quarterfinals, played across 8-17 September, feature five Brazilian clubs: holders Flamengo, Palmeiras, Fluminense, Cruzeiro and Corinthians. They are joined by Estudiantes of Argentina, Ecuador’s LDU Quito and Independiente del Valle, and surprise package Platense.

The draw has already produced drama. Flamengo landed a heavyweight all-Brazilian tie against Cruzeiro in the round of 16 and survived it, while Palmeiras extended its remarkable away form to stay on course for a second straight final. Our round-of-16 draw analysis mapped the bracket in detail.

Semifinals run 13-22 October, after which the finalists get five weeks to prepare — and their fans get five weeks to find tickets and transport to Uruguay. Both finalists also know that a congested calendar awaits, with the post-World Cup scheduling squeeze already shaping squad rotation.

Favorites: Flamengo, Palmeiras and the Brazilian streak

Flamengo starts as favorite. The Rio club is defending champion, owns the deepest squad on the continent and has reached four finals in seven years, a run detailed in our coverage of their 2025 semifinal grind.

Palmeiras, beaten 1-0 in last year’s Lima final, is built for knockout football and remains the most likely challenger. Fluminense and Cruzeiro are dangerous outsiders, while Corinthians carries the largest traveling fan base of the surviving field.

The numbers explain the confidence: Brazilian clubs have won seven straight Libertadores titles, powered by television revenue that dwarfs their rivals. Estudiantes, a four-time champion, is the best hope of breaking the streak, while LDU and Independiente del Valle have both won continental titles before.

Tickets: how and when to buy for Montevideo

CONMEBOL sells final tickets through its official ticketing platform, with the main sales window opening only after the semifinals confirm the two finalists. Each finalist receives an allocation for its own supporters; neutral sections go on general sale at the same time.

Prices for recent finals have ranged from affordable upper-tier seats to premium hospitality, and demand spikes instantly when a Brazilian giant qualifies. Buy only through official channels: counterfeit tickets and resale fraud are recurring problems around the final.

Fans planning to travel should book accommodation before the semifinals end. Montevideo hotels fill within days once a finalist with a mass following — Flamengo or Corinthians above all — is confirmed, and prices climb sharply.

Travel guide: getting to Montevideo and the stadium

From Brazil, direct flights run from São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro to Carrasco airport, and many fans cross via Buenos Aires, where ferries connect to Montevideo in about two hours. Argentine fans typically arrive by ferry or by road through the northern border crossings.

Inside the city, the Centenario sits in Parque Batlle, reachable by bus and taxi from the center and from the Tres Cruces bus terminal. On final day, expect road closures around the park and heavy security perimeters opening several hours before kickoff.

Late November is late spring in Uruguay, with mild evenings around 15-20°C. The city is compact and walkable, and the Rambla waterfront becomes the informal fan zone in the days around the match.

What the winner takes home

The champion’s package is the richest in South American club football: around US$25 million in accumulated prize money across the campaign, a place in the Recopa Sudamericana 2027 against the Sudamericana winner, and a confirmed slot at the FIFA Club World Cup 2029.

For Flamengo, a fifth title would cement the club’s status as the dominant South American institution of the era; the financial side of that machine is laid out in our report on Flamengo’s lucrative 2025 campaign. For any challenger, beating the Brazilian bloc in Montevideo would reshape the continental balance.

Copa Libertadores 2026 — Key Dates Quarterfinals: First legs 8-10 September, second legs 15-17 September 2026. Semifinals: First legs 13-15 October, second legs 20-22 October 2026. Final: Saturday 28 November 2026, Estadio Centenario, Montevideo — single match. Champion’s rewards: ~US$25 million prize money, Recopa Sudamericana 2027, FIFA Club World Cup 2029. Ticket sales: Open after the semifinals via CONMEBOL’s official platform only. Dates as announced by CONMEBOL; kickoff time confirmed after the semifinals.

This is reporting, not travel or ticketing advice. Conditions vary by year, vendor and individual circumstance. Confirm current schedules, prices and entry rules with official sources before booking.

It is a single match at a neutral venue, decided by extra time and penalties if level after 90 minutes. CONMEBOL confirms the kickoff time after the semifinals in October.

Who is favorite to win the 2026 Copa Libertadores? Defending champion Flamengo is the favorite, with the deepest squad in South America and four finals in seven years. Palmeiras, runner-up in 2025, is the closest challenger. Brazilian clubs have won seven consecutive titles, though Estudiantes and Ecuador’s LDU and Independiente del Valle remain threats.

World.title: Police Seize Seven Weapons in Raid Targeting Deputy Mario Frias
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —The weapons. Federal Police found seven firearms registered to deputy Mario Frias (PL-SP) at an address that is not his, opening a separate case for illegal weapons possession. —The operation. The raid was part of Operation Make Up, authorized by Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino, with 49 search warrants executed in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Ceará and the Federal District. —The money. Investigators suspect R$2 million (about US$394,000) in parliamentary amendments was diverted to two NGOs tied to Karina Ferreira da Gama, producer of the film “Dark Horse.” —The seizure. Frias’s cell phone was confiscated. Police say money flows in the broader scheme run into the hundreds of millions of reais. —The parallel track. A separate inquiry by Justice André Mendonça is examining payments linked to Banco Master that were allegedly steered to the same film.

Brazil’s Federal Police went looking for evidence about a film-financing scheme at the homes and offices of deputy Mario Frias — and walked out with his cell phone and a separate criminal case: seven guns registered in his name, stored at an address where he does not live.

Police Seize Seven Weapons in Raid Targeting Deputy Mario Frias

Seven Guns at an Address That Is Not His

The weapons were found during one of the 49 searches executed on Thursday, September 10, across São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Ceará and the Federal District. All seven firearms are registered to Mario Frias, the former culture secretary under Jair Bolsonaro and now a first-term federal deputy for São Paulo. None of them was supposed to be where officers found them: the address is not Frias’s declared residence.

That mismatch matters under Brazilian law. A registered gun owner must keep weapons at the address filed with the Federal Police or the Army. Storing them elsewhere converts a paperwork problem into a criminal one — and police said the discovery will be investigated separately, as suspected illegal possession of a firearm. It is, in other words, a second legal front for Frias, independent of whatever the corruption probe eventually concludes.

Operation Make Up and the NGO Money Trail

The operation that brought officers to Frias’s door is called Make Up, and it was authorized by Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino. Investigators suspect that roughly R$2 million (about US$394,000 at the current rate of around 5.08 reais per dollar) in parliamentary budget amendments was diverted to two non-profits linked to Karina Ferreira da Gama — the ICB institute and the National Academy of Culture, known as ANC.

Ferreira da Gama is the owner of Go Up Entertainment, the production company behind “Dark Horse,” a film project about the collapse of Banco Master. Go Up itself is not a target of the warrants; the two NGOs are. Police are investigating embezzlement, document forgery, money laundering, criminal organization and bidding-related crimes, and describe money flows in the wider scheme as running into the hundreds of millions of reais — at least US$20 million.

One strand predates the raid. Reporting in June had already flagged a R$1 million (about US$197,000) amendment destined for an entrepreneurship program that was never carried out. In May, questioned by the Supreme Court, Frias denied that his amendments had gone to “any film production.” Thursday’s searches — including the seizure of his phone — suggest investigators intend to test that denial against his messages and financial records.

The amendment web reaches further. Deputies Bia Kicis and General Pollon also assigned funds that were never disbursed; a former campaign aide to Senator Flávio Bolsonaro directed R$1 million (about US$197,000) to the producer’s orbit; and investigators noted that Ferreira da Gama bought an SUV with R$100,000 (about US$19,700) in cash — a classic red flag in money-laundering investigations.

The Dark Horse Connection

Operation Make Up does not exist in a vacuum. A parallel inquiry led by Justice André Mendonça is examining a plea bargain alleging that Banco Master money was channeled to the same “Dark Horse” film project at the request of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro — the story The Rio Times detailed in its coverage of the plea deal behind Brazil’s judicial crisis. Master’s collapse has already rippled through Brasília, including the cancelled Moraes speech that signaled how radioactive the bank’s name has become.

The senator reacted within hours, accusing Justice Dino of political interference — a charge with an obvious subtext. Flávio Bolsonaro is leading President Lula in runoff polling for October’s election, and an investigation touching his family’s allies, his former campaign staff and a film about a bank whose downfall embarrasses the establishment lands in the middle of the campaign. Dino, a former Lula justice minister, is precisely the villain the Bolsonaro camp would script for such a moment.

Frias, for his part, is one of the most visible culture-war figures of the Brazilian right — an actor turned politician who ran the culture portfolio in the Bolsonaro government. That profile guarantees the case will be fought as much on social media and campaign stages as in court.

What Comes Next

Three things to watch. First, the weapons case: whether prosecutors file illegal-possession charges is now largely a technical question, and it moves faster than a corruption trial. Second, the forensic accounting on the ICB and ANC transfers — and whether Frias’s seized phone contradicts his May testimony to the Supreme Court. Third, convergence: if Dino’s Make Up probe and Mendonça’s Dark Horse inquiry begin citing the same money flows, the two cases merge into the largest campaign-season scandal of 2026. With the first round weeks away, every procedural step will be read as a poll intervention — by both sides.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was Mario Frias targeted by Federal Police?

Operation Make Up, authorized by Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino, investigates the suspected diversion of about R$2 million (about US$394,000) in parliamentary amendments to two NGOs linked to Karina Ferreira da Gama, producer of the film “Dark Horse.” Police executed 49 search warrants in four states on September 10, 2026, and seized Frias’s cell phone.

What happened with the weapons found in the raid?

Officers found seven firearms registered to Mario Frias at an address that is not his declared residence. Because Brazilian law requires registered guns to be kept at the filed address, the discovery opened a separate investigation into illegal weapons possession, independent of the corruption probe.

What is the Dark Horse film case?

“Dark Horse” is a film project about the collapse of Banco Master, produced by Go Up Entertainment. A parallel Supreme Court inquiry is examining allegations, detailed in a plea bargain, that Banco Master funds were steered to the film at the request of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Operation Make Up now investigates whether congressional amendments also flowed to the producer’s NGOs.

SPORTS · FORMULA 1, 10 SEPTEMBER 2026

Key Facts —Dates — The São Paulo Grand Prix 2026 runs Friday 6 to Sunday 8 November 2026 at Interlagos, officially the Autódromo José Carlos Pace. —Race — The Grand Prix starts Sunday 8 November at 14:00 local time (17:00 UTC), over 71 laps of the 4.309-kilometre circuit. —Format — 2026 is a classic weekend with no sprint race: two Friday practice sessions, final practice and qualifying on Saturday, race on Sunday. —Championship stakes — Interlagos is round 21 of 24, the penultimate flyaway before Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi decide the 2026 title. —Attendance — The 2025 edition drew a record crowd of roughly 304,000 across the weekend, the largest in the event’s modern era. —Name — The race carries the official title Grande Prêmio de São Paulo, with MSC Cruises as title sponsor, and Brazil’s contract runs until 2030. —Weather — Early November marks the start of São Paulo’s rainy season; covered grandstand seats are the safest choice.

The São Paulo Grand Prix 2026 brings Formula 1 back to Interlagos from 6 to 8 November, and few races on the calendar carry this much history and this much noise. The title fight often arrives in Brazil still open, the crowd of more than 300,000 turns the bowl into a wall of sound, and rain is always lurking. This guide covers dates, the full schedule, tickets, transport, where to stay, and what to watch for.

São Paulo Grand Prix 2026: dates and full schedule

Formula 1 confirms Interlagos for the weekend of 6-8 November 2026, slot 21 in a 24-round season. It is the last South American stop and, in most scenarios, the race where the championship picture hardens before the final triple-header.

Unlike recent editions, 2026 returns to a traditional format with no sprint. Friday holds free practice one at 12:30 and free practice two at 16:00 local time. Saturday brings final practice at 11:30 and qualifying at 15:00. Gates open at 08:00 each day.

The Grand Prix itself starts Sunday at 14:00 local, which is 17:00 UTC and noon on the US East Coast. The race covers 71 laps, roughly 306 kilometres, and historically lasts between 90 minutes and two hours when rain or safety cars intervene.

Session times remain subject to final confirmation by Formula 1 in the weeks before the event. Check the official F1 schedule again in late October, since support races and concert programming can shift gate and session times slightly.

Why Interlagos matters: Senna’s home and a title decider

Interlagos, officially the Autódromo José Carlos Pace, sits in the south of São Paulo between the Guarapiranga reservoir and the Billings dam. The anti-clockwise 4.309-kilometre layout is short, bumpy and steep, with the famous Senna S opening the lap and the long uphill drag to the finish line rewarding bravery.

The circuit is synonymous with Ayrton Senna, who grew up in the city and won here in 1991 and 1993. His 1991 victory, sealed with a failing gearbox in pouring rain, remains the defining image of the Brazilian Grand Prix and the reason the crowd’s emotion is unlike anywhere else.

Championships have repeatedly been settled on this hillside. Lewis Hamilton clinched his first title on the final corner in 2008, and Max Verstappen produced one of the great wet-weather drives here in 2024. When the points are close, Interlagos rarely stays quiet.

Tickets: where to sit and what to expect

Tickets sell through the official São Paulo Grand Prix channels, typically in waves, and the 2025 record crowd of about 304,000 means popular grandstands go early. Three-day passes dominate, with single-day Sunday tickets the most expensive per day.

Grandstand A, on the run to the Senna S, offers overtaking action and big screens but no roof. The covered sectors near the final corner and main straight cost more and protect against November rain, which is a real consideration: showers hit the circuit in most editions.

Budget options include general admission on the grass banks, which deliver atmosphere at a fraction of grandstand prices but no guaranteed view of a screen. Whichever sector you choose, buy only through official vendors; resale scams around this event are common.

How to get to Interlagos: metro, shuttles and traffic

The standard route is Metro Line 5-Lilac to Capão Redondo, where official shuttle buses run to the circuit gates on race weekend. The combination avoids the worst of the road congestion that locks the district of Interlagos for hours after the checkered flag.

Ride-hailing works but expect surge pricing and long waits after the race; drivers often cannot reach the perimeter roads. If you drive, pre-booked parking is essential, and leaving before the final laps saves an hour or more.

The economic stakes behind this logistics machine are enormous: the Grand Prix weekend has become São Paulo’s most lucrative long weekend, pumping hundreds of millions of dollars into hotels, restaurants and transport. Our report on the Grand Prix’s record economic haul details the numbers.

Where to stay: districts that work for race weekend

Most international visitors base themselves in Pinheiros, Vila Olímpia or along Avenida Paulista, trading a longer commute for better hotels, restaurants and safety. From these districts, the metro connection to Line 5 is direct or requires a single change.

Staying near the circuit itself cuts travel time but limits evening options. Book early: occupancy across the city approaches capacity for race week, and rates climb sharply once the championship narrative becomes clear in September and October.

The broader tourism picture supports the hype. Earlier editions generated an estimated US$350 million windfall for São Paulo’s economy, a figure city officials expect the 2026 race to match or beat given the record crowds.

Weather, safety and what to pack

Early November in São Paulo means warm afternoons around 24-28 degrees Celsius and a high chance of afternoon thunderstorms. Bring a light rain jacket, sunscreen and a hat; umbrellas are usually restricted inside grandstands, and ponchos sell out fast at the circuit.

Safety around the event has improved with heavy policing on metro routes, but standard big-city caution applies: keep phones and wallets out of sight in crowds, use official shuttles after dark, and avoid walking alone between the circuit and distant parking areas.

Ear protection is worth packing, especially for children, since the current cars remain extremely loud in the bowl’s confined space. Binoculars help in the grass-bank sections where screens are scarce.

What is at stake in the 2026 title fight

With three rounds left after Brazil, Interlagos sits exactly where championship math gets brutal. A driver arriving with a 25-to-40-point lead can be crowned here; a tighter fight turns the weekend into the season’s pivotal swing, as it has so many times before.

The 2026 season also runs under Formula 1’s new power-unit and chassis regulations, which reset the competitive order in the opening races. How the grid adapts by November — and who has developed fastest — will decide whether São Paulo hosts a coronation or a showdown.

For the wider Latin American leg of the calendar, Brazil anchors the region alongside Mexico City the weekend before. Fans planning both races should follow our coverage across the Brazil section as tickets and travel logistics evolve.

São Paulo Grand Prix 2026 — Weekend at a Glance Friday 6 November: Free Practice 1 at 12:30, Free Practice 2 at 16:00 local; gates open 08:00. Saturday 7 November: Free Practice 3 at 11:30, Qualifying at 15:00 local. Sunday 8 November: Race at 14:00 local (17:00 UTC), 71 laps, 4.309 km per lap. Venue: Autódromo José Carlos Pace (Interlagos), São Paulo — round 21 of 24. Getting there: Metro Line 5 to Capão Redondo plus official shuttle buses; avoid driving after the race. World.title: Fuse Failure Shuts 161 Ecuador Oil Wells at Referendum-Hit ITT Block
World.content:
Ecuador · Energy

Key Facts —What happened. A blown fuse at a processing plant triggered the emergency shutdown system at Ecuador’s Block 43-ITT, automatically switching off 161 oil wells between September 5 and 7, 2026. —The cost. Petroecuador puts the lost volume at about 25,000 barrels. National output fell from roughly 375,000 barrels per day to a trough of 344,000 before recovering. —The recovery. Crews reactivated the wells progressively; the hydrocarbons regulator recorded a rebound to nearly 361,000 bpd on Wednesday, and full stabilization was expected by Thursday, September 10. —The block. ITT sits inside the Yasuní National Park — the field Ecuadorians voted to close in a 2023 referendum. It still produces around 40,000 bpd. —The backdrop. Ecuador ran a US$5.3 billion fiscal deficit in 2025, oil is its top export, and Brent crude just broke US$105 — every lost barrel is expensive, and every produced one unusually valuable. —The plan. Petroecuador is investing US$632 million in 2026, roughly 50% more than last year, to hold national production near 370,000 bpd.

A single faulty fuse switched off 161 wells in Ecuador’s most controversial oil field last weekend, briefly knocking national output down by some 30,000 barrels a day — a small accident with an outsized political echo, because the field in question is the one voters ordered closed three years ago.

Fuse Failure Shuts 161 Ecuador Oil Wells at Referendum-Hit ITT Block

A Fuse, a Pressure Spike and 161 Silent Wells

Petroecuador’s explanation, delivered after reporters noticed a sharp production drop, is almost banal. A fuse failed at one of the block’s plants. Pressure rose in the pipelines carrying crude out of the field. The emergency shutdown system did exactly what it is designed to do — and turned off 161 wells at once, sometime over the weekend of September 5 to 7.

The state company estimates the lost volume at around 25,000 barrels. The national production curve tells the story more vividly: output had been running near 375,000 barrels per day, fell to 344,000 at the trough, and had already climbed back to nearly 361,000 by Wednesday, according to the Regulation and Control Agency for Hydrocarbons (ARCH). Petroecuador said systems would be fully stabilized by Thursday, September 10.

No spill, no injuries, no sabotage — a safety system working as intended. But the location turned a routine incident into national news.

The Most Political Oil Field in Ecuador

Block 43, known as ITT — for the Ishpingo, Tambococha and Tiputini fields — lies beneath the Yasuní National Park in the Amazon, one of the most biodiverse places on Earth. In August 2023, Ecuadorians voted in a national referendum to keep the ITT crude in the ground forever. Three years later, the block still produces around 40,000 barrels per day, down just 3.6% year on year in the first four months of 2026.

President Daniel Noboa’s government says it respects the vote but argues that closing the field properly will take years — and Petroecuador has warned of multibillion-dollar losses over two decades if the wells are cemented. Environmental groups counter that every month of delay is a breach of the popular mandate. A weekend in which 161 ITT wells sat idle gave both sides a preview of the argument to come: for activists, proof that the shutdown is technically trivial; for the treasury, a reminder of what disappears.

The Fiscal Math Behind Every Barrel

Ecuador can ill afford idle wells. The country’s fiscal deficit widened to US$5.3 billion in 2025 from US$3.11 billion the year before, according to the Observatorio de Política Fiscal. Crude is the country’s top export earner, and last year’s numbers were already grim: production fell 9% to an average of 349,167 bpd, exports dropped 7% in volume, and the average realized price slipped to US$58.63 a barrel from US$68.56 in 2024. Starved of cash, Petroecuador cut investment by 80% between January and November 2025, to US$357 million.

This year was supposed to be the turnaround. The company plans US$632 million of investment in 2026 — nearly 50% more — with a 36-well drilling campaign, seven contracted rigs and a production target of 369,000 to 370,000 bpd. High prices are helping: exports reached US$2.98 billion between January and April, up 3.8% year on year despite volumes falling 7.7%. And with Brent crude now above US$105 a barrel, the price umbrella over Quito’s budget is wide — as long as the oil actually flows.

A Fragile System, Once Again

The fuse incident is small compared to what Ecuador’s oil infrastructure has already survived. In July 2025, regressive erosion of the Coca and Loco rivers forced the shutdown of both major pipelines, the SOTE and the OCP, dragging national output to an all-time low of 146,000 bpd and shutting the country’s three biggest blocks for most of the month. Recovery took weeks.

That is the uncomfortable context of a blown fuse: a system this centralized, this underinvested and this exposed to nature does not need sabotage to stop. It needs only a weak component — and a country that cannot decide whether it wants the oil at all.

What Comes Next

Watch the ARCH daily production figures over the coming days for confirmation that the 375,000-bpd baseline is holding. The larger fight — over when, and whether, Block 43-ITT will ever be switched off deliberately, well by well — returns to the courts and the streets. This weekend, Ecuador got an accidental rehearsal of both outcomes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Ecuador shut 161 oil wells?

A fuse failed at a plant in Block 43-ITT between September 5 and 7, 2026. The resulting pressure increase in the crude pipelines activated the automatic emergency shutdown system, which switched off 161 wells as a safety measure. There was no spill or sabotage.

How much oil production did Ecuador lose?

Petroecuador estimates about 25,000 barrels in total. National output fell from roughly 375,000 barrels per day to a low of 344,000, then recovered to nearly 361,000 by Wednesday, September 9, with full stabilization expected by September 10.

Why is Block 43-ITT controversial?

The block lies under the Yasuní National Park in the Amazon. In an August 2023 referendum, Ecuadorians voted to keep its crude permanently underground — yet it still produces around 40,000 barrels per day while the government argues an orderly closure will take years.

World.title: Senegal’s Ruling Party Demands Loyal Dialogue After Prime Minister’s Speech
World.content:
Key Facts — What happened Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko called for a loyal dialogue with President Bassirou Diomaye Faye after his speech on 8 September 2026.

— The power base Pastef, the majority party, holds 130 of the 165 seats in the National Assembly.

— The money The African Development Bank approved CFAF 20 billion, about 35 million dollars, in July 2026 for public finance management.

— The constraint Senegal runs an International Monetary Fund programme of about SDR 453 million, roughly 650 million dollars.

— What comes next Investors and creditors will watch whether the loyal dialogue stabilises reforms under Vision 2050.

Senegal · POLITICS

Senegal’s ruling Pastef party has demanded a loyal dialogue between President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko, exposing a cohabitation crisis at the top of the state.

Senegal’s Ruling Party Demands Loyal Dialogue After Prime Minister’s Speech

Senegal’s majority party has called for a loyal dialogue between President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko. The demand follows Sonko’s speech on 8 September 2026, in which he rejected any permanent hostility between the two leaders.

A cohabitation crisis inside Pastef

Pastef, the party that dominates Senegal’s National Assembly, now finds itself split between two competing poles of power. President Faye and Prime Minister Sonko, once close allies, have drifted into an internal cohabitation crisis.

Sonko used his 8 September address to call for a loyal dialogue with Faye. He also insisted that the state needs standing institutions, not institutions aligned to one camp.

The prime minister’s language was careful but firm. He rejected what he called permanent hostility, while making clear that the executive and the legislature must not simply align.

A dominant majority with decisive power

Pastef holds 130 of the 165 seats in the National Assembly. That gives the party decisive control over laws and the budget.

This majority has already been linked to tensions over economic policy. The relationship between the executive and the legislature has become a central fault line.

For investors, the split matters because it can delay or reshape reforms. A divided majority can slow budget decisions even when one party formally controls the chamber.

The money and power stakes

Senegal remains under heavy financial constraint. In July 2026, the African Development Bank approved CFAF 20 billion, about 35 million dollars, for public finance management and revenue mobilisation.

The funding sits within the reform agenda of Vision 2050. It is designed to strengthen how the state collects and manages public money.

Senegal also runs a programme supported by the International Monetary Fund of about SDR 453 million, roughly 650 million dollars. Fiscal discipline is therefore at the heart of the current power struggle.

Why creditors are watching the loyal dialogue

The International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the African Development Bank all frame Dakar’s room for manoeuvre on debt, revenue and subsidies. Political tension inside the ruling party directly affects the credibility of reforms.

Western partners and creditors want stable institutions that can deliver on commitments. A prolonged dispute between the president and the prime minister could complicate that picture.

The loyal dialogue is not just a domestic affair. It conditions how reliably Senegal can implement the fiscal adjustments its lenders expect.

The regional read-through

Senegal is a benchmark for political stability in French-speaking West Africa. Its internal cohabitation test is being watched in Dakar, Abidjan and beyond.

The country’s role in the wider scramble for influence and capital in Africa makes the standoff more consequential. Political predictability helps determine where money flows.

For readers tracking the continent’s shifting power map, the Senegal case fits a broader pattern. It shows how domestic political friction can shape access to finance and reform momentum, as covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The immediate test is whether the loyal dialogue produces a working arrangement between Faye and Sonko. No formal date for direct talks has been announced.

Investors will monitor the next budget cycle and any signals from the International Monetary Fund. The strength of Senegal’s institutions will be measured by how the two leaders manage their rivalry.

The coming weeks will show whether the majority party can turn its parliamentary dominance into stable government. For now, the call for dialogue has lowered the temperature without resolving the underlying competition.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Senegal’s ruling party demand after the prime minister’s speech? Pastef demanded a loyal dialogue between President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko after Sonko’s speech on 8 September 2026. How many seats does Pastef hold in Senegal’s National Assembly? Pastef holds 130 of the 165 seats in the National Assembly, giving it decisive control over laws and the budget. Why does the political tension matter for Senegal’s creditors? Senegal runs an International Monetary Fund programme of about SDR 453 million, roughly 650 million dollars, and fiscal discipline depends on stable institutions and reform credibility.

World.title: Somaliland Pushes UN Recognition Drive on Sidelines of General Assembly
World.content:
Key Facts — What happened Somaliland is using the United Nations General Assembly season in New York to press its long-running campaign for international recognition as a sovereign state.

— The push Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise Somaliland in December 2025, and the United Arab Emirates is lobbying several more countries to follow.

— The money The United Arab Emirates has hired lobbying firms such as FGS Global, paying about $2.6 million in six months with an annual budget projected near $5 million to promote recognition.

— The asset A $442 million, 30-year concession with Dubai-based DP World is transforming the port of Berbera into a regional hub, with ownership split 51% DP World, 30% Somaliland and 19% Ethiopia.

— The flashpoint On 1 January 2024, Ethiopia and Somaliland signed a memorandum granting Ethiopia 20 km of coastline for 50 years in return for a promise to recognise Somaliland; Somalia called the deal “null and void.”

— What comes next Somalia, backed by several allies, is lobbying United Nations members during the General Assembly to block any recognition moves and preserve Somali territorial integrity.

Somalia · GEOPOLITICS

Somaliland is using the United Nations General Assembly season in New York to intensify its campaign for international recognition, offering Red Sea security and Berbera port access in exchange for diplomatic support.

Somaliland Pushes UN Recognition Drive on Sidelines of General Assembly

Somaliland is turning the corridors of the United Nations General Assembly into a lobbying stage. Its leaders want the world to treat the self-declared republic as a sovereign state, not a breakaway region of Somalia.

A diplomatic push in New York

Somaliland declared independence from Somalia on 18 May 1991. Its claim rests on an earlier sovereignty: it was briefly recognised by more than 30 states after its 26 June 1960 independence as British Somaliland, before entering an unratified union with Somalia.

In August 2025, Somaliland actors submitted a detailed legal case to the United Nations Secretary-General. They argued that the original statehood “continues” and that Somaliland is not a secessionist entity, urging re-admission to the United Nations system.

President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi “Irro” has campaigned for recognition throughout 2025 and 2026. The breakthrough came in December 2025, when Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise Somaliland; Irro made a state visit to Jerusalem in June 2026.

Paid lobbying and the United Arab Emirates connection

Parallel to the diplomatic outreach, Somaliland relies heavily on paid lobbying in Western capitals. Reports indicate the United Arab Emirates has hired major firms such as FGS Global to promote recognition and shape media narratives.

The lobbying effort is substantial: about $2.6 million was paid in six months, with an annual budget projected near $5 million. That money buys access, messaging and pressure in Washington and European capitals.

The United Arab Emirates is not acting out of sentiment. Its interest runs through the port of Berbera on the Gulf of Aden, where a $442 million, 30-year concession with Dubai-based DP World is transforming the harbour into a regional hub.

Berbera, Ethiopia and the Red Sea chessboard

Ownership of the Berbera concession is split 51% DP World, 30% Somaliland and 19% Ethiopia. Berbera and nearby Bosaso have attracted Emirati investment in both commercial and prospective military facilities.

The aim is to compete with China’s corridor via Djibouti and to give landlocked Ethiopia alternative sea access for its 120 million people. On 1 January 2024, Ethiopia and Somaliland signed a memorandum of understanding granting Ethiopia 20 km of coastline for 50 years to develop a commercial port and naval base.

In return, Ethiopia promised to recognise Somaliland’s independence. Somalia’s federal government immediately denounced the deal as “null and void,” reasserting its sovereignty over Somaliland and warning foreign partners against recognition.

Great-power rivalry at the Bab el-Mandeb

These arrangements have turned Somaliland into a node of great-power competition at the southern entrance to the Bab el-Mandeb. Analysts describe converging contests: United States–China rivalry over basing and maritime routes, and Egypt–Ethiopia tensions over Nile and regional primacy.

A regional split has emerged between a Turkey–Saudi–Qatar bloc backing Somali territorial integrity and an emerging “Berbera axis” of Somaliland–United Arab Emirates–Ethiopia, with some reporting also pointing to Israel. For Western powers, Somaliland’s offer combines military basing rights at Berbera, participation in Red Sea security and potential access to critical minerals in exchange for diplomatic recognition.

In the United States, draft legislation such as H.R. 3992 in June 2025 has proposed formal recognition, though it remains stalled. The broader scramble for influence fits the pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

Somalia’s counter-campaign at the United Nations

Somalia, backed by several allies, continues to lobby United Nations members and international partners during the General Assembly to block any recognition moves. Its core argument is the principle of Somali territorial integrity.

The federal government in Mogadishu treats the Ethiopia–Somaliland memorandum as an attack on its sovereignty. It has warned foreign partners that engagement with Hargeisa undermines the Somali state.

The contest is now playing out in New York, where both sides are working the same corridors. The outcome will shape not only Somaliland’s future but also the balance of power across the Horn of Africa.

What to watch next

The immediate test is whether any additional United Nations member states signal openness to recognition during or shortly after the General Assembly session. Israel recognised Somaliland in December 2025, and Somali sources say the United Arab Emirates is lobbying countries including Eswatini, Argentina, Zambia and the Dominican Republic to follow.

The United States Congress could also move on H.R. 3992, though the legislation has stalled. Any progress there would dramatically shift the diplomatic calculus.

Meanwhile, the Berbera port expansion continues to anchor the economic case for recognition. The $442 million DP World concession runs for 30 years, giving outside powers a long-term stake in Somaliland’s status.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Somaliland want United Nations recognition? Somaliland declared independence from Somalia on 18 May 1991 and argues its original statehood from 26 June 1960 continues. Recognition would open access to international finance, treaties and security partnerships. What role does the Berbera port play in the recognition campaign? The $442 million, 30-year DP World concession at Berbera gives the United Arab Emirates and Ethiopia a commercial and strategic stake in Somaliland. Access to the port and Red Sea security are central bargaining chips in the lobbying effort. How has Somalia responded to the recognition push? Somalia has called the Ethiopia–Somaliland memorandum “null and void” and is lobbying United Nations members during the General Assembly to block recognition. It argues the moves violate Somali territorial integrity.

World.title: AFRICOM Announces New Military Equipment Delivery to Nigeria in West Africa
World.content:
Nigeria · DEFENSE

Key Facts — What happened The United States Africa Command delivered critical military supplies to Nigerian forces in Abuja in January 2026.

— The catch AFRICOM did not disclose the type or quantity of equipment in the delivery.

— The numbers Washington approved a possible Foreign Military Sale worth about $346 million in munitions to Nigeria in August 2025.

— Why it matters Nigeria is emerging as a key security pivot for Washington in West Africa against jihadist groups and Russian and Chinese influence.

— What comes next AFRICOM has prepared operational plans for counter-terrorism in Nigeria, including possible deployment of U.S. combat aircraft.

The United States Africa Command has delivered critical military supplies to Nigerian forces in Abuja, deepening a security partnership against jihadist and criminal groups across the country.

The United States Africa Command (AFRICOM) announced a new delivery of critical military supplies to Nigeria’s security forces in Abuja in January 2026. The shipment supports Nigeria’s ongoing operations and underscores a shared security partnership between Washington and Abuja.

What AFRICOM delivered to Nigeria

AFRICOM confirmed the delivery in a post on X, stating that U.S. forces delivered critical military supplies to Nigerian partners in Abuja. The command said the delivery supports Nigeria’s ongoing operations and emphasises the shared security partnership.

Photos released by U.S. authorities show sealed pallets being offloaded from a military transport aircraft. AFRICOM did not disclose the type or quantity of equipment in the shipment.

The delivery follows U.S. airstrikes targeting Islamic State fighters in Sokoto State in northwest Nigeria on Christmas Day 2025. Those strikes were conducted in coordination with Nigerian authorities.

The money behind the AFRICOM Nigeria military supplies

This delivery sits within a wider defence framework between Washington and Abuja. In August 2025, the United States approved a possible Foreign Military Sale worth about $346 million of munitions, precision bombs and rockets to Nigeria.

A broader $413 million envelope for counter-insurgency and security operations in Nigeria and West Africa was included in the U.S. fiscal year 2026 defence budget. These figures reflect Washington’s growing investment in Nigerian security capabilities.

Nigeria has battled Islamist insurgencies for around 15 years in the northeast. The country also faces widespread banditry and kidnapping in the northwest and Middle Belt regions.

Why Nigeria matters to Washington now

For Washington, Nigeria is emerging as a key security pivot in West Africa. The United States seeks to maintain influence against jihadist groups operating across the Sahel and Lake Chad Basin.

Russia and China have expanded their military and security footprint in other African states. This great-power competition is reshaping defence partnerships across the continent, a dynamic explored in Africa: The New Scramble.

AFRICOM has prepared several operational plans for counter-terrorism in Nigeria. These include options to deploy U.S. combat aircraft in-country, signalling a potential deepening of direct American military involvement.

The regional read-through for West Africa

The delivery to Abuja comes as several West African states have shifted away from traditional Western security partners. Military juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have turned to Russian military support in recent years.

Nigeria, by contrast, has maintained and deepened its security relationship with Washington. This makes Abuja an increasingly important anchor for U.S. strategy in the region.

The Sokoto State airstrikes in December 2025 demonstrated a willingness by both sides to coordinate on kinetic operations. The latest supply delivery reinforces that operational tempo.

What to watch next in the U.S.-Nigeria security partnership

The undisclosed nature of the equipment leaves open questions about the scale and capability of the shipment. Analysts will watch for further announcements on whether the delivery includes advanced munitions or surveillance systems.

The possible deployment of U.S. combat aircraft to Nigeria would mark a significant escalation in direct American involvement. No timeline for such a deployment has been announced.

Nigerian security forces continue to face pressure from multiple fronts, including Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province in the northeast. The effectiveness of new supplies will be tested in upcoming operations across the country.

Frequently asked questions

What did AFRICOM deliver to Nigeria in January 2026? AFRICOM delivered critical military supplies to Nigerian forces in Abuja, but did not disclose the type or quantity of equipment. How much has the United States approved for Nigeria’s security operations? Washington approved a possible Foreign Military Sale worth about $346 million in August 2025, plus a broader $413 million envelope in the U.S. fiscal year 2026 defence budget. Why is Nigeria important to U.S. strategy in West Africa? Nigeria is emerging as a key security pivot for Washington against jihadist groups and to compete with Russian and Chinese influence in the region.

World.title: Why Africa’s smart cities will also need smarter finance
World.content:
Key Facts — What happened Kenya’s Konza Technopolis, a 2,024-hectare smart city launched in 2008, has an estimated total project cost of about US$14.5 billion.

— The money Phase 1 infrastructure was financed by Italy’s UniCredit SpA at roughly KSh 50.4 billion (about US$391 million), while Huawei built core systems under a China Eximbank loan of RMB 1.225 billion (about US$172 million) signed on 26 April 2019.

— The catch The China Eximbank loan carries 2% interest and matures on 21 September 2038, deepening Kenya’s exposure to Chinese digital-infrastructure credit.

— The shift In December 2025 Kenya’s PPP Unit approved a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer expansion model for the Konza cloud and smart-city facilities.

— What comes next In August 2026 Konza signed a framework with China’s Guodong Network for a proposed KSh 38.8 billion (about US$300 million) programme covering towers, data centres, fibre and cloud.

Kenya · INFRASTRUCTURE

Africa’s smart-city ambitions will fail without equally smart, diversified finance. Kenya’s Konza Technopolis shows how Chinese credit, Italian engineering and local public-private partnerships are now shaping the continent’s urban future.

Why Africa’s smart cities will also need smarter finance
