World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation was in Poland this week to visit potential locations for the base and discuss the issue further. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The candidate of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), one of Poland’s main political groups, has been disqualified from Kraków’s mayoral election after over 2,000 of the signatures from local residents collected in support of his candidacy were found to be invalid. One of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, admitted that the situation was an “embarrassment” and “catastrophe”. He responded by dismissing the candidate, Bartosz Bocheńczak, as head of his party’s local structures in Kraków and launching an investigation into how the blunder occurred. Podobnie jak i wielu naszych działaczy, wolontariuszy, sympatyków i wyborców, czuję się bardzo zawiedziony brakiem rejestracji kandydatury Bartosza Bocheńczaka w Krakowie. Przyczyną braku rejestracji było to, że spośród około 5000 zebranych podpisów, ponad 2000 były błędnych.… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) September 7, 2026 Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, is holding a mayoral election this month after the previous incumbent, Aleksander Miszalski, was removed mid-term in a rare recall referendum earlier this year. Over a dozen potential candidates announced plans to stand. But, in order to be registered, they had to collect at least 3,000 signatures from residents of the city supporting their candidacy, then submit them to the municipal electoral commission by 3 September. Twelve candidates made such submissions, after which the commission began assessing all signatures to ensure that each candidate had at least 3,000 that were valid. On Monday, reports began to emerge that, although Bocheńczak had submitted just over 4,600 signatures, the commission had found that fewer than 3,000 of them were valid. That evening, the candidate himself confirmed the news. Mentzen, who is leader of the far-right libertarian New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja) party that makes up one half of Confederation, revealed that over 2,000 signatories had listed their address as their place of residence rather than where they are officially registered as living. In Poland, it is common for people to live somewhere different from where they are officially registered. That is particularly the case for young people, who are often registered at their parents’ address while residing elsewhere. Confederation is particularly popular among young people, and Kraków has a large student population. Moja kandydatura na Prezydenta Krakowa nie została zarejestrowana. Zabrakło ważnych podpisów. Nie będę snuł teorii spiskowych, szukał winnych ani przerzucał odpowiedzialności na kogokolwiek. Uważałem, że złożenie niemal 5000 podpisów zapewni nam wystarczający margines… — Bartosz Bocheńczak (@BBochenczak) September 7, 2026 Mentzen said that the regulations regarding collecting signatures for candidates are “absurd”, yet admitted that Bocheńczak’s campaign should have done a better job of complying with the rules. There must now be “consequences from this embarrassment”, said Mentzen, who announced that Bocheńczak had been dismissed as New Hope’s local leader in Kraków and that a party commission would “determine responsibility for this disaster”. Confederation also faced scrutiny last year when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected its financial report for the 2024 European elections after it found irregularities. The party also failed to submit the required documents on time. As a result, it lost access to state subsidies. The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal by the far-right Confederation against the electoral commission's decision to reject its financial report for last year's European elections due to irregularities. The group will now lose access to state subsidies https://t.co/hNGu2Zvzii — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 Bocheńczak is not the only candidate who has struggled with collecting signatures. Last week, just days before the deadline, it emerged that over 3,000 signatures collected in support of the favourite in the elections, Łukasz Gibała, an independent, were invalid because the word “Kraków” was missing from the form. Gibała – a perennial candidate in mayoral elections who finished runner-up to Miszalski in 2024 – quickly scrambled to collect more signatures, and his team managed to gather an additional 9,000 in three days. On Monday this week, it also emerged that three other independent candidates, Marian Banaś, Stanisław Kułach and Marta Ratuszyńska, had failed to gather enough signatures. All three have taken up their right to appeal against the commission’s decision to reject their candidacies. Dziś złożymy dodatkowe podpisy do komisji wyborczej – ponad 9 tysięcy (oprócz wcześniejszych 5,5 tys.). Skala Waszego zaangażowania i pomocy była bezprecedensowa – w 3 dni zebraliśmy więcej podpisów niż którykolwiek z naszych rywali przez 3 tygodnie 💪 Bardzo Wam dziękuję i… — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) September 3, 2026 Six candidates have so far been accepted, including Gibała; Monika Piątkowska, who is supported by the centrist Civil Coalition (KO) and Polish People’s Party (PSL); Michał Drewnicki of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS); Aleksandra Owca of the left-wing Together (Razem); and Michał Klimek of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). Two candidates, Daria Gosek-Popiołek of The Left (Lewica) and Sławomir Pietrzyk of Social Democracy of Poland (Socjaldemokracja Polska), are still awaiting confirmation from the electoral commission that they submitted enough valid signatures. A decision is due to be announced today. The first round of the election will take place on Sunday 27 September. If any candidate receives over 50% of the vote, they will become mayor. If not, a run-off between the top two candidates will take place on 11 October. There has been little polling on support for candidates, but one survey by the Opinia24 agency for Polityka Insight two weeks ago showed Gibała with 25.2%, ahead of Piątkowska (15.3%) and Gosek-Popiołek (8.7%). World.title: Poland urges EU to deny asylum to migrants who violently cross its borders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus. “This is about depriving people who illegally cross the border in organised groups, using violence or destroying border security measures, of the right to international protection,” Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister who oversees migration policy, told broadcaster RMF. Polska zabiega o to, by Unia Europejska przyjęła jej interpretację przepisów dotyczących ochrony międzynarodowej. „Chodzi o pozbawienie prawa do ochrony międzynarodowej osób, które nielegalnie przekraczają granicę w zorganizowanych grupach, z użyciem przemocy albo niszcząc… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) September 6, 2026 The station reports that, at a meeting of the European Council next month, Poland will propose expanding the interpretation of article 33 of the United Nations’ Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. That section outlines the principle of “refoulement”, under which states are barred from expelling or returning refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened. The article includes a clause saying that the principle does not apply if “there are reasonable grounds for regarding [a refugee] as a danger to the security of the country” in which they have arrived, or if they have a criminal conviction that makes them “a danger to the community of that country”. Poland wants that clause to be applied in situations where someone applies for asylum after being part of an organised and aggressive border crossing. Since last year, Poland has itself banned asylum claims from people who illegally cross the border from Belarus. Since 2021, the Belarusian authorities have encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to irregularly – and often aggressively – enter the EU. Poland’s asylum ban, which has exceptions for certain vulnerable categories of people, was introduced as a temporary measure in March 2025 but has been repeatedly renewed since then. Warsaw now wants a similar interpretation of international refugee law to be applied across the EU Its proposals come in the wake of July’s incident in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands of migrants irregularly entered from Morocco. Soon afterwards, Poland urged the EU to adopt tougher measures, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. Prime Minister Donald Tusk was also one of 22 EU leaders who signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. After last week's migration crisis in Ceuta, Poland has called for tougher EU measures, including an automatic ban on residence for anyone who enters illegally. It pointed to its own experience of dealing with "weaponised" migration from Belarus https://t.co/2VHn5ZUJx7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 5, 2026 Poland has long argued that the situation on the Belarus border is an example of how migration has been “weaponised” by Russia and its allies to sow social discord in EU countries. In response, Poland has invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, has deployed thousands of additional officers there (and granted them expanded rights to use firearms), and has banned asylum claims. In 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, and the figure remained as high as 30,000 in 2025. However, in the first half of this year, only 235 attempted crossings were recorded, which the Polish government has hailed as evidence of the success of its tough measures. However, Poland’s human rights commission recently raised concern at how long the technically “temporary” asylum ban has been in place. Some Polish courts have also ruled that Polish border guards acted unlawfully when forcing migrants back into Belarus. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Prague to Host Central Europe’s First Climate Week
World.content:
Prague will host the first international climate week in Central Europe from September 14 to 20, with more than 50 conferences, seminars, workshops and other events planned across the city.

Climate Week Prague will bring together representatives from climate research, finance, government, business and other sectors to discuss how cities and economies can respond to climate change.

The official opening will take place at the Prague Planetarium on Monday, September 14, at 2:30 p.m.



Speakers will include former European Commissioner for Climate Action Connie Hedegaard, Deputy Director-General for Climate Policy at the European Commission and a former Czech environment minister Jan Dusík, and Prague Mayor Bohuslav Svoboda of the ODS party, who is supporting the event.

The program will cover a broad range of issues, including how cities can adapt to rising temperatures, water management, energy, construction, agriculture and transport.

Finance will be a major part of the agenda. The CEE Sustainable Finance Summit, running from September 14 to 16, will examine the impact of geopolitics and artificial intelligence on Europe’s economic competitiveness.

Climate Week Prague has been organized by a coalition of independent organizations led by the International Sustainable Finance Centre. The group also includes research institutions, the Climate Facts think tank, banks, investors and trade unions representing workers in the construction and energy sectors.

The organizers say the increasing effects of climate change, including more frequent heat waves, were among the main reasons for launching the event.

Data cited by Fakta o klimatu illustrates the change in Prague’s summer temperatures.

Between 1961 and 1990, the city recorded seven tropical nights, when temperatures remained at or above 20 degrees Celsius throughout the night. Over the following 35 years, that number increased to 165, according to data from the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institute for Global Change Research.

Average summer minimum temperatures in Prague also increased during the period, rising from 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, according to Fakta o klimatu.

The local figures come as international assessments warn of further warming. Reuters reported earlier in September, citing the United Nations Environment Programme, that global temperatures are expected to exceed the key 1.5-degree-Celsius threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.

Further warming is expected to contribute to more extreme weather and increase pressure on ecosystems, glaciers and low-lying coastal cities.

World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: September 28 Holiday in Czechia: What Will Be Open and Closed
World.content:
Czech Statehood Day falls on Monday, September 28, giving people across Czechia a three-day weekend. But anyone planning to shop should be aware that many large stores will be required to close.

The public holiday commemorates Saint Wenceslas, the patron saint of the Czech lands and one of the most important figures in Czech history. September 28 has been observed as Czech Statehood Day since 2000 and is a statutory day off.



For shoppers, however, the key issue is the country’s restrictions on retail opening hours.

Which shops will be closed on September 28

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square metres must close on September 28.

This means most large supermarkets, hypermarkets and shopping centres will not be able to operate as normal.

The restriction does not apply to all businesses. Smaller shops with a sales area of up to 200 square metres can remain open, although individual owners decide whether to operate during the holiday.

Some types of businesses are also exempt from the restrictions. These include pharmacies, petrol stations and shops located at airports and major railway stations.

Restaurants, cafés and most other services are not covered by the retail law and can therefore open according to their normal schedules or the decision of their operators.

People planning to use smaller independent shops should still check opening hours in advance. Many owners choose to close during public holidays, particularly when the holiday creates a long weekend.

Why is September 28 a public holiday

Czech Statehood Day is linked to Saint Wenceslas, the medieval ruler who became the patron saint of the Czech lands.

Wenceslas was the son of Duke Vratislav I and Drahomíra. His grandmother, Ludmila, who was later canonised, played a major role in his upbringing and is traditionally credited with influencing his Christian education.

Wenceslas is believed to have been killed in Stará Boleslav on September 28, either in 929 or 935, depending on the historical source.

His death turned him into a martyr and helped establish his lasting importance in Czech religious and national traditions.

World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague by Saffa Maso Bistro
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can can buy a basic ticket or a ticket with a braai package, which includes traditional South African boerewors sausage (500g) and a portion of biltong (150g).

On-site you’ll also find original Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices, and more for sale.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Saffa Maso | Biltong | Bistro | Obchod (@saffamaso)

Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.

Tickets are available via SMSTicket at this link. Children under 12 enter free.

World.title: Prague Unemployment Reaches 4% with 40,509 Job Seekers
World.content:
Unemployment in Prague rises to 4% at the end of August, with 40,509 people registered as job seekers at the Labour Office.

The figure was 2.1% higher than in July and 15.7% higher than a year earlier.

Despite the increase, Prague continued to record the lowest unemployment rate among Czechia’s regions. The national unemployment rate stood at 5% at the end of August.



More people registered as job seekers

A total of 5,368 people registered with the Prague Labour Office in August. That was 133 fewer than in July but 1,033 more than in August 2025.

At the end of August, Prague had 37,811 people considered reachable for employment. This category covers people aged 15 to 64 who are not temporarily unable to work and are not taking part in retraining.

The number of reachable job seekers increased by 822 compared with July and by 5,475 compared with the same month last year.

Women accounted for 55.2% of all registered job seekers, with 22,378 women listed in the Labour Office records.

More than 22,000 vacancies remain available

Employers in Prague had 22,519 registered vacancies at the end of August. That was 708 fewer positions than in July and 565 fewer than a year earlier.

There were an average of 1.8 registered job seekers for every vacancy.

Of the total number of registered vacancies, 1,676 were not marked as positions available to foreign workers. Employers could recruit workers from abroad for a further 20,843 positions.

Construction, accommodation and food services, and wholesale and retail were among the sectors with the largest number of vacancies.

World.title: Central bank chief on the scenario for introducing the Hungarian euro
World.content:
Hungary’s central bank governor has spoken of the pitfalls of euro adoption: this, he says, is how a Hungarian euro can be made to work.

Only one criterion met

The president of the Magyar Nemzeti Bank emphasised that the aim is not a swift, but a successful euro introduction. In his view, three things are needed for this: societal support, a coordinated strategy and a prepared real economy, index.hu writes.

Public backing is already in place: among countries on the verge of adopting the euro, Hungary has the highest proportion of supporters, with roughly four in five Hungarians favouring the single currency. At the same time, an equally large share believe the country is not yet economically ready for it.

The figures so far bear out this caution. According to Mihály Varga, Hungary currently meets just one accession criterion – the inflation reference value. This has, however, already improved the country’s standing in financial markets, while over the past year and a half the forint has become one of the world’s best-performing emerging-market currencies.

Risk from energy dependence and sluggish growth

Hungarian economic cycles move closely in step with those of the eurozone, which is a favourable sign. A more serious risk, however, is inflation: because of the greater energy dependence of central and eastern European countries, prices can more easily diverge from trends seen in the euro area.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

There is also work to be done on catching up. Between 2020 and 2025, Hungary grew by an average of 1.2 per cent a year, while several neighbouring countries expanded more quickly.

On the basis of Mr Varga’s message, then, adopting the euro has again become a more realistic political goal, but actual accession is not yet close. Societal support is strong, certain economic indicators are improving, but significant economic-policy work is still required to meet the necessary convergence criteria.

The European Commission has broken its silence: the Hungarian euro remains light-years away — can Péter Magyar’s plan succeed?

This is what the “Hungarian euro” looks like

As we reported last year, the first Hungarian euro coin is available for purchase on Vatera, and its price was not excessively high at the time. The obverse features King Matthias and Queen Beatrix, while the reverse shows the Phoenix, one of the largest sailing vessels on Lake Balaton, which sailed on the “Hungarian sea” in the ownership of the Festetics family, founders of the Georgikon in Keszthely. Why these particular images appear on the front and back, and why this coin was produced in the first place, can be read in our article.

World.title: PM Magyar’s stern message to Ukraine: no EU accession without progress
World.content:
Ukraine must take concrete steps to secure the rights of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia before further EU accession clusters can be opened, Prime Minister Péter Magyar told a doorstep press briefing in Bratislava on Thursday.

PM Magyar insists performance-based accession

He said political agreement was reached in June between the Hungarian and Ukrainian governments on the educational, cultural, linguistic and administrative rights of the Transcarpathian Hungarians, but the promised concrete measures had yet to be implemented.

Magyar said the Tisza Party had supported the opening of the first and sixth clusters, but further chapters should only be opened on a performance-based accession.

Péter Magyar and Volodimir Zelensky at the EU Summit on 18 June 2026. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

The prime minister cited Serbia, which started its accession process 12 years ago, yet only two of the six clusters have been opened for it, and noted that nearly 300,000 Hungarians live in Serbia, many of whom commute to Hungary for work or study, often queuing for hours at the Schengen border.

“For this reason … and out of honesty, it isn’t fair that everyone is now demanding that we open clusters for Ukraine, when there has been no progress in the negotiations on the first and sixth clusters.” Magyar said it would be unfair if Ukraine advanced faster in EU accession than candidates that had been fulfilling the conditions for many years. “This is a very long process, and it is by no means certain that it will be successful in the end,” he said.

No progress yet on Slovakia’s Benes Decrees

Magyar said that no progress had been made yet on disputed issues between Hungary and Slovakia such as the confiscation of land without compensation, the threat of imprisonment for expressing opinions, or the Benes Decrees, adding, however, that he was confident this would happen soon.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Speaking at a press conference in Bratislava after a meeting of Visegrad Four prime ministers and their Irish counterpart, Magyar said he and Slovak PM Robert Fico had previously agreed, and reaffirmed on Thursday, that these issues needed to be prepared at an expert level, but this had not yet happened. “I am confident that, as with any Slovak prime minister, it is in the interest of the Slovak prime minister to find solutions to these issues,” Magyar said.

He added it was clear that progress at the bilateral level could not be made until there was movement on at least the confiscation of land without compensation or the threat of imprisonment for expressing opinions. Last year, Slovakia passed a law that criminalises criticism of the Benes Decrees with up to six months in prison.

If you missed: Hungarian government to fight for annulment of Benes decrees

Potential in central European cooperation greater than current reality

There is greater potential in strengthening cooperation between central European countries than has been exploited so far, Prime Minister Peter Magyar told MTI on Thursday in a press briefing in Bratislava. Speaking about the economic and trade success indicators of Visegrad Four (V4) cooperation, Magyar said he could not specify a concrete target figure for trade growth, but he was interested in growth.

He highlighted the development of north-south transport links, such as the Warsaw-Prague-Bratislava-Budapest high-speed rail project, which could also extend to Vienna, as well as cooperation opportunities in energy, the defence industry, digitalisation, health care, agriculture and the food industry. Magyar said the V4 countries could form the basis of a strong central Europe, to which other countries, including Austria, Romania and the Balkan states, could later join.

World.title: Breaking – Magyar names Tisza’s five Constitutional Court nominees
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar, leader of the Tisza Party, on Thursday announced his party’s five nominees for the Constitutional Court on Facebook.

Magyar named his five Constitutional Court candidates

The nominees are Nóra Chronowski, a university professor, doctor of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and constitutional lawyer; Miklós Ligeti, an ombudsman, criminal lawyer and legal director of Transparency International Hungary; András György Kovács, a Kúria (supreme court) council chair judge and administrative lawyer with a PhD; Árpád Gábor Orosz, former head of the Kúria’s Civil College, a council chair judge, civil lawyer and European legal expert who has taught at the University of Szeged since 1993; and Zsolt Szomora, deputy director of the Institute of Criminal Sciences at the University of Szeged’s Faculty of Law and Public Administration and a habilitated university professor.

Magyar said the nominees’ committee hearings would be held on Monday, and parliament would elect the five new Constitutional Court judges on Tuesday morning.

The Prime Minister added that, true to the Tisza party’s pledge, he would propose Constitutional Court nominees who meet not only the requirements of the Fundamental Law but every professional criterion.He added that over recent weeks the government had held extensive consultations with a number of outstanding jurists, weighing considerations of irreproachability, integrity, independence and genuine professional achievement.Care had also been taken, he wrote, to ensure that the candidates would cover all branches of law: constitutional law, criminal law, administrative law, civil law and fundamental rights.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Background to the vacancies

The mandates of four Constitutional Court judges – among them Péter Polt, the Court’s president – expired on 1 September, after the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, adopted in July, stipulated that “the mandate of a member of the Constitutional Court shall terminate upon reaching the age of 70”.In addition to Mr Polt, this age limit had already been reached by Mária Haszonicsné Ádám, Miklós Juhász and Zoltán Lomnici.

Under the law, the National Assembly has 60 days to elect new Constitutional Court judges to replace those who have left. Parliament elects the new judges by secret ballot, requiring a two-thirds majority of MPs, for nine-year terms. The 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law reduced the length of judges’ mandates from 12 years to nine.

Further changes at the Court

Ágnes Czine, the Court’s vice-president, will see her 12-year mandate as a Constitutional Court judge expire in November.

One judge, Csaba Hende – a former MDF and later Fidesz MP and defence minister – had already left the 15-member body in July, as a result of the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law and the rules of the Constitutional Court Act. In his place, Parliament elected Pál Sonnevend, a university professor and former dean who heads a department at ELTE’s Faculty of Law, as a Constitutional Court judge.

It is “not right” that Hungary is paying 1 million euros a day to protect Europe’s common borders, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said at the meeting of Visegrád Four prime ministers and their Irish counterpart in Bratislava on Thursday.

PM Magyar: not a good message from the EU

Some 19-20 member states now agreed on the need for consistent, strict action and support for border protection, he added, expressing hope for an agreement at the October European Council meeting.

World.title: Hungary admits “embarrassing blunder” over King Charles III’s Lipizzaner horses – updated: another twist
World.content:
The Hungarian agriculture ministry has acknowledged an “embarrassing blunder” after a poorly worded letter sparked claims that Budapest was demanding the return of two Lipizzaner horses gifted to King Charles for his coronation.

A diplomatic wobble in the royal stables

The row broke after the Daily Mail reported that Hungary was seeking to take back the pair, Nelson and Iveco, from the Royal Mews at Windsor, prompting a flurry of speculation that the move amounted to a diplomatic slight. Courtiers were said to be “baffled” by what was described as a “strongly worded” communication from Budapest’s agriculture ministry insisting the animals be returned to the Szilvásvárad state stud farm.

The two Lipizzaners were handed over by former Defence Minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky. Source: Facebook/Szalay-Bobrovniczky Kristóf

In a late-night statement, the Agrár- és Élelmiszergazdaságért Felelős Minisztérium (Ministry of Agriculture and Food Economy) conceded that a July letter had indeed proposed terminating the loan agreement, but insisted the wording had been “inaccurate” and the mistake swiftly corrected. Officials said they had made it “unequivocally clear” to the British side that Hungary did not intend to bring the horses home.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

“Here, everyone is stupid” – Orbán weighs in

The episode took on a domestic political edge when former prime minister Viktor Orbán weighed in on social media after the ministry and embassy had already denied any recall. Quoting the cult Hungarian film Üvegtigris, he posted: “‘Here, everyone is stupid?’ asks Dr Csopkai in the well-known film. ‘Here? Everyone,’ replies Gaben,” in a swipe at the new Tisza-led government.

Loan, not gift: the Lipizzaner horses’ status clarified

According to the ministry, the horses were placed with the Royal Mews in 2024 under a loan agreement and remain the property of the Hungarian state, even as they are used by the British royal household. The pair – formally Neopolitano XXVII-44 (Nelson) and Incitato XVIII-3 (Iveco) – were selected from the Szilvásvárad State Stud with input from royal staff and specially trained for ceremonial duties, including harness and riding work.

If you missed: Hungarian conservation project sends Przewalski’s horse back to native steppe in Kazakhstan

Though the offer was made to mark the 2023 coronation, the formal handover took place in June 2024 in London, when then defence minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky presented the animals to the Royal Mews.

All’s well that ends well (in the Buckingham)

The Hungarian embassy in London later confirmed that the matter had been “resolved” and that the horses would “of course, remain in the United Kingdom as originally intended”. Royal sources similarly said there was no outstanding dispute, with Nelson and Iveco set to stay on at Windsor as living symbols of Anglo-Hungarian ties – and of the perils of imprecise diplomatic prose.

Another twist: world‑champion driver stripped of one of his Lipizzans?

According to 24.hu, the previous Hungarian government confiscated one of the Lipizzan horses from world‑champion carriage driver Marcell Dani — a horse that remains in Her Majesty’s service for ceremonial duties.

World.title: (Party) loyalty over expertise? Political appointees instead of career diplomats in Szijjártó’s foreign ministry
World.content:
According to internal sources, Péter Szijjártó was never particularly fond of career diplomats — some say because he himself was a political appointee, installed without any diplomatic training. Rather than the slow, convoluted machinery of traditional diplomacy, he preferred direct, results-driven showcases, chiefly in economic and foreign-trade matters; his favourite photo opportunity was, reportedly, the ribbon-cutting at a new factory. Now, startling figures have emerged concerning the personnel policy pursued during his tenure.

Appointments without open competition in the Szijjártó ministry

According to an investigation by 444.hu, which consulted numerous sources familiar with the relevant procedures, well over a third of diplomatic posts were filled not through open competition but by direct political appointment.

Ministry data obtained by the outlet show that between 2022 and 2026, 3,177 foreign-service positions were advertised, yet only 1,502 were filled on the basis of competitive applications. In a further 919 cases, the ministry’s leadership directly selected the individuals dispatched to particular posts.

This practice extended even to the most sought-after overseas assignments. In North America, for instance, more diplomats were appointed by direct decision than through successful competition: 58 to 47. In Europe the gap was narrower: 393 recruited via competition, compared with 326 directly nominated.

Three-quarters of staff turned over

Sources within the foreign ministry told 444.hu that this formed part of a broader personnel strategy. Szijjártó is said to have regarded the traditional model — in which officials with formal diplomatic training advance over many years through the ranks — as secondary. Between 2014 and 2026, roughly three-quarters of the ministry’s staff were replaced.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán in the parliament. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

The paper reported that the ministry also admitted individuals linked to Fidelity (Fidelitas), the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC), Szijjártó’s sporting contacts, or the families of governing-party politicians and NER-affiliated entrepreneurs. Some hires, sources claimed, were determined by instructions from above.The resulting system thus operated alongside the classical diplomatic career path a more direct, leadership-driven personnel model — and, according to the numbers, this was not exceptional but routine.

How former PM Orbán’s ex-secretary informed media about the shady businesses and was threatened with his kids

A lucrative BYD post for the former foreign minister

Péter Szijjártó was one of the principal campaign figures for Fidesz in April’s election, alongside former prime minister Viktor Orbán and former construction and transport minister János Lázár. After the poll he won a seat in parliament, but resigned it a few weeks ago upon revealing that he had accepted a senior international position with the Chinese BYD group — a firm he (and the Hungarian state) had previously supported with hundreds of billions of forints.

BYD’s first European factory, currently under construction in Szeged, is due to begin operations in the fourth quarter of 2026.Police have since declined to open a criminal investigation into allegations of bribery connected with the appointment, citing lack of suspicion of an offence; however, the parliamentary National Security Committee continues to examine potential national-security risks arising from Szijjártó’s new role.

World.title: Croatia Buys South Korean Rocket Launchers as Regional Arms Race Accelerates
World.content:
Boo-hwan Lee, chairman of Hanwha’s board of directors (L) and Croatian Defence Minister Ivan Anusic. Photo: MORH/F.Klen.

Croatia signed contracts on Thursday with South Korean company Hanwha Aerospace to buy 18 Chunmoo K239 self-propelled multiple rocket launchers worth 435.2 million euros, excluding VAT, which Hanwha will deliver by 2029. The total cost of the deal, including VAT, training, missiles and spare parts, was not disclosed.

The government in Zagreb previously said the system’s advantages include its ability to use missiles of different calibres, flexibility, strong firepower and a very short reaction time.

The same launchers have already been purchased by Norway, Estonia and Poland, which also produce missiles for the system.

On Thursday, Defence Minister Ivan Anusic also signed a contract with Polish company WB Electronics to deliver and integrate a command-and-control system for the launchers.

“With this type of weaponry, Croatia is gaining capabilities that it does not currently have, or has ever had,” Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said at the contract-signing ceremony.

The Chunmoo K239 launchers “will complement the contracted HIMARS systems, increase the range and firepower of the Croatian Army, diversify supply routes and further strengthen deterrence,” the Prime Minister added, referring to the missile system that Croatia previously ordered from the United States.

Anusic said the Chunmoo launchers, “along with the [French] Rafale [fighter jets] will be the strongest and most striking force” of the Croatian armed forces.

He stressed that this is not a “one-way relationship” with South Korea, as the Croatian company Koncar will also be involved in implementing the project.

The Defence Minister praised the South Korean arms industry for its “very affordable price, top quality and very fast delivery”, which he said was crucial in current geopolitical circumstances.

Boo-hwan Lee, chairman of Hanwha’s board of directors, emphasised that the company wants to “continue and deepen cooperation with Croatia” and “focus on the transfer of technology and knowledge”. He called Croatia a “long-term partner” and expressed hope that South Korea’s defence industry will “find a place” there.

Beside the contract with the Korean company, Croatia’s and South Korea’s defence ministries signed a memorandum of understanding.

Croatia’s eastern neighbour, Serbia, is meanwhile also arming itself, as a kind of arms race continues to develop in the region.

During the official visit of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to Serbia and the Serbia-Uzbekistan Business Forum held in Belgrade on Tuesday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announced that Serbia will start producing long-range ballistic missiles.

“Within a year, we will start producing long-range ballistic missiles, and we are ready to cooperate with you [Uzbekistan] on that matter as well,” Vucic said to Mirziyoyev, adding that Serbia is already producing shorter-range ballistic missiles.

“We are making progress in our defence industry. We are receiving technology transfers from some powers, while we are providing [technology] to others,” Vucic said.

World.title: Hague Prosecutors Seek Six Years for Kosovo’s Thaci for Obstructing Justice
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Hashim Thaci in court on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Photo: Screenshot/Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The Kosovo Specialist Prosecutor’s Office in The Hague on Thursday demanded six years’ imprisonment for former President Hashim Thaci on obstruction of justice charges, days before the announcement of the verdict in his other trial for war crimes.

Thaci is being tried alongside four co-defendants in the obstruction of justice case for interfering with witnesses in his war crimes trial.

“The prosecution asks that you impose … nine months of imprisonment for [Hajredin] Kuci; three years for [Fadil] Fazliu; three years for [Isni] Kilaj; three years for [Bashkim] Smakaj; and six years for Thaci,” prosecutor Joshua Hafetz said during closing statements.

The prosecution claims Thaci told the other four defendants to give instructions to certain witnesses in the war-crimes case about to what to say in court. Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Prosecutor Hafetz highlighted that the prosecution wants the six years in prison for Thaci “to be served consecutively to any sentence that might be imposed” at his war crimes and crimes against humanity trial alongside three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders: Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi.

The verdict in the war crimes case will be announced on September 16. All four have plead not guilty.

Hafetz told the court on Thursday that the evidence of obstruction of justice consists of around 28 hours of recordings of Thaci during nine separate visits over four months at the Detention Centre in The Hague.

“What was important to Thaci and his co-defendants was that the witnesses Thaci had chosen for intervention should say and do what Thaci wanted,” Hafetz told the court.

He added that whenever Thaci instructed Kuci, Fazliu, Kilaj and Smakaj, he “lowered his voice and whispered to give specific instructions on what the visitors should say to the witnesses. He did this for months and his instructions had a similar practice; to dilute the charges in [the war crimes case]”.

Prosecutor Kimberly West told the court during the closing statements that Thaci, “together with his collaborators in this process, attempted to obstruct this process by interfering with the testimonies of these witnesses and was caught. He was caught with many hours of recordings and documents confirming the recordings in question.”

West said the instructions went from asking witnesses to change their testimony to denying Thaci’s presence in a place where crimes were allegedly committed, so that the testimonies fit “his narrative”.

The prosecution claimed that the evidence, parts of which were found at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci, was printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use, and discussed during visits to the same centre.

Hafetz also claimed that Thaci tried to influence two former KLA fighters, Bislim Zyrapi and Rrustem Mustafa, who were testifying in his war crimes case. The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

In his testimony in 2023, former KLA area commander Mustafa claimed that the KLA zone commanders made operational decisions, not the guerrilla force’s General Staff. He said the KLA’s leaders, who included Thaci, did not have control over lower-ranking fighters – testimony that bolstered the defence’s case.

Zyrapi, former chief of the KLA’s General Staff, gave his testimony in 2024.

During defence questioning, he said the General Staff often was not informed of the actions of fighters in the KLA’s operational zones and that, despite attempts, it had not been possible for the KLA to fully exercise control over its lower-level units, partly because of Serbian offensives.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Convicted Bosnian Serb Wartime Minister Makes New Release Plea
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

A lawyer for the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mico Stanisic has asked the UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in The Hague to free him early on the grounds that he has served two-thirds of his sentence.

Stanisic previously requested early release in November 2024, but was turned down.

His lawyer, Slobodan Zecevic, said the amount of jail time he had served reaches the threshold required for early release under the law in Poland, where Stanisic is serving his sentence.

Stanisic was the interior minister of Bosnia’s Serb-dominated entity, Republika Srpska, during Bosnia’s 1992-5 war.

The Hague Tribunal sentenced him to 22 years in prison for persecution, murder and torture under a final verdict in 2016.

As evidence of Stanisic’s rehabilitation, his submission to the International Residual Mechanism states that Stanisic served his sentence in a multi-ethnic prison and has had friendly relations with inmates of different ethnic backgrounds.

It also notes that during his time in prison no disciplinary proceedings were brought against him.

“The petitioner claims that, especially given the length of his sentence, his behaviour manifests a great level of re-socialisation,” the submission says.

“After almost 20 years from his voluntary surrender, and more than 32 years from the time the crimes were committed, the sentence already served by the petitioner not only reduces the likelihood of further criminal conduct but also contributes to reconciliation within the community where the crimes had been committed,” it adds.

Stanisic voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal in March 2005 and his trial began in September 2009, alongside his co-defandant, Stojan Zupljanin, the wartime head of the regional police centre in Banja Luka. Zupljanin was convicted of persecution, murder, torture and extermination.

According to Stanisic’s application for early release, if he is permitted to leave prison he will live at the family home in Belgrade and has the financial resources – a pension – to support himself.
