World.title: The innovative and lucrative athletics format sidelining some of its stars
World.content:
World Athletics is set for its latest attempt at a slimmed-down, cashed-up event, with the so-called Ultimate Championship starting Saturday morning (AEST) in Budapest.

The event starts less than a week after the conclusion of the Diamond League season, with all the bells and whistles expected from a track and field meet trying to cut through on a global stage.

Winners will receive US$150,000 ($209,530) and even the eighth-placed athletes picking up a six-figure pay cheque as part of an overall US$10 million ($14 million) purse.

Held over three straight night sessions, the track at Hungary's Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre will illuminate to highlight the event happening in that moment.

Rather than a lengthy program including qualifying runs, there will be just one final for many events and semis in the 100m, 200m, 400m and hurdles races.

Loading Instagram content

In a year without an Olympics or world championships, World Athletics president Sebastian Coe said the event will answer a simple but important question.

"Who's the best?" he said.

"Nobody goes into the sport to figure out who's second best, they go in wanting to know who the best is. And I think at the end of these championships we will have gone a long way to identifying that."

To confirm that, there will be no podiums, only weighty prize purses and bragging rights between the 381 fierce competitors.

Patterson claims Diamond League final title Eleanor Patterson continues her outstanding season by winning the women's high jump at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Most of the traditional track events will be contested (although 3,000m steeplechase, 10,000m and race walking are out) with only Olympic gold medallists, world champions and the current top-ranked athletes invited.

That includes Australian sprint stars Lachlan Kennedy in the 100m and Torrie Lewis in the 200m; Sarah Billings in the 800m; Abbey Caldwell, Jessica Hull and Cameron Myers in the 1,500m; and Ky Robinson, Rose Davies and Hull in the 5,000m.

Diamond League winner Eleanor Patterson and world champion Nicola Olyslagers will compete in the women's high jump, while Commonwealth Games gold medallists Kurtis Marchall (pole vault) and Mackenzie Little (javelin) are also competing.

As part of the hype around the meet, World Athletics held a catwalk fashion event before a televised lane draft for the 200m, allowing athletes to choose which heat and lane they will run in.

Torrie Lewis will race in a stacked semifinal heat. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot/World Athletics)

The draft order was based on world rankings, with American Olympic champion Gabby Thomas picking first and placing herself in lane seven of the first semifinal heat.

World 100m and 200m champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, made the next selection and placed herself right inside her US teammate, kicking off the mind games early.

Lewis, choosing 10th, selected the outside lane in that first race and immediately going up against the best of the best.

"It is the confidence for me," 2008 Olympic 100m hurdles gold medallist Dawn Harper-Nelson said as she hosted the event.

"This is what the lane draft is about."

Coe said the innovations on display would show what the sport can be in the future, but that may sound some alarm bells for those athletes and disciplines without an invitation to Budapest.

Discus did not make the cut for the Ultimate Championship. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The field program is very restrictive, with men's and women's events for high jump, javelin, long jump and pole vault, while only men's hammer throw and women's triple jump made the cut.

That left many on the outside looking in, including Australian discus star Matt Denny, who said the Ultimate Championship highlighted "a bigger issue in our sport".

The payday and spotlight could be life changing for track and field athletes who travel the world to compete without many opportunities for the sort of prize money afforded to other sports stars.

"I support the concept of the Ultimate Championships," Denny wrote on Instagram.

"Athletics needs innovation. We need to improve the broadcast product, attract new audiences and find better ways to grow the sport.

"But innovation should not come at the expense of opportunity."

Loading Instagram content

The main argument for the disciplines that were included boiled down to a lack of audience interest in those that missed out, but Denny said that was an unfair metric when it is not athletes who make broadcasting decisions.

"When events are minimally shown on broadcasts for the last 20 years, you lose the reasoning to say people don't want to watch," he wrote.

"You cannot control what gets shown, what gets promoted, whose stories are told and which events receive the greatest exposure, then simply point to the result numbers as proof that people do not care about everything else.

"If an event is struggling for attention, before deciding the event is the problem, we should be asking whether we have genuinely given it the opportunity to succeed."

The post received praise from fellow omitted athletes like Australian hammer throw national champion Steph Ratcliffe, race walker Rhydian Cowley and American shot put great Chase Jackson.

But even invited athletes like Dutch 400m star Lieke Klaver and European javelin champion Julian Weber backed Denny's sentiments, with Weber praising the post as "so true".

World.title: Nursing graduates face 'trial by fire' during rural program, study finds
World.content:
Danielle Rogers did not know what to expect when she moved to Monto — more than 400 kilometres north-west of Brisbane — to complete her graduate nursing program in 2010.

"I think I cried all the way there," she said.

But her three-year stint in the rural town inspired the Hervey Bay researcher's post-doctoral study.

While Dr Rogers learned a lot through her experience, she discovered newly graduated nurses were underprepared for the medical challenges common in rural and remote health facilities.

Danielle Rogers completed her post-graduate training nursing program in the rural Queensland town of Monto. (Supplied: CQ University)

A CQUniversity report, authored by Dr Rogers and released last month, found rural and remote nurses were expected to provide medical assistance for a range of highly complex health issues with limited training and resources.

Advocates believe funding for programs designed to prepare nurses for remote work is key to retaining people in areas with chronic staff shortages.

'Sink or swim'

For her report, Dr Rogers interviewed more than 60 nurses and medical experts about their experiences working at health services in Australia's remote regions.

Roughly half of these respondents completed nursing programs in rural Queensland.

A key concern identified was the onboarding process for new nurses, which involved senior staff explaining the new responsibilities and how the service operated.

Dr Rogers examined how prepared newly graduated nurses were before completing their one-year program at a rural health facility. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Dr Rogers said rural nurses must be equipped to respond to "a diverse range of [medical] presentations" not often seen in metropolitan areas, such as farming accidents, with limited support.

But multiple participants reported feeling overwhelmed by their new workload because it did not always align with their skill level or prior training.

"There were a lot of comments about [how] they were sent in to sink or swim or felt it was a trial by fire," Dr Rogers said.

Queensland Nurses and Midwives Union secretary Sarah Beaman said it was tricky for new nurses to make the transition into rural health centres.

"Any clinician entering these sites are job ready but if they've come from a metropolitan environment, they feel underprepared particularly when faced with emergency presentations and limited on-site support," Ms Beaman said.

Several respondents said they were underprepared for the complex medical challenges found in rural and remote communities. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Most interviewees were forced to use their professional development leave to attend essential courses about improving their existing skills.

But they said the sessions largely focused on the experience of metropolitan nurses.

"One person said they did a course [about] advanced life support and the instructor told them to hit a button and the team would come," Dr Rogers said.

"They asked, 'Well, there's only two nurses, what do we do in a situation like that?' And the instructor said, 'Oh well, that's not what we're teaching today'."

Minimal support available

Nurses were told the best place to voice concerns was with their direct line managers.

But staffing constraints meant it was not always practical to seek guidance from veteran workers.

"Because senior nurses were so tired and burnt out, the education and support which may have been available was difficult to access," Dr Rogers said.

"They [graduates] felt like they had to learn and debrief from each other."

Multiple nurses reported their mental health declined over the course of their training program due to geographical isolation, financial woes and growing workloads. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Many nurses said that, over time, their mental health declined due to geographic isolation, growing caseloads and financial insecurity.

"The increased pressure to look after patients with persistent shortages can lead to burnout and stress," Ms Beaman said.

The report found the ongoing pressures often resulted in nurses moving to metropolitan areas upon completing their graduate program.

Support options are available for rural nurses in Queensland, including a 24/7 crisis hotline and grants to cover initial accommodation and travel costs.

But Ms Beaman said more incentives were desperately needed.

More training opportunities needed

Queensland Health's 2025 Workplace Gap Analysis found more than 17 per cent of nurses in rural facilities were entry-level employees.

A separate statistic from the Wide Bay Health and Hospital Service revealed about 5 per cent of the 234 nurses currently working at rural health services across the region were newly graduated nurses.

Despite the negative experiences uncovered in Dr Rogers's study, Ms Beaman said rural placements were an incredible training ground for prospective graduates.

"You get to work to an optimised scope of practice and provide high-level care when needed," she said.

Sarah Beaman says more funding is needed for education courses focused on rural nursing experience. (ABC News: Jack McKay)

But she said prospective workers were deterred from accepting rural nursing programs due to inequitable access to learning and limited professional development options.

Ms Beaman said the current curriculum should be updated to include "transition programs specific to the daily experience of rural and remote nurses".

"They need to look at low-cost staff housing options and training support to entice people to work in communities with low staffing numbers," she said.

A Queensland Health spokesperson said the department was "building more staff accommodation and providing incentives such as paid professional-development leave, relocation costs and bonus payments".

World.title: Sydney Olympic Park Metro Station development plans released
World.content:
Sydney Olympic Park will be home to a four-platform metro station, the only one its size on Sydney's rapidly expanding metro network, aimed at easing transport headaches at the major events hub.

Plans for the new Olympic Park Metro Station, unveiled on Friday, also include a public plaza and two new high-rise residential towers.

The station will be designed to accommodate about 25,000 passengers per hour, in addition to the existing heavy rail station that has capacity for 40,000 passengers per hour.

The station will be designed to accommodate about 25,000 passengers per hour. (Supplied: NSW government)

Transport Minister John Graham said Olympic Park's potential had been "hampered" by a lack of transport links.

"That will change as this metro opens.

"Above all, it'll mean an end to that rush for the train at the end of a big event as people try and get out of there," he said.

"Instead, they'll be much more open to hanging around the precinct, staying for a good time after the event rather than racing for the train."

The station will also have wider walkways, extra escalators and a special configuration allowing those arriving to exit off one platform, while those waiting to board would enter from another.

A render of the proposed metro station's mezzanine. (Supplied: NSW government)

Business Western Sydney executive director David Borger said the four platforms would help deal with "massive crowd surges" during major events.

"At the moment, we know that the loop train line that was built for the Olympics is challenging, people have to interchange at Lidcombe," he said.

"This is going to improve access for major sporting events. Olympic Park often lacks people, the people are coming and the trains are going to ensure that they come."

Hopes metro link will spur housing development

A render of the proposed metro station platform. (Supplied: NSW government)

The new residential towers associated with the development will each be 42 and 32 storeys, containing about 500 apartments.

Mr Graham said while it was a "good start", the new metro station would make housing development in surrounding areas more attractive.

"As this precinct becomes more connected, what you're going to see is it really comes to life, and that'll be true both in a sports and entertainment sense, but also from a housing point of view," he said.

Work has already begun on the steel rail track. (Supplied: NSW government)

A master plan by the NSW government for the wider Sydney Olympic Park contains plans for up to 15,000 homes by 2050.

That would include up to 20 per cent affordable housing on government-owned land and five per cent on private land.

Mr Borger said once the metro opens, people living in the area would be within a half-hour commute of more than 800,000 jobs, compared with the current 70,000 jobs.

Construction on the new metro station is expected to begin about mid-2027, with the Metro West currently slated for completion in 2032.

World.title: BHP subsidiary class action begins over public holiday work
World.content:
A class action has been launched against Australia's biggest mining company, BHP, months after the Federal Court found one of its subsidiaries improperly required employees to work on public holidays.

The Federal Court ruled last year that Operations Services (OS), a subsidiary of BHP, breached the Fair Work Act by requiring 85 employees to work on Christmas Day 2019 at the Daunia mine near Moranbah, in Central Queensland.

The new class action, which will be run by Sydney-based AEN Legal on behalf of two lead plaintiffs, will be funded by the Mining and Energy Union (MEU).

MEU Queensland president Mitch Hughes said the action potentially covered about 7,000 employees, which included workers who were employed by OS between December 2019 and March 2023.

BHP subsidiary Operations Services employs workers in WA, Qld, SA and NSW. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

During that time, OS employed people across coal mines in Queensland and NSW, iron ore operations in WA and copper mines in SA.

"That'll probably narrow down, depending on the scope," he said.

Mr Hughes said the employees' concerns included a lack of consultation by OS management before allocating shifts.

"In some cases, we heard accounts from the workforce where everyone's name was simply put into a hat, and they were selected [to work public holidays]."

He said BHP would typically run a "skeleton crew" across Christmas and Boxing Day and described the decision to keep the mines running at full production in recent years as "ruling with an iron fist".

Operations Services provides a variety of production and maintenance services to BHP mines. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

In a statement, BHP said the "proceedings remain before the Court and no findings have been made in relation to the claims".

It said it would not comment further because the matter was "ongoing".

Mr Hughes said the court action was designed to build on last year's Federal Court decision, which was specific to the Daunia mine workers of 2019.

In his judgement, Justice Darryl Rangiah detailed some of the circumstances in which the miners left their families to work on Christmas and Boxing Day.

BHP ordered to backpay for holidays The Mining and Energy Union wins an appeal, arguing the mine operated for the pure purpose of profit over the public holiday period.

In one instance, a single mother paid $500 for a babysitter for her two children when she went to work.

In another, a man missed out on time in New Zealand with his young daughter, who he had planned to visit.

Others said they were able to spend some time at Christmas celebrations, but were forced to depart early to attend work, upsetting family members.

BHP has appealed the Federal Court decision, which is set to be heard on November 9.

World.title: Farmer's legacy lives on in wildflower he discovered before tragic death
World.content:
A West Australian farmer who died fighting a devastating bushfire has been posthumously honoured with a native flowering plant he discovered two years before his death.

Ravensthorpe Shire deputy president and farmer Mark Mudie died in December last year while battling a blaze at West River that destroyed more than 5,000 hectares of farmland.

The plant, believed to be a hybrid species of hakea, is being planted today in Ravensthorpe, about 500 kilometres south of Perth, to remember and celebrate his life.

Nathan Mudie says his father often picked wildflowers for his mother. (ABC Esperance: Andrew Williams)

Mr Mudie's son Nathan said his father often wandered the bushland around the community, drawn to region's native flora.

"I remember the day dad found it, driving in the truck during seeding, and he called me up and said, 'I found a plant that I've never seen before'," he said.

"I didn't think much of it, but he was very excited about it and got some samples taken away.

" It was a bit of a rare thing to have out in our area, but Dad was very proud to find it. "

Mark Mudie discovered the plant in a gravel pit in Ravensthorpe. (Supplied: Sue Leighton)

Sitting adjacent to the Fitzgerald River National Park, the region's biodiversity attracts visitors from around Australia every year for its natural wildflower displays.

Nathan Mudie said the flowers were one of his father's passions, which he often shared with the family.

"He quite enjoyed the wildflower season in Ravensthorpe and used to always pick a bunch of wildflowers and bring it back home for Mum," he said.

"He was right into his wildflowers."

Sue Leighton believes the plant discovered is a hakea hybrid. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding )

Plant returned to family

Ravensthorpe Wildflower Show and Herbarium coordinator Sue Leighton said Mark Mudie would often send her photos of flowers he saw to learn their names.

When he discovered the unusual hakea, she was one of the first people he called.

"He sent me a photo and said, 'Sue, I don't know what this is, I've never seen it before?'" Ms Leighton said.

"He sent a picture of this hakea that was about two-and-a-half metres high and about two-and-a-half wide and full of big blooms on it."

Wildflowers on display at the Ravensthorpe Herbarium. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Ms Leighton said three of the herbarium staff went out to examine the plant and take cuttings for further examination.

"One taxonomist has said that it's just a subspecies of another one, but there's never been any seed on it at all, so we do believe it is a hybrid," she said.

"I've got those two plants that Kings Park has given us, and we're doing a ceremony planting of the one that will go in the herbarium garden at Ravensthorpe, and the other one will go to his wife, Elaine."

Digby Growns says the plant warranted horticultural attention. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Kings Park senior plant breeder Digby Growns said it was an impressive specimen, and worthy of horticultural attention.

"It was covered in these globular flowers, similar to Hakea laurina, and we presumed it was a hybrid with that species and another unknown species," he said.

Mr Growns took several cuttings in a bid to propagate the plant.

"First to bring it into cultivation and protect it, given there was only a single plant," he said.

"And then to have a look at it, to see if there was any opportunity for making it commercially available."

Digby Growns says the plant was similar to the Hakea laurina known to grow in the area. (Supplied: Sue Leighton)

Mudie Surprise

Ms Leighton said it could take years for the taxonomy of the plant to be finalised, but the herbarium was hoping, in time, the hakea could be named in honour of Mark Mudie.

"If it was something that could be grown as a hybrid, it could be given a name," she said.

" It won't have a species name on it, it will just have a trade name ... It could be called Mudie Surprise. "

Nathan Mudie said with just the planting of the hakea, the remembrance and recognition of his father's discovery had touched the family.

"It's a very nice tribute that the community and everyone's decided to do, and for us as a family, it was very, very touching for us, and it's very nice to be here," he said.

"I think he'll be very proud of that and of how the community rallied together, and it shows the person that he was."

World.title: Houthis advance along Yemeni coast, threaten Saudi oil exports in Red Sea
World.content:
Iran-aligned Houthis have seized Yemen's port city of Mocha and advanced towards strategic islands overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as Iranian strikes have damaged US fighter aircraft at a base in Jordan.

The developments marked an escalation on two fronts of the Iran war on Thursday, hours after US President Donald Trump said he expected the conflict to end after the US midterm elections.

Yemeni government military sources said the Houthis had gained further leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes, and had reached the Hanish Islands.

If the Houthis gain control of the waterway, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their backer Iran leverage over a second major transit corridor and further disrupt global energy supplies.

It could also complicate Mr Trump's efforts to find an exit from a war that has hurt his Republican Party's electoral prospects ahead of the November midterms.

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces react during what they say to be clashes with Iran-aligned Houthis in Al-Hazm, Yemen. (Reuters: Media Centre of the Yemeni Armed Forces)

Yemen's Houthi-run humanitarian operations coordination centre said Red Sea navigation was safe for all shipping companies except Saudi vessels.

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, has relied heavily on the Red Sea route since the Iran conflict effectively closed Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of global oil supplies previously flowed.

Yemeni government forces and their allies are relocating south along the Red Sea coast to Dhubab on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, across from Perim Island, government military sources said. Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said.

UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg told the Security Council on Thursday that the international community must act to address "a new and more dangerous phase" in the Yemen war.

The Houthis' capture of Mocha gave them "a direct presence on the approaches to one of the world's most vital straits", raising serious concerns about freedom of navigation, he said.

Yemeni government forces and their allies are relocating south along the Red Sea coast. (Reuters)

Jenifer Neidhart de Ortiz, the US representative at the meeting, accused the Houthis of acting as "agents and tools of Iran".

"This escalation is unacceptable, and those who enable it bear responsibility for its consequences," she said.

Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources told Reuters the Houthi advance down the coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said, without elaborating, that the group's operations were defensive and would stop once attacks on Yemen stopped.

Brent crude rose as much as 4 per cent on Thursday to above $US105 a barrel as traders weighed the threat to another major shipping route.

Yemen's Houthi rebels march during a mobilisation campaign in Sanaa, Yemen. (AP Photo)

The US national average diesel price also surpassed $US6 a gallon for the first time, according to price tracker GasBuddy.

After joining the war with an attack on Israel in March, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July and escalated attacks this month.

Houthis launch fresh strikes on Saudi oil facilities The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have the potential to disrupt the world's energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi civil defence authorities issued emergency alerts in the south-western city of Khamis Mushait for the fourth time in 24 hours as the Houthis attacked.

Pakistan has delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in the Houthis in an effort to prevent the crisis from spiralling, Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources said.

A senior Iranian official said Tehran's response was: "Iran does not control the Houthis".

The fighting comes during the biggest declared wave of US-Iran tit-for-tat attacks on Gulf shipping since the war began in late February.

Iran strikes damage US aircraft in Jordan

Iranian strikes on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan damaged several US military aircraft this week, a US official told Reuters.

One A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, lost a wing in Tuesday's attack, while about eight F-15 fighter jets sustained light damage and were returned to service, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The losses add to mounting damage to US military assets since the war began.

A May report from the Congressional Research Service said 42 US military aircraft had already been lost or damaged in the conflict, including more than two dozen drones.

Iran attacks US base in Jordan Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it fired ballistic missiles at a base in Jordan used by the US military and attacked 10 ships on Wednesday after the US said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers.

Eighteen US service members have been killed and more than 800 injured since the war began in February.

The attack on the Jordan base came after US forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. Washington said the strikes were retaliation for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps twice targeting a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles over the previous two days.

US forces fired about 30 Patriot interceptors to counter the Iranian missiles, the US official said, amid growing concern about US stocks of air defence missiles.

While inventory numbers are classified, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated about 65 per cent of US Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, leaving fewer than 850 on hand compared with 2,330 before the war.

Iran has also struck the US Navy's Fifth Fleet headquarters at Naval Support Activity Bahrain.

Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao described the extent of the damage in an interview with the Epoch Times, saying Iran had "blew the hell out of Bahrain".

Trump sees war ending after midterms

The war and higher fuel prices have helped drive Mr Trump's popularity to record lows, according to polls.

He accused Iran of trying to influence the midterm elections, which will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress.

Donald Trump at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas. (Reuters: Callaghan O'Hare)

"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," Mr Trump told reporters on Wednesday.

The US president has previously set other deadlines for the war to end.

Trump looks for exit in protracted war The Iran war is showing signs it could drag on into next year as Iran seemingly looks to prolong Donald Trump's political pain for as long as possible.

In recent weeks, Washington had cited increasing success guiding tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.

But renewed fighting this month appears to have set back efforts to reopen the waterway.

Just seven vessels transited the strait on Wednesday, about half the 10-day average, preliminary ship-tracking data showed.

Iranian state media said on Thursday the Revolutionary Guards Navy had struck a US unmanned vessel at the entrance to Hormuz.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: NSW premier's top staffer in High Court showdown over arrest powers
World.content:
A showdown between the New South Wales premier's top staffer and the upper house has played out in the High Court over whether he can be arrested and hauled before a parliamentary inquiry.

Powers dating back to the 19th century were declared non-existent by the NSW Court of Appeal last December after Chris Minns's chief of staff, James Cullen, launched a legal challenge.

Mr Cullen faced detention and being forced to give evidence before a committee after he refused to attend its inquiry into the leaking of confidential minutes.

Others have since used the ruling to dodge questioning by the state's elected representatives.

James Cullen, who appeared at the Dural caravan plot inquiry last June, is involved in a High Court showdown. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

An appeal by Legislative Council president Ben Franklin was heard on Thursday before Chief Justice Stephen Gageler, and Justices Michelle Gordon, James Edelman, Jacqueline Gleeson and Robert Beech-Jones.

A phalanx of 14 barristers spread across the bar table in Canberra, with the Commonwealth, South Australia and Northern Territory intervening in the case and Liberal MLC Damien Tudehope appearing as a non-party helping the court.

The case concerns the validity of sections 7 to 9 of the Parliamentary Evidence Act 1901, which provide a process for arresting a witness who fails to appear and give evidence when summoned.

The president may "certify" the witness's non-attendance to a Supreme Court judge, who then "shall" issue an arrest warrant to bring the person before a chamber or committee to give evidence.

The NSW premier's top chief of staff is in a high court showdown over whether he can be arrested. (ABC News: Liam Patrick )

It is the role of the judge that the Court of Appeal deemed the "constitutional vice" of the scheme because it made the judge a "mere functionary" with "no choice but to sign and seal the warrant".

The Court decided this substantially impaired the "institutional integrity" required of state courts under the Australian Constitution, as it gave an "appearance of judicial authority" to a decision already made "in substance" by the president.

Taxpayers set to foot huge legal bill

The president's legal team, led by Bret Walker, SC, argued the Court of Appeal's conclusion was "inconsistent with the history of the constitution and the assumptions on which it was framed".

In written submissions, Mr Walker pointed to the fact the warrant power in the 1901 Act was first conferred upon the Supreme Court 20 years earlier in the Parliamentary Evidence Act 1881.

"That suggests that, at the time of Federation, the function was not thought to be incompatible with the independence and impartiality of the Supreme Court," Mr Walker wrote.

"The Constitution assumes that, at Federation, the Supreme Courts were independent and impartial tribunals."

Taxpayers are set to foot a huge legal bill regardless of the winner. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

According to an outline of his oral argument, Mr Walker said if a judge could scrutinise the basis for an arrest warrant, it would be inconsistent with a Bill of Rights prohibition on courts interfering with proceedings in parliament.

Brendan Lim, SC, for Mr Cullen, said this principle was "a shield, not a sword", according to a summary of his oral argument.

"[It] can explain why a court does not interfere with the intra-mural affairs of Parliament but not why a court may be required to lend its authority to such an intra-mural affair," Mr Lim said.

Whoever wins, taxpayers will foot a huge legal bill.

At budget estimates in August, Clerk of the Parliaments and Clerk of the Legislative Council Steven Reynolds revealed the original action cost $443,518 to defend.

The case is about the validity of sections 7 to 9 of the Parliamentary Evidence Act 1901. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The High Court appeal, Mr Reynolds said, cost $384,620 as of July.

He added the president was ordered to pay costs of about $250,000 to Mr Cullen, whose fees are being covered by a government grant.

NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said on Thursday it was "absolutely appalling".

"The premier's own chief of staff is using hundreds of thousands of dollars of taxpayers' money to avoid scrutiny," Ms Sloane said.

"It is an outrageous undermining of our democracy in NSW."

Mr Cullen declined to comment.

Kellie Sloane commented on the situation. (ABC News: Warick Ford)

Public paying more than legal bill

The public is paying another price: its capacity to interrogate government activity and other matters of public importance, through its elected representatives, is diminished.

NSW premier's fight with chamber that keeps him in check The NSW premier faced an extraordinary question this week amid a deteriorating relationship between his government and the Legislative Council.

As Mr Reynolds told estimates, three key witnesses declined to appear at an inquiry into identity protections, citing the Cullen ruling, and numerous others refused to front a committee probing data centres.

"Witnesses now, it's widely known that they can't be compelled to attend," Mr Reynold said.

Mr Franklin told estimates the issue caused him significant concern.

"The problem with this broadly is that the people who we particularly need to appear and want to appear, I suspect, are the ones going to be most likely to avail themselves of the opportunity not to appear," Mr Franklin said.

The Coalition has introduced legislation to restore the powers to force witnesses to front inquiries, but the government has refused to consider it pending the High Court appeal.

World.title: Alleged arsonist charged over 11 fires across northern Tasmania
World.content:
A man has been charged with arson and other offences in relation to 11 separate fires in northern Tasmania, including a significant blaze that destroyed power poles and took 20 fire crews to contain.

Tasmania Police charged a 29-year-old Nile man with arson earlier this year over three fires, including a fire at a public toilet block in the town of Perth.

Longford Police and the Tasmania Fire Service have been investigating a spate of fires between August 2025 and April 2026 spanning from Perth to Ulverstone.

Police say he has been charged over eight other allegedly deliberately lit fires, including at Longford, Sassafras, Whitemore and Breadalbane.

The Breadalbane fire burnt through thick gorse and vegetation alongside the Midland Highway on April 20.

Police said the Breadalbane fire damaged local power infrastructure. (ABC News)

Police described the fire as "significant", saying it resulted in power poles being destroyed and local power outages.

There were no injuries.

Inspector Craig Fox said the Breadalbane fire had placed the public at risk.

He said investigations into other fires were ongoing.

"We are continuing to look at several fires within the region," Inspector Fox said.

The man will next appear in court on September 24.

World.title: The raw, moving reality check Australian fiction needs
World.content:
CultureBooksReview The raw, moving reality check Australian fiction needs David Free September 11, 2026 — 11:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The world chronicled in Max Easton’s Now, Autonomy is both familiar and foreign. Set in Sydney’s inner west, the novel is peppered with local landmarks and place names: Newtown, Homebush, Parramatta Road, Central Station, Hyde Park, the QVB, the Marrickville Bowling Club. In that sense, the terrain of Easton’s book is commonplace. But the social world his characters live in is offbeat, at least by the standards of Australian fiction. Most Australian novels are – let’s face it – middle-class affairs. The characters in them don’t tend to be haunted, on a monthly basis, by the question of how to keep a roof over their heads. Writer Max Easton has a gift of caring for his characters. Lauren Eiko This is why Easton’s work feels like a breath of fresh air, even if the air is thick with the smell of traffic fumes and pub carpets and inner-city squats. Easton’s characters belong to the urban working class, or perhaps underclass. They’re smart young people who’ve been shut out of the modern economy or have voluntarily subtracted themselves from it. Either way, Easton’s people are outsiders. They work menial jobs, never getting enough shifts to lift themselves beyond a hand-to-mouth existence. They play punk music, publish zines and find a sense of purpose in radical politics. They love their city but feel alienated by its materialism. Walking up George Street en route to a march for Palestine, they pass franchise stores they’ve never heard of, “whole shops dedicated to watches and handbags and cosmetics”.



Photo: Now, Autonomy is the third novel in a trilogy that has followed the same group of characters from the 1990s up to the present. The connection between the three books is loose. You don’t need to have read the earlier novels to follow the action of this one – or indeed to be seriously moved by it, as I unexpectedly found myself being. I say “unexpectedly” because Easton’s book sneaks up on you. If you don’t come from the same world as his characters, and don’t share their sometimes crude political views, you may start by seeing them as types, defined by their more conspicuous social markers. There’s Sunny, the non-binary they/them firebrand. Pat, the ageing radical. Helen, the bottle-shop clerk and part-time punk bass player who is always “one bad roster away from declaring bankruptcy.” Easton cares about these characters, and has a gift for making you care about them, too. As his older characters slip from youth into middle age, they’re visited by the same grim epiphanies that await us all at that time of life. “At some point,” Pat finds, “life had stopped feeling like something he was living, and more like something he’d lived.” But even in ageing, there’s a class dimension. Easton’s older characters don’t just feel that life has passed them by. They also finally see that the economy has left them behind, and isn’t coming back for them. They want autonomy, but autonomy costs more money than they’ll ever have. Helen, at 38, feels as if she’s holding the social ladder that all her former friends have ascended. “We’re still living like we’re in our 20s,” her girlfriend says. “It’s not easy to be our age and still be fighting for scraps.”



Editor's pick Literature prizes Looking for your child’s next favourite book? Start with these award winners The irony, for Easton’s characters, is that they never craved social advancement in the first place. They’ve missed a bus they didn’t want to catch. Their ambitions, as the book proceeds, zero in on a more modest goal, a kind of parody of the great Australian dream. All they want is a squat to call their own — a place where they can rehearse their music and put on shows. The city around them is full of boarded-up buildings that developers have purchased and then left to rot. Is it too much to ask to “take a space back”, and put one of these abandoned ghost-buildings to civilised use? The lives of Easton’s characters aren’t wholly defined by the raw economic deal they’re getting. In the course of being fiscally shafted, they still laugh, love, have relationships, make music, create, age, die. Their lives are as real as any others being lived in today’s Australia. Easton humanely documents a social underworld we think too little about, even though it exists right under our noses. Now, Autonomy by Max Easton is published by Giramondo ($32.95).

World.title: A giant Mao looms over Hong Kong. Welcome to 2030
World.content:
CultureBooksReview A giant Mao looms over Hong Kong. Welcome to 2030 Declan Fry September 11, 2026 — 11:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I first knew Badiucao as the rebel heart dissident exiled in Australia, penning pictures of koalas suckling on Chairman Mao, pandas in red-star caps brandishing severed kangaroo heads decked out in scholarly mortarboards to protest “soft power in Australia”, you name it. He was that kind of guy. Didn’t mind, didn’t take prisoners; if you wanted to see world leaders sodomising each other, he was your man. Some of that spirit animates his and journalist Melissa Chan’s debut graphic novel, You Must Take Part in Revolution, as three young activists befriend each other during Hong Kong’s 2019 Umbrella protests. Dissident and artist Badiucao has released a graphic novel with Melissa Chan called You Must Take Part in Revolution. Wayne Taylor After a bomb attack goes horribly wrong, we skip forward to 2030. Andy, an Asian-American veterinarian, is re-examining his past. Mainlander Maggie’s radicalism sees her imprisoned. Rounding out the trio, Olivia has fled to Taiwan, where the US – now ruled by a right-wing autocrat who seized power in a coup – has an increased presence. (China has taken up shop over in Cuba.) In this future, a giant Mao statue stands over Hong Kong. Neon signs advertise, in simplified Chinese, a two-child policy. It’s all a bit ridiculous: even the mainland has officially (and famously) dubbed Mao “30 per cent wrong”, and a two-child policy was encouraged during British governance of Hong Kong. At least when Chuck Norris saved a Florida mall from those dastardly commies in Joseph Zito’s 1985 hamfest Invasion USA, things were fun!



Photo: Andy remains a good boy, even when he seeks to rebel a little – “American exceptionalism, and American optimism. Too cute,” a wise older activist tells him. That is, until he journeys to Taiwan and becomes a soldier for the US military. Andy doesn’t really know what he’s fighting for (Hong Kong’s freedom, he consoles himself). The narrative, trying to convey multiple cultural, political and linguistic points at once, sometimes gets bogged down in detours. It’s as if it cannot decide which audience to speak to. When Andy writes jia you during the Umbrella protests – an expression meaning “fighting” or “hell yeah” – a conversation ensues between Olivia and Maggie that seems to mock his poor Chinese handwriting. It seems intended for readers who do not understand Chinese but, for those who do, it’s mostly confusing – why would Olivia, a native Chinese speaker, mock Andy’s (basically fine, maybe awkward) handwriting? It doesn’t feel credible or consistent with their camaraderie as three ethnically Chinese comrades from different contexts and geographies finding friendship. At its worst, the book takes itself far more seriously than some of the more gung-ho beats of the plot warrant. More realistic are all the high-tech goggles folks wear in the future: who needs dystopia when tech giants are tightening the screws?



Editor's pick Special feature Watched, followed, threatened. Now an impostor is claiming to be me Life is continually surveilled. An online emoji can cost you your job (a dystopia many local public figures are sadly all too familiar with). Each day, life becomes more unlivable, more poorly serviced, more underpaid – but with more tracking and monitoring as a trade-off. No need to travel to China, either: a quick journey to our Coles/Woolworths duopoly brings you face to face with surveillance and weapons companies like Palantir, whether you’re out shopping, delivering, or in the warehouse. What a deal! During one excellent section, Olivia descends into a hellscape of skulls. Badiucao’s art shines as the narrative shows us a world where hope feels distant: the promises of socialism, capitalism, democracy, communism, take your pick – all compromised by history’s weight, the loss of ideals, the tightening noose of technology and the violence done in the names of all of them. Editor's pick China relations How this brutal work of fiction is becoming terrifying reality A reference to the tragedy of the SARS epidemic that seems to blame China for fatalities in Hong Kong feels on the nose by comparison: at best, it’s ambivalent about political accountability and mishandling of the kind that has beleaguered countless disasters, from Hurricane Katrina to Fukushima in 2011; at worst, it’s tired China-bashing that mixes inferiority complexes (Hong Kong, colonised by EuroAmerica, never quite able to actually be EuroAmerica) with superiority ones (at least we’re not mainlanders!). Of course, any bullied people know it’s easier to be a crab in a bucket and drag down those around you rather than face yourself – never mind the colonial boot that’s actually crushing your face.



Editor's pick Review This 700-page biography, 40 years in the making, is a miracle Olivia, with her conflicting loyalties, is perhaps the book’s strongest and most compelling representation of this dilemma. She shows how a person’s choices – not necessarily their culture or language, their citizenship or political allegiances – can really define who they are. In this respect, the Mao lines that provide the book’s title – “If you want to know the theory and methods of revolution, you must take part in revolution. All genuine knowledge originates in direct experience” – feel both ironic and deadly serious. This is the story of people who are in mourning, dealing with feelings of helplessness and loss. For each of them, China means many things. A language, a culture, but, at the same time, different languages, different cultures, different histories. A place … or is it places? Taiwan, mainland China, Hong Kong, Singapore, more, less? Which dynasty? Qin? Yuan? Which ethnicity? Han? Mongol? Leader? CCP, Chiang Kai-shek, Mao, Kublai Khan? All of which suggests “China” is never a continuous historical entity. There are as many Chinas as there are people who identify with that big, generous word. The grievances, hurts, and pain of different communities, whether they identify as “Chinese” or otherwise – including Asian-Americans; or those who fled the mainland for the West after Tiananmen; or Hong Kong after 1997; or Tibetans, Taiwanese, countless others – have formed all sorts of ways of belonging. Their grip upon the past, Chan and Badiucao suggest, can be an act of courage, of resistance. Yet it can also, they warn, mean fossilising, repeating a narrative instead of recognising that the world has changed and will go on changing.



While our world remains crushed inside a trauma loop of surveillance, bullying and abject violence, what choices will we make? It’s when this question comes into focus that You Must Take Part in Revolution shines. You Must Take Part in Revolution by Melissa Chan and Badiucao is published by Affirm ($40). Badiucao is a cartoonist at The Age. What else is happening in the book world? Looking for a last-minute Father’s Day gift? Try these books Brilliant or boring? World.title: Fierce finals furnace burns on slow-starting Dockers
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Fierce finals furnace burns on slow-starting Dockers Justin Chadwick September 11, 2026 — 11:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fremantle’s horror first-quarter efforts in recent finals will be well and truly in the spotlight when they take on Geelong in Friday night’s blockbuster semi-final showdown in Perth. The Dockers won a club-record 19 games in the regular season on the way to the minor premiership, but are now staring down the barrel of a straight-sets September exit following last week’s shock 32-point loss to Hawthorn. Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir speaks to captain Alex Pearce during last week’s final against Hawthorn. Paul Kane/Getty Images The Hawks kicked four goals to one in the opening term to get a crucial early edge, with the slow start continuing a worrying finals trend for the Dockers. In the four finals played under Justin Longmuir, Fremantle have lost the opening quarters by a combined total of 99-19.



That included returns of 0.1 (1) in both the elimination-final win over the Western Bulldogs in 2022 and the semi-final loss to Collingwood a week later. Against Gold Coast in last year’s elimination final, Fremantle managed 1.2 (8) in the opening quarter. The Suns only managed one goal themselves, but broke the game open with a seven-goal second-quarter blitz on the way to a famous one-point win. The slow starts across four finals have raised big questions about whether Fremantle can handle the big occasion. Longmuir said it was imperative for his team to handle the pressure early against Geelong in order to buck the recent trend.



“A lot of it comes down to what you do off the contest,” Longmuir said. “Finals are more contested. There’s more pressure, both perceived pressure and real pressure, and we just haven’t handled that as well as we could early in games.” Fremantle have recalled former Demons defender Judd McVee to replace the injured Brandon Walker (ankle), while Nathan O’Driscoll was axed in favour of utility Corey Wagner. Geelong go in unchanged from the team that beat Carlton by 33 points in last week’s elimination final, meaning key defender Sam De Koning misses again. Cats veteran Patrick Dangerfield kicked five goals against the Blues and looms as a huge threat to Fremantle’s hopes of winning through to a preliminary final against Sydney at the SCG.



View post on X “Clearly we can’t allow him to have the sort of game he had last week,” Longmuir said. “He’s a star of the competition. He’s been in these situations a lot, and we’ve got to make sure we limit the supply to their forward line, because he’s not the only dangerous forward down there.” Fremantle’s star spearhead trio of Josh Treacy, Jye Amiss and Patrick Voss kicked just two goals between them last week, and the pressure is on them to bounce back against Geelong. World.title: Former Blues president Luke Sayers issues apology to end high-stakes defamation case with ex-wife
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCourts Former Blues president Luke Sayers issues apology to end high-stakes defamation case with ex-wife Christine Lacy September 11, 2026 — 10:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Carlton president Luke Sayers has settled his bitter defamation battle with his ex-wife Cate, with the businessman issuing an apology for the extreme hurt and harm he had caused to the mother of his four daughters. The confidential, eleventh-hour agreement staves off potentially explosive court proceedings that could have severely embarrassed the AFL and several of its most senior executives. Luke and Cate Sayers at the 2023 Brownlow Medal night, before their split. WireImage Cate Sayers sued her ex-husband for defamation in the Supreme Court of Victoria, claiming he had falsely blamed her for publishing a photograph of his penis on his X account in January last year. A female executive at one of Carlton’s sponsors was also tagged in the post. On Friday, lawyers for the former couple told the court they had reached a settlement which would end the proceedings.



The court heard Sayers apologised unreservedly for the suggestion that his former wife had been responsible for posting the lewd picture. “I acknowledge the extreme hurt and harm to Cate Sayers occasioned by the suggestion that has been circulating that she posted or may have posted an explicit image on my X account. I accept that she did not do this. To the extent that I may have suggested otherwise, I apologise unreservedly to her.” In a statement outside the court, Cate said she acknowledged Luke’s public apology. “This brings to a close a painful and difficult chapter that began with extraordinary claims made about me that were accepted without challenge by powerful institutions and powerful people,” she said. “I commenced these proceedings to establish the truth clearly and finally, with Luke’s apology today, I feel I have achieved what I set out to do.”



Cate said she had been overwhelmed by the support she had received from “so many women and others, including many whose reputations have been treated as expendable”. Related Article AFL off-field behaviour Court opens door to keeping AFL documents secret in Sayers defamation battle “I hope today’s outcome gives some strength to you all and to others who may find themselves subjected to circumstances where they too have to stand up and insist that the truth be recognised. “I now intend to move forward with my life with dignity.” She declined to comment on whether the apology from her former husband was accompanied by a monetary settlement.



The court date had already been postponed twice by the warring parties as representatives for Luke, who was a former chief executive of PwC, sought to reach a negotiated settlement with Cate to avoid exposure of how he and his advisers, the AFL and Carlton each handled their roles in managing the explicit picture scandal. Cate Sayers had been asking the court for damages for the “significant distress, hurt and embarrassment” caused by the saga. A statutory declaration sworn by Luke was key to him being cleared of wrongdoing by the AFL for the nude photo publication, but then became the basis for his ex-wife’s defamation case. The document declared that Cate’s denials about posting the explicit picture couldn’t be trusted, that she suffered from mental illness and at times refused to take her medication. It also contained an express request that neither the police nor the AFL interview Cate. Cate claimed the allegations against her spread through AFL circles via the “grapevine effect”, sparking widespread gossip within the football community.



“Cate has been the subject of substantial discussion and gossip within the AFL community, in particular in Victoria, and also Australia wide,” her statement of claim alleged. “Cate has been shunned and avoided by persons she knew and had relationships with, who are involved with the AFL, Carlton, the game of AFL generally and others who knew Luke and Cate.” The AFL’s integrity unit investigation and an internal process at Carlton both found Sayers was not responsible for posting the photo, that his account had been “compromised” and he had not breached any rules. He stepped down as Carlton’s president shortly after those findings. However, both investigations accepted Luke’s sworn statement on face value and did not investigate its veracity. The role of two of the AFL’s most senior executives - executive general manager of corporate affairs Sharon McCrohan and general counsel Stephen Meade - as well as its integrity unit, which is led by Tony Keane, were expected to come under intense scrutiny in the court.



The case had been set to hear the businessman’s arguments to keep material relating to the AFL’s investigation into the scandal secret via legal privilege. Luke was represented in his legal battle with his wife by Arnold Bloch Liebler partner Leon Zwier and Matt Collins, KC. Cate was represented by Rebekah Giles from Giles George and Sue Chrysanthou, SC. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mining stocks tumble to weigh down ASX; oil climbs to its highest mark since May
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Mining stocks tumble to weigh down ASX; oil climbs to its highest mark since May Staff writers Updated September 11, 2026 — 10:34am ,first published September 11, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has fallen sharply at the open with mining stocks plunging, while oil prices climbed to their highest mark since May overnight as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 91.1 points, or 1 per cent, in early trade to 8728.3, with seven of 11 industry sectors in negative territory, led by materials after a Reuters report said the White House has not yet ​made a decision on refined copper tariffs. It comes after the ASX shed 1 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.56¢. Oil climbed to its highest mark since March. AP Australian bonds slid, tracking an overnight slump in Treasuries after escalating Middle East tensions drove up oil prices and fuelled concerns about inflation. The yield on Australia’s three-year notes surged as much as 18 basis points to 5.03 per cent, the highest since May 2011. The yield on 10-year debt jumped 13 basis points to 5.38 per cent. Both levels were the highest since May 2011.



The pain continued for the miners, with losses across the board. BHP dove 4.4 per cent, Rio Tinto 2.9 per cent and Fortescue 2.8 per cent. Bullion was little changed near $US4315 ($6023) an ounce on Friday, after dropping 1.8 per cent in the previous session to the lowest since early August. Northern Star slumped 4 per cent and Evolution Mining 4.2 per cent. Financial stocks climbed, clawing back some of Thursday’s losses. Commonwealth Bank rose 0.3 per cent, National Australia Bank 1.6 per cent, Westpac 0.7 per cent and ANZ Bank 0.6 per cent. Energy stocks advanced as Brent oil rose over $US107 a barrel as deteriorating conditions in the Middle East stoked concerns over global supplies. Fighting has intensified over the past two weeks, including US strikes on Iranian oil tankers, ballistic missile attacks on Jordan, and Houthi assaults on Saudi energy facilities that have forced some operations to halt. A recent pickup in crude purchases by China has also tightened the oil market. “Further attacks on fuel tankers and rhetoric suggest the conflict could extend longer than analysts had modelled,” said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC Private Wealth Group. “Trader chatter remains sceptical of the rally but the reality is that both the expected timeline of the conflict and hopes for a significant normalisation in Gulf flows are being pushed out.” Local energy stocks rose on the jump in crude prices, with Woodside Energy up 1.4 per cent and Santos 1.6 per cent. The refiners also had strong gains, with Ampol up 1.3 per cent and Viva Energy 1.9 per cent.



Related Article Energy Australia softens local gas supply rules, easing fears in Asia Technology stocks followed their Wall Street peers lower with WiseTech down 2.6 per cent, Xero 1.3 per cent, Technology One 1.4 per cent and NEXTDC 2.2 per cent. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.60¢. Overnight, rising crude prices worsened worries about inflation and cranked up pressure within the bond market, helping to send stocks lower again on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent for a fourth-straight loss, its longest such streak since June, though it’s not far from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent.



A report on Thursday said inflation at the US wholesale level accelerated to 5.4 per cent last month from 4.8 per cent in July, and retailers could eventually pass such increases in prices on to shoppers. A report is coming on Friday that will show how much inflation US consumers are feeling. The typical move to rein in high inflation is for the Federal Reserve to raise its main interest rate, the federal funds rate. Such a move then filters out through the rest of the bond market, makes it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money, slows the overall economy and undercuts prices for investments. That, hopefully, would remove some of inflation’s fuel. A report on Thursday suggested the US job market may remain solid, with fewer workers applying for unemployment benefits last week. That could give the Fed more confidence that the economy could withstand higher interest rates. Following Thursday’s reports, traders see a roughly 73 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the 61 per cent probability seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That’s also despite Trump’s consistent lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. The Fed’s counterpart in Europe, the European Central Bank, raised its own interest rates on Thursday in hopes of getting inflation in check. It cited “the conflict in the Middle East” and how it “continues to generate inflation pressures”.



It all pushed the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.95 per cent from 4.83 per cent late Wednesday, which is a significant move for the bond market. It’s up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began, and is back to where it was in the autumn of 2023. That was after the Fed cranked the federal funds rate higher to get super-high inflation coming out of the COVID pandemic under better control. Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Higher yields mean investors can make more money putting their money into bonds, which can in turn make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments that are riskier than bonds. Some investors see a 5 per cent yield on the 10-year Treasury as the next potential flashpoint. But strategists at Bank of America’s Research Investment Committee suggest 7 per cent may be the more important threshold, pointing to peaks for expensive stocks around that point in the past.



In the meantime the rising 10-year Treasury yield is making mortgages more expensive and hurting the housing industry. One report on Thursday said the average long-term US mortgage rate hit its highest level in more than 14 months, while a second one said sales of previously occupied US homes fell in August to their slowest pace in more than a year. That helped sent stocks of home builders lower, including drops of 3.5 per cent for Lennar and 2.4 per cent for D.R. Horton. Elsewhere on Wall Street, Macy’s fell 4.7 per cent, even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. While raising its forecast for earnings this fiscal year, it warned that “there are macroeconomic and geopolitical factors that could influence” how much its customers feel comfortable spending. Macy’s said it received $US116 million in tariff refunds from the government – $US98 million during the quarter and another $US18 million after the quarter ended. Macy’s chief executive Tony Spring told the Associated Press on Thursday that it’s using some of the proceeds to lower prices on certain items like furniture and other big-ticket purchases. In sharemarkets abroad, indexes slipped across much of Europe.

World.title: Voting shake-up to favour the Greens in Melbourne’s next lord mayoral race
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCity life Voting shake-up to favour the Greens in Melbourne’s next lord mayoral race Angelica Snowden September 11, 2026 — 10:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Greens are set to benefit from a shake-up of complicated rules governing City of Melbourne elections, potentially paving the way for the minor party to claim the mayoralty. The changes to the City of Melbourne Act, passed by state parliament on Thursday evening, mean businesses and non-resident property owners will no longer be automatically enrolled to vote in council elections, which is likely to increase the weight of resident votes in future polls. Rule changes have passed the upper house that will impact Melbourne City council elections. Luis Enrique Ascui In 2020, the City of Melbourne electoral roll was made up of 55.09 per cent business owners and non-resident property owners. Locals made up only 44.91 per cent of the roll. Similar amendments which removed automatic enrolment for non-resident owners were applied to all other 78 councils from 2020, via changes to the Local Government Act. The City of Melbourne is unique because it is the only municipality to be governed by its own act.



Those amendments “resulted in a significant reduction in the number of council-enrolled voters on voters’ rolls across all local councils”, according to the Victorian Electoral Commission’s report on the last local government elections in 2024. Related Article City life ‘I made a mistake’: Charities still waiting for Reece’s promised $9 million for the homeless Residents in the City of Melbourne are younger – 28 is the median age of the area’s 43,000 residents, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics – but their electoral influence is offset by business owners and non-resident property owners who comprise the majority of the electoral roll. The next council elections will be held in October 2028. The changes also include the abolition of group voting tickets. The City of Melbourne was the last remaining jurisdiction in the country still using the complicated preference-swapping system.



The Greens, who negotiated the amendments to the act that were supported by Labor MPs, did not secure support to scrap the contentious rule that hands businesses two votes in council elections. They also fell short in a bid to ban donations from gambling and property developers. Banning donations from property developers was a key recommendation from the anti-corruption watchdog’s Operation Sandon report into a scandal that engulfed the City of Casey. Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the party had improved transparency in the City of Melbourne. Eddie Jim Both amendments were voted down by Labor and Coalition MPs. Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the changes would improve democracy and make sure “City of Melbourne elections are decided by the people who actually live here, not by big business or dodgy backroom preference deals”.



“Residents are the ones who have to live with the decisions of council, and people who actually live here should decide who represents them, not big corporations or property investors who live somewhere else,” she told The Age. “Melbourne is a progressive city, and people here want leaders who put people and the planet before corporate profits, that’s why so many people vote Greens in Melbourne. “These reforms will make sure elections are decided by residents who live here, not big business, and if that means more Greens are elected, that will be a good outcome for democracy and for our wonderful city.” Lord Mayor of Melbourne Nick Reece. Eamon Gallagher Group voting tickets allow political parties to direct where candidate preferences flow. The abolition of the complex scheme will stop candidates being elected as councillors with a tiny fraction of the primary vote.



Related Article City life ‘Hard to understand’: Allan government fails to act on council donations Group voting tickets were also banned in elections for Victoria’s Legislative Council after laws passed parliament in August with support from both major parties. The changes bring the City of Melbourne in line with all other local government areas. Former premier Jeff Kennett introduced automatic enrolment for corporations in the City of Melbourne in 1995. He also handed corporations two votes instead of one in 1993. Sandell declared the rule changes a win for the party. “The Greens have finally killed off dodgy, undemocratic ‘preference whispering’ and ripped out some of the worst parts of the City of Melbourne’s warped electoral system,” she said.
