World.title: Super Rugby Pacific's 'Super Round' to return to Christchurch in 2027
World.content:
Super Rugby Pacific's Super Round will return to Christchurch for the second year running in 2027.

The Super Round - in which all ten teams in the competition play at the same venue over three days - was a big success at the new Te Kaha Stadium in Ōtautahi on Anzac weekend this year, with strong indications given by organisers afterwards that there would be a repeat next year.

ChristchurchNZ, Super Rugby Pacific and the government confirmed that on Friday, with the round to take place from 2-4 April. The partnership is backed by the government's one-off Events Attraction Package.

The Friday match will involve home team the Crusaders against the ACT Brumbies, while the Saturday double-header will see the Chiefs take on Western Force, followed by the Blues playing the NSW Waratahs.

On the Sunday, the Highlanders will play the Drua, followed by the Hurricanes meeting the Queensland Reds.

Super Rugby Pacific CEO Jack Mesley said the round last year delivered one of the best weekends in the competition's history.

"Its positioning in Round 8 provides the perfect springboard into a very exciting stretch in our season, as we build towards the first-ever Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup match in Round 11.

"Ten teams, one city, and an unforgettable weekend for the fans."

Tourism and Hospitality Minister Louise Upston said Super Round was ''exactly the kind of event the government's one-off Events Attraction Package was created to attract. It's a fantastic opportunity to fill hotels, restaurants and cafes, welcome visitors to Christchurch, and celebrate the best of Super Rugby Pacific in one action-packed weekend."

2027 Super Round Fixtures

Friday 2 April

Game 1: Crusaders v ACT Brumbies - 7.35pm kick-off

Saturday 3 April

Game 2: Chiefs v Western Force - 5.05pm kick-off

Game 3: Blues v NSW Waratahs - 7.35pm kick-off

Sunday 4 April

Game 4: Highlanders v Fijian Drua - 2.00pm kick-off

World.title: NZ First promises two-year clemency for Pacific overstayers
World.content:
New Zealand First will offer a two-year clemency period for Pacific Islanders who overstay their visas, the Winston Peters-led party has announced.

While announcing a suite of immigration policies on Friday, the party said the extra time would not be available to any other nationalities, in recognition of its "unique and close bond" with the Pacific.

NZ First leader Winston Peters Calvin Samuel

It said the 24-month period would be "to facilitate any Pacific overstayer to apply to remain in the country legally on a valid visa", and those who failed to do so would be deported after the period lapsed, "permanently ineligible to apply for any visa in the future, due to their heightened risk of reoffending."

Other policies included a referendum on a 20,000 resident visa cap, stricter birthright citizenship rules, and broader liability for deportation.

Peters has previously accepted a petition by migrant rights campaigner Anae Arthur Anae that advocates a visa-waiver for Pacific nationals for up to three months, which is an entitlement given to over 130 countries elsewhere.

Anae, praising the new policy, said it's all too common for Pacific islanders, relying on immigration consultants, to have incomplete documentation.

"Since 2008, [Immigration NZ] has been dealing with third parties on behalf of Pacific people," he said.

"It goes like this: someone comes along, says 'I can help you'. They pay them a fee to do all the documentation, and they sit back and wait, thinking everything has been done."

"Meanwhile, it's only partially done, no follow-up, and then these people are regarded as overstayers and deported."

He said the extra time to allow for islanders to get their affairs in order could help them avoid this kind of situation.

"Why do they keep hammering us about overstaying all the time as excuses to their incompetence in providing a service for people fairly?"

RNZ

Immigration NZ officials have recently batted off scrutiny in Parliament over how the agency determines overstay risk per nationality, which tends to single out Pacific countries despite a relatively small number of arrivals.

It revealed that this risk, combined with factors such as national security and biosecurity, has given INZ cause to advise cabinet against visa waivers to Pacific nationals direct from their home country.

In its most recent estimate, INZ said around 20,980 people currently in the country had overstayed their visa - 2599 of whom were Tongan, 2577 Chinese, and 2213 American.

Between July 2023 and 2025, Tonga had the highest overstay risk: 472 of their 24,425 temporary arrivals, or nearly two percent. Samoa followed, at 1.7 percent.

The United States had nearly double the amount of overstayers as Tonga did at 894. However, INZ deemed them a lower risk because that figure was just 0.13 percent of their arrivals.

The US, Great Britain, India and China, whose nationals receive an NZeTA on arrival in New Zealand for three months, all had higher overstay levels than Samoa.

"We consider that there is a strong rationale for maintaining current policy settings," Immigration policy manager Stacey O'Dowd told Parliament's Petitions Select Committee.

Anae, whose petition is still being considered by the Select Committee, said it was an injustice that weighs heavy on the Pasifika community.

"We've got to make applications, can't even get here for a funeral," he said.

"I had a case recently of someone who submitted an application to come to her brother's funeral. She gave them the death certificate, she got her visa to come to his funeral 1 month after the funeral. Explain that one to me.

Visa waivers for Fijians, Samoans and Tongans were abolished in February 1987, three months after they were introduced. Waivers for Tuvaluans, Ni-Kiribati and Dei-Naoero were similarly scrapped in 2003.

World.title: Auckland CBD business owner eager for CRL opening after years of disruption
World.content:
Businesses gear up for opening of City Rail Link Morning Report Download MP3 4m

The City Rail Link has held its official opening in Auckland, with a bar owner saying he's looking forward to reaping the rewards of staying afloat during its construction.

A symbolic ribbon was cut on Friday morning at the vast Te Waihorotiu Station, which runs between Victoria Street West and Wellesly St. It's expected to become New Zealand's busiest train station.

The ceremony was attended by a large contingent of officials and politicians, including Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown and representatives from Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei .

Minister for Rail Winston Peters spoke at the opening too - and even showed off his singing skills with his best Johnny Cash impression.

The City Rail Link took ten years to complete and cost $5.5 billion dollars.

It has also caused significant disruption for businesses along the route.

Craig Wright told Morning Report it's been a long slog to keep Northern Line Bar and Social open near Karanga-a-Hape Station, and he's hoping for consistency and continuity once the new rail loop is running.

"When you're faced with three metre hoardings, literally, you know, a metre and a half from your doorway, the view isn't great for the customers to sit and look at.

"Neither is the noise or the smell or the dust."

Auckland City rail link construction on Karanga-a-Hape road in 2019. RNZ / Kymberlee Fernandes

He said the business made it through those years with "good luck and duct tape".

"I think it's probably a testament to the staff that I have have been consistent over the few years that we just stuck in there, we could see, pardon the pun, light at the end of the tunnel."

He said the support of the local Karanga-a-Hape road community went a long way and everyone had pitched in to help eachother.

As construction hoardings came down and first look events took place, there have been some better days but Wright said he was now hoping for more consistency.

"We need people to be coming into the city to work and to enjoy activities in the city, but also that they can leave from our stations to go on to other events."

He said as exciting as the opening was he was hoping the stations and rail link would be maintained well over a long period of time.

"Without sounding pessimistic, the day we see rail replacement buses, our hearts are going to drop.

"So hopefully the maintenance and the future proofing is going to be the proof in the pudding."

World.title: Live: 49ers and Rams locked in tight contest early at the MCG
World.content:
Two of the 49ers best players on either side of the ball, defensive end Nick Bosa and tight end George Kittle, are coming off serious injuries from last season, so all eyes will be on how they go this year.

George Kittle (Getty Images)

On the defensive side, the 49ers pass rush is a genuine concern, especially if Bosa can't return from the ACL injury that ended his season, which means former Dallas Cowboy Osa Odighizuwa may need to really up his game at defensive tackle.

Offensively, Brock Purdy will be desperate to stay fit for long enough to really get into a rhythm this season.

Brock Purdy (Getty Images)

Last year, the young quarterback started just nine games and managed a TD/INT ratio of 20/10. That's too many interceptions for an elite quarterback and, given the addition of quality wide receivers Mike Evans and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling, Niners fans will hope he can find his accuracy.

Given all those new toys for Purdy to play with, running back Christian McCaffrey shouldn't need to be thrown to as many times as he was last year.

Christian McCaffrey (Getty Images)

The running back had an astonishing 102 receptions (catches) — the sixth-most of any player in the league — for 924 yards and seven touchdowns last season.

That's in addition to his day job of running with the ball, where he had 1,202 yards from 311 rushes (runs) for 10 touchdowns, the eighth-most rushing yards of anyone in the league.

His backup is likely to be Kaelon Black, so keep an eye on him to see whether he can carry some of that running load this season.

World.title: Opals knocked out of World Cup as luckless captain's torn ACL confirmed
World.content:
The Opals have been knocked out in the quarterfinals of the Women's Basketball World Cup in a 23-point loss to Spain just hours after receiving more devastating injury news about captain Ezi Magbegor.

Half an hour before the tip-off in what turned out to be a comprehensive 89-66 loss to Spain, Magbegor's WNBA team, the Seattle Storm, revealed the star forward had torn her ACL.

Magbegor, who only returned to the court in early July after partially tearing her Achilles in March, went down early after taking a knock to her right knee in Australia's qualification final win over Italy.

"It makes me emotional when I see anyone go down," Opals coach Sandy Brondello said after the loss to Spain.

"But Ezi's come back from an injury and it's just another injury. [It's] just really unfortunate. She's a key part of what we want to do. It sucks, but that's sport isn't it?

"She's got to have a great recovery and she'll get back, I don't have a doubt about that. Just disappointed for Ezi that she's going through another rehabilitation."

The inexperienced Opals struggled without some of their biggest stars. (Supplied: FIBA)

Magbegor joined fellow stars Alanna Smith (leg injury) and Jade Melbourne (illness) on the sidelines, while veteran Sami Whitcomb was ruled out before the tournament with injury and Cayla George did not play due to pregnancy.

Smith suffered a lower-leg injury in the opening game of the tournament, while Melbourne played only three minutes against Italy and could not take the floor in the quarterfinal.

The Opals made a great escape after surrendering a 20-point three-quarter-time lead against the Azzurre thanks largely to a 30-point explosion by 21-year-old Izzy Borlase, but the missing players were too much to overcome in the final-eight showdown.

Ally Wilson was Australia's top scorer with 13 points as the team shot just 40 per cent from the field and had 23 turnovers.

Veteran Steph Talbot said she her young team's lack of big-tournament experience was evident in the game, and said it was a strange experience hitting the court with only eight teammates.

"It's very weird. It was very quiet, very unusual. We were all looking around like, 'Is this it?'" she said.

"But a job's a job and we fought hard to the end. I'm really proud of the effort they put in. It's definitely a different experience."

Brondello said the difficult World Cup would be valuable experience for the team, which boasted seven players in their first major international tournament, with the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics looming large on the horizon.

World.title: Crows' quest for premiership glory just beginning as they prepare to take on Lions
World.content:
A week is a long time in footy, but an hour can feel like a lifetime.

In the space of 30 minutes last Saturday, Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks jumped from zero to hero, whilst hours earlier at the SCG the Lions went from premiership favourites to staring down a straight sets exit.

When the Bulldogs piled on three rapid fire goals to erode the Crows' 20-point lead, the tension at Adelaide Oval was palpable; but after Izak Rankine snapped a magical goal to seal Adelaide's first finals victory in nine years, everything changed.

The home crowd rose as one to give their embattled senior coach a standing ovation; drawing a smile from the man whose future was publicly in the spotlight and uniting a football club that has been fractured since its 2017 grand final collapse.

Izak Rankine sealed Adelaide’s first finals victory in nine years with a spectacular goal from a ridiculous angle. (AAP: Matt Turner)

Adelaide premiership player and former board member Rod Jameson couldn't hold back his emotions post-game on ABC Sport.

"'Get stuffed' is probably what you want to say," he said.

"It's been against the odds.

"I feel really happy for Matthew Nicks that he's actually got one … so what's the narrative now next week?"

That's the big question in a relentless news cycle. Despite the pressure valve being released, Adelaide's quest for glory is just beginning with an upcoming semi-final at the Gabba to face a Lions side who handed them their biggest loss of the season back in round 7.

But the heat has certainly shifted to the qualifying final losers Fremantle and Brisbane, with both teams facing the daunting possibility of becoming the 13th side in 13 years to be eliminated in straight sets.

Matthew Nicks claimed his first AFL finals win since he began coaching the Crows. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Reigning premiers Brisbane were stunningly blown away by an undermanned Swans. Sydney's passion was unrelenting; winning the tackle count by 15, contested possessions by 19 and beating the Lions at their game with a whopping six goals to one from centre bounce.

"They were desperate from the start, and all you want as a fan is the effort … that was perfect finals footy," dual premiership winning Swan Ryan O'Keefe said on ABC Sport.

"When was the last time 36 scoring shots were kicked against an opposition in a final? That's unbelievable."

It’s a blueprint that will build belief for the Crows ahead of Saturday’s semi and could dictate the result. Adelaide is one of the best pressure sides in the competition. The six times they have lost pressure differential this season they’ve been defeated, whilst the Lions are 13-0 when winning it.



Adelaide’s other advantage is their forward firepower, with the team averaging 109 points per game in their last five matches. The Lions conceded 14 goals to key forwards last week, have leaked 100 points eight times this season and are sitting 13th for points against per game.



"The defence is the difference this year," premiership Magpie Luke Ball said after the Lions loss at the SCG.

"It looked too easy to score against them. They're going to have to defy history."

Lachie Neale starred for the Brisbane Lions with 42 disposals. (AAP: James Ross)

The final and most pivotal factor is likely to be the midfield. The Lions kicked five goals to none from centre bounce back in their round 7 mauling on top of 27 extra points from stoppage. Lachie Neale starred with 42 disposals and Will Ashcroft had 36 touches and a goal.



It's a concern for the Crows who conceded three unanswered goals from the middle against the Bulldogs on Saturday night. They made up for it in their defence with Josh Worrell nabbing a career high 34 disposals and a massive 19 intercepts. Adelaide kept the Bulldogs to a 14 per cent inside 50 to goal efficiency.



Brisbane are no strangers to doing it the hard way. This is the eighth consecutive year they’ve made it to a preliminary final or semi-final with a record of 3-2 in the latter.

The Crows, meanwhile, have got the monkey off their back, snapping their September shackles and now can take a swing at the reigning premiers at a venue they haven't won at since 2018.

"I don't think it can be understated how much pressure was on this side coming into this contest," All-Australian midfielder Josh Francou said after the elimination final.

"They were challenged and in the end they got the job done and in the end they go to up to Brisbane with a free hit."

You can hear ABC Sport call the semi-final between Adelaide and the Brisbane Lions from 5:30pm CST on 891 ABC Adelaide and on ABC Listen.

World.title: Recent finals history is against Freo, but these numbers could save them
World.content:
Keeping hold of form and momentum on the footy field is often like trying to catch lightning in a bottle. Just ask Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir.

Few, if any, would question that Fremantle has been the best and most complete football team across the 2026 AFL season.

The shortest player in the AFL has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over by all 18 AFL clubs at the national draft, Isaiah Dudley reflects on his improbable rise as the Dockers look to bounce back in the finals.

The Dockers' excellence has spanned weeks, months, time zones and weather seasons.

In the middle of the year, the question was more of when they were going to lose rather than if anyone would challenge them for the minor premiership.

But just as winter turns to spring the fortunes of all football teams change.

Now instead of wondering about the pack chasing them, the Dockers are now frantically searching for how they can regain that torrid early season form.

The development of how we play football in Australia — in all codes — often means that the best team of the year doesn't win the title.

Instead, it is often taken out by the team in the best form or with the best fitness when the finals comes around.

Once upon a time, it was almost a foregone conclusion that a side in Fremantle's current position would rally to redemption in week two of the finals.

In the first decade of this century, more qualifying final losers went on to win a premiership than to suffer the indignity of a straight-sets exit.

But as the Dockers would remember better than many sides, things have changed since then.

Fremantle, along with Geelong, broke new ground in 2014 when both experienced back-to-back finals losses.

With rising performance standards and more equalisation measures in the league, footy is more competitive than ever, and straight-sets exits have been the single most common fate for top-four losers since those breakthrough losses.

Half of the two dozen semifinals since 2014 have been won by the nominal underdog.

With time rapidly running out on season 2026, Fremantle is looking for that ephemeral sense of what kept them ahead of the pack before their season is over.

Standing in Freo's way this week is the side with the current longest winning streak — and a side who knows how to measure efforts for September — Geelong.

Winning the whole thing

Fremantle's loss to Hawthorn last week was its first home defeat in 13 games at Perth Stadium this season. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Usually when a team starts to dip there is a reason. It is very rare for the rest of the league to raise their level to that of the competition heavyweights.

The league leaders are always the most studied, and the most scrutinised.

Over the course of the season threads are pulled at potential weaknesses until they are unravelled by the best of the rest.

When looking Fremantle's dip the biggest story is what is happening at the contest — or more importantly what isn't happening.

Fremantle's midfield and front half group is blessed with attacking talent, able to turn a half-chance into a broken line or shot at goal.

They are sometimes less able to control the ball when it hits the deck, especially when there are even numbers at the contest.

Against disciplined midfields, the Dockers have struggled to find the supply they need to churn the scoreboard over.

While they are still outsourcing teams at stoppage, the Dockers are beginning to be outscored when the ball hits the deck in general play.

Opposition sides have become increasingly accustomed to not overcommitting to competing in the air to counter the Dockers plethora of tall contested marking options, and instead focusing the ball on the inevitable battle when it hits the deck.

When GWS downed Fremantle in round 17, the Giants were able to win the post-clearance ground ball battle 65 to 49.

Despite losing ground in the air, the Giants were more than able to make it up on the ground.

It is a template other sides have been able to follow, cruelling the ability for the Dockers to score from broken play.

Last week, Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell was very clear on their focus around keeping extra numbers at the contest.

Hawthorn's smalls such as Nick Watson (right) dominated groundballs all night in the qualifying final. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"Our forwards' work rate was a real highlight. We didn't always use the ball at our best, but the way they created outnumber after outnumber was huge," Mitchell said after the win over Fremantle.

While the Dockers broke even at post clearance contests in the game, the Hawks scored an extra 27 points from intercepts.

This was the big difference in the contest, and the key reason that the Dockers are playing again this week.

"I just thought [the] contest was pretty even, but I thought their contest method was a lot better than ours. I thought they were probably a little bit more decisive to get it to the outside [and] buffer pressure," Longmuir said after the match.

Part of the deal that Mitchell made with the outnumber was to leave their defence more isolated against the dominant Dockers key forward set up.

But that was a calculated gamble due to the match-ups that presented themselves.

Hawthorn captain James Sicily (right) was excellent in defence and nullified Fremantle's tall forwards time and time again. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"I think having a bit of extra time to watch them. Credit to Kade Simpson, the backline coach, he did a great job preparing the boys. Whether it was, you know, Barrass, Battle, Sicily, Weddle, we sort of had good match-ups [on Fremantle's forwards]," Mitchell said.

The Dockers were only able to get two goals from their tall forward triumvirate of Josh Treacy, Patrick Voss and Jye Amiss — the first time since round 6 that they were kept to less than three as a group.

Although the Dockers managed nine marks inside 50, the set shots they managed were from unfavourable situations and none are renowned sharpshooters from those positions.

But despite the downward turn in form, there is definitely still a clear path to the club's maiden AFL premiership cup.

The path back

Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir has put up a defiant front in the lead-up to the semifinal against Geelong. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The silver lining for Fremantle is last week's loss wasn't a season-ender.

Instead, Longmuir has a fair amount of hope for their chances to come.

"There's still a path there. So everything we've been working on across the course of the year, we've got to lean into that now," Longmuir surmised in the wake of the loss to Hawthorn.

"[I] understand that the outside noise might turn a little bit from positivity to negativity. I understand that aspect of it, but as a group, we've got to lean into each other and try [to] find our best footy before next week," he said.

" We're not dead and buried. "

But the road to glory has become significantly harder than it looked a week ago.

Instead of a week off to recoup before a home preliminary final, the Dockers instead face one of the most feared sights in footy; Geelong when it matters most.

After floating through the season in fits and spurts, Geelong found its feet as September drew closer.

Geelong rode a six-match winning streak coming into the finals, albeit against some softer opposition.

Last week's win over Carlton was dominant but still left the indication that there is room to grow.

The Cats are also one of the few sides who know what it is like to beat the Dockers this year, splitting their two home and away clashes with the minor premiers.

In both games, control over the ball was perhaps the most critical element.

In round 1 the Cats claimed 50 more marks than the Dockers on their way to a 10-point win, while in round 15, the Dockers gained a 22-mark edge over the Cats in their nine-point win.

Limiting the Dockers ability to control the ball via the kick-mark game — and instead forcing the ball to deck — is one of the ways that teams can blunt their attacking influence.

Notably, Fremantle has suffered three losses in four of its matches where it has registered its lowest marking totals of the season.

The messier the game is, the harder it often is for the Dockers to dominate.

However, the Cats present a vastly easier challenge to the Dockers inside defensive 50 than Hawthorn did last week.

Geelong's defence has not been as strong as it has been in previous years and most key defensive indicators have deteriorated in the last part of the year.

Geelong has conceded marks and shots inside 50 at a bottom-four rate in the last ten matches, and during that time, the Dockers probably should have beaten them by more in their return match.

There's a quiet — if not cautious — confidence that the Dockers will be able to break the trend of straight sets exits if they can get the game back on their terms.

"I think you [have] to lean into physicality from the start. Contest is really key and then [we need to] try and lock it in our front half," Fremantle co-captain Andy Brayshaw told the media during the week.

If the Dockers can return to their brand of football, their hopes of their maiden premiership may still be alive in 2026.

World.title: The FIFO Rams may have lost the battle for hearts and minds
World.content:
The NFL has long been a pioneer in blending the barrier between entertainment and legitimate sporting competition.

Today's clash at the MCG between the San Francisco 49ers and the LA Rams is a historic moment for the league — after all, playing a regular-season game on the other side of the world is pretty outlandish.

But as close to 100,000 people cram into the Melbourne Cricket Club's hallowed halls and stare into the far distance at the gridiron imprinted upon its hallowed turf, the question has to be raised as to why it's happening, who is benefiting most, and why the two teams are taking such wildly contrasting approaches to the contest ahead of a busy season.

First things first. Why is this happening?

Modern Australian sports fans are far too educated to be left staring in wonder at the strange code of football being played in front of them when they turn up.

Most, if not all, of the people in the stands later today will not only know the rules, but have their favourite players and likely even have a team they can claim to support year in, year out.

This Australian San Francisco 49ers fan has been a fan long before there was ever a suggestion of a game being played on these shores. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Josh Chadwick)

More than a handful of Australia-based supporters would likely confess to spending Monday mornings with one eye on a pop-out window on their computer screen — or at their phone — to keep up with Sunday Night Football as it plays out Stateside.

In short, people already have their favourites.

Anecdotally, when attending previous international matches as a supporter in London over the years, you are far more likely to see fans wearing unrelated jerseys to those teams actually playing — especially in the nascent years of the NFL's English experiment.

So those people heading to the MCG today will, by the law of averages, be watching two teams they don't support.

This should clearly be a detrimental situation to the nominal home team, the Los Angeles Rams.

However, the Rams' pitiful backing from locals at SoFi Stadium, which results in more away-team invasions than anywhere else in the NFL, especially against San Francisco, suggests that playing in front of a hostile crowd at home probably isn't anything they're not used to.

"It's cool for us always to have an advantage of having, what I see, as one home game a year in LA," coach Kyle Shanahan told reporters earlier this week.

"Just the way our fans take over that stadium … [but] I have a feeling they won't be much different here. I expect to have a good showing."

The San Francisco 49ers have been training at AAMI Park this week. (AP Photo: Asanka Brendon Ratnayake)

Shanahan made those comments in Melbourne on Monday.

The Rams didn't even arrive until Thursday morning, about 24 hours before kick-off, in a bold fly-in fly-out plan to avoid the jet lag that comes from a 12,748-kilometre, 16-hour trans-Pacific flight.

Melbourne's NFL game is a battle of opposing jet lag strategies The San Francisco 49ers arrived a week in advance of their Melbourne NFL game, while the Rams will arrive the day before. A sleep expert says both strategies have merit, but one may have a slight edge.

How effective this plan will be on the field will come in time — not just after the MCG contest, but in the next couple of games and throughout the year.

But off the field, it's hard not to think that the Rams have fumbled the ball in their own end zone and given a free pass to San Francisco to take over the running of the narrative, which gets us onto the question of who is benefiting.

According to an investigation by The Athletic, the 49ers are the most popular team in Australia.

NFL games were first being shown on Australian TV during the 1980s, first by Channel Nine, Channel 10 and then the ABC, with effervescent host Don Lane bringing a new audience to professional American Football.

Joe Montana led the 49ers during their greatest era. (Getty Images)

Given that the 1980s were the 49ers' greatest era, with the side winning four of their five Super Bowls that decade thanks to Bill Walsh's famed West Coast Offence and the talents of quarterback Joe Montana, the Niners' enduring appeal makes sense.

Australians love a winner.

So having the 49ers play the first game on Australian soil makes perfect sense.

But there is a complication.

Starting in January 2022, the NFL launched its Global Markets Program, a formalised approach that gives NFL clubs access to international territories for marketing and fan engagement.

The (Inter)National Football League The NFL will open its 2026 season with a match in Melbourne, Australia, this week, one of a record nine matches to take place overseas this season. And it shows no signs of slowing down yet.

All 32 teams now have an overseas presence via this program, with 22 different countries targeted, including Australia.

These markets are not exclusive. Germany is the most popular market, with 11 NFL teams snapping up their options there, while some areas, including Colombia, Japan, Greece, Ghana and Nigeria, have been taken by just one team each.

But Australia is proving to be of interest too, with four teams nominating this great southern land as their territory to harvest in the NFL's own brand of sporting and commercial imperialism.

Those four teams that picked Australia are the Las Vegas Raiders, Philadelphia Eagles, Seattle Seahawks and the Los Angeles Rams.

So, if the Rams have commercial rights in Australia, why did they fly in the day before the game and not spend time winning over hearts and minds among supporters in the build-up?

Loading Instagram content

Have they missed a trick by failing to turn up to their own party?

It's almost as if the Rams are turning up to their holiday home, only to find that the 49ers have already unpacked the suitcase in the master bedroom and are sitting on the couch with their feet on the coffee table.

For a start, Australia is not the Rams' only overseas operation; they also have the rights in China, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, New Zealand and the United Arab Emirates, with Japan, South Korea and China exclusively theirs.

It would be wrong to say the Rams organisation has done nothing in Melbourne.

The cheerleaders have been out and about all week, and the team has collaborated with Melbourne fashion label-turned-homeless charity HoMie and various events at "Rams House" on the Crown Riverwalk.

But San Francisco has done all that too, and then some.

Melbourne Victory players Louis D'Arrigo and Philipp Ziereis exchanged jerseys with San Francisco 49ers star Fred Warner at AAMI Park. (Supplied: Melbourne Victory)

The 49ers' stated aim is to paint Melbourne red, and it seems, externally at least, to be doing a great job: hosting open training sessions in front of 2,000 local children at AAMI Park, watching the Geelong-Carlton game at the MCG on Friday night, a training run with Special Olympics athletes, setting a cheerleading record at Federation Square, visiting the local children's hospital, partaking in a Bunnings sausage sizzle. This is hearts and minds 101 from the 49ers team.

Shanahan and the 49ers' decision to give the players a week to adjust to the time zone and the rigours of international travel seems to make sense to anyone who has travelled across the world and then had to work.

"It took a couple of days to adjust," he said on Monday.

"But [I'm] feeling real good today."

The biggest interest for sports science types will be how two sets of experts came to such wildly different conclusions about how to approach the longest road trip in NFL history.

The San Francisco 49ers Gold Rush cheerleaders led 1,424 people in a record-breaking cheer dance event. (Getty Images: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Ye Myo Khant)

The Rams felt that the team would be far better served doing all their prep at home and keeping the players' body clocks on US Pacific Coast time.

They did something similar last year when playing the Jaguars in London, a 10-and-a-half-hour, 8,780km journey from LA, a game they won comprehensively.

The 49ers have decided that getting into the Melbourne time zone would serve them best, training in the late morning to adapt to the earlier-than-usual kick-off time.

Which perhaps leads to the crux of the issue: the purpose of these international games.

Are they meant to spread the gospel of the NFL into new markets, or are they primarily about building commercial relationships?

"For us, this is a year-round effort," Kevin Demoff, president of the Rams, told CNB.

"I would much rather win the game and grow the market the other 51 weeks a year than focus on having our players here for that week."

That said, questions about the approach have clearly struck a nerve, as Demoff responded to San Francisco Standard reporter David Lombardi's tweet criticising the strategy.

Lombardi wrote on X: "An actual 'business trip' would involve the Rams taking the time actually to grow their brand. There's a reason the Rams don't even own LA. It's related to their current mentality. Moving to Anaheim and then St. Louis severely hurt the cultivation of a fan base. 49ers benefit."

Demoff accused the writer of being "obsessed with the Rams brand" in a startlingly thin-skinned response.

As much razzmatazz as the NFL collects around itself, this is also a serious sports league where, with just 17 regular-season games to establish your case for sporting immortality, teams simply cannot afford to throw away a single chance for a win.

The conflict between the front-of-house commercial imperatives and the back-end business of winning football games is being thrown into stark relief this week.

The Los Angeles Rams are coming to Australia for one thing only, to win. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Greg Fiore)

The 49ers have embraced Australia, and Australia has embraced them in turn.

The Rams, as a sporting operation, are treating this like a business trip, focused on getting a W to start their season, commercial considerations be damned.

And who knows, should the Rams' smash-and-grab approach work out, and they claim the victory, that puts them on the path to Super Bowl LXI — which is taking place at their actual home, SoFi Stadium, next February — then it might not matter how many proverbial babies they kissed or hands they shook.

That would give the Rams the unique status of being able to say they won a Super Bowl on home turf, after starting the season by laying down roots at a distant home away from home.

Such a victory would forever tie Australia to a team of winners.

And Australian sports fans do love a winner.

World.title: Joyce vague on details, Albanese wins tennis match amid golf grant saga
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Barnaby Joyce has always been a disruptor; it’s one of the reasons Pauline Hanson wanted to woo him to One Nation.

Few have had a career quite like Joyce, who was once described by Tony Abbott as Australia’s best retail politician. The man who had two turns as Nationals leader could connect with voters. He was loved and despised (in some seats) in equal measure.

His defection to One Nation was designed to bolster the party’s legitimacy. His performance as its Treasury spokesperson this week did anything but.

Joyce struggled as he was sent out to sell the party’s superannuation policy. Under the plan, renters and mortgage borrowers would be able to divert a quarter of their super contributions to their income for up to three years.

Across a series of interviews (including one he conducted from the Qantas Chairman’s Lounge) he was asked about the proposal’s inflationary impact and what this would mean for a person's foregone retirement savings.

“Interest rates keep rising,” Hanson had said as she announced the policy at a rare press conference in Parliament House. Economists told the ABC the policy, if ever adopted, would only tempt the Reserve Bank to push them higher.

Loading...

Joyce claimed the extra cash wouldn't drive up inflation because the money already sits in superannuation funds, so it's already in the economy. Economists don't share that view, with history suggesting people would most likely spend and not invest any extra money.

Joyce snapped at the ABC's Sarah Ferguson on 7.30 on Monday night for not providing questions on retirement savings losses ahead of time. He declared he was not Jesus Christ, as if that was ever in question.

He is, though, an accountant by trade (a fact he pointed out) and someone who has been on the policy sell many a time. It became clear One Nation never modelled the proposal. Joyce later claimed they didn't have the staff to do so — an argument that fails to acknowledge One Nation could've asked the Parliamentary Budget Office to help as other parties do.

Whether the policy has merit is one thing. But inflation is already running hot. Having some idea of the inflationary impact before releasing should be the bare minimum for a Treasury spokesperson.

A subplot to this is it's the second time in as many months the Coalition was reportedly gazumped by One Nation on policy (first being the tobacco excise). A similar proposal was said to have been drafted under Sussan Ley. The opposition downplayed the question of a leaker within their ranks, but it again begs the question of discipline.

The similarity between offerings from the Coalition and One Nation is something the government continues to leap on. It plays into the argument the government thinks it can win and is probably why a noticeable chunk of Labor's questions to itself in QT were about super.

Hastie v Hanson

A fight between Hanson and Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie has been brewing for a while.

The spat came to a head this week over a One Nation cartoon that called the former SAS captain a "traitor" eight times across nine minutes for testifying in Ben Roberts-Smith's failed defamation case. He was subpoenaed to do so.

"It's a slur on me. It's a slur on other veterans who have given under oath evidence to the federal court," Hastie said.

Several Liberals also condemned the cartoon. As did fellow veteran Jacqui Lambie, who echoed Hastie in calling the One Nation leader a "bloody coward".

Hastie served in Afghanistan. He's drawn the ire of One Nation and backer Gina Rinehart for giving evidence against the Victorian Cross recipient. Hanson and Rinehart say Roberts-Smith has been unfairly targeted over war crime allegations.

Andrew Hastie is taking issue with a cartoon published on Pauline Hanson's X account. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Roberts-Smith was this year charged with five counts of the war crime of murder over the alleged killings of five Afghan men between 2009 and 2012. He has not yet entered a plea but has denied the allegations.

Hastie's seat of Canning covers a large part of the state electorate of Secret Harbour, which One Nation won in a by-election last month. It's put a target on the seat as one the party thinks it can win at the next federal election.

Hastie's ruled out legal action over the video. It would be too costly of an exercise, he says, thanks to Rinehart's backing. Instead, he wants to "impose costs politically".

Hanson, and Joyce, have insisted she hasn't personally called Hastie a traitor despite the video. Earlier this week though, she did say she'd call him a "wanker".

Coalition deals it itself out

While he wouldn't agree with Hastie's description of Hanson having a "glass jaw," Opposition Leader Angus Taylor did back the call for the video to be pulled down.

It's an ironic point for him to make at the press conference where he was rallying against the government's Digital Duty of Care legislation – a bill he declared amounted to political censorship.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

The government released draft legislation earlier this week. It's designed to force social media companies to identify and mitigate harm on their platforms. It would also force platforms to provide users with choice between an algorithmic feed and a feed simply made up of people you actually follow.

But on Thursday the Coalition effectively dealt itself out of negotiations, confirming it won't support the bill amid concerns it hands the communication minister too much power to determine what constitutes online harm.

Shadow Communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson urged reporters to not conflate the concerns about the algorithm with the part of the bill the Coalition had problems with, ignoring the fact Matt Canavan, who was standing next to her, and others had been doing so all week.

Loading

Albanese gets tetchy

You might think with all this going it, the prime minister's week must have been smooth sailing.

After the ABC revealed the PM had an honorary membership with the Marrickville Golf Club, Albanese was under pressure over a $6m grant he promised the club for upgrades.

The $560 million Major and Local Community Infrastructure Fund was investigated by the Centre for Public Integrity and found 73 per cent of the funding went to notionally Labor-held seats.

Labor essentially spent the week insisting there was nothing to see here. The scheme was invitation only so the government could deliver its election promises. The crossbench labelled it pork-barrelling by design, calling for guidelines to be rewritten.

Loading...

Albanese turned the story into a bigger spectacle in a tetchy interview with the ABC, where he denied knowledge of the membership and took aim at the public broadcaster.

"I don't have a card. I don't go in there. I haven't been in there for years. I used to walk my dog along the path, as lots of people do because it's a community club," he said.

"The ABC should do better."

At least the prime minister can take comfort in the victory he did have in his preferred sport of tennis. Albanese defeated mortgage broker Joseph Daoud in a charity tennis match.

Daoud, a vocal critic of the government's housing tax changes, purchased the hit-out with Albanese for $16,500 in the Mid-Winter Ball's silent auction.

Despite telling reporters he'd been practising for months, Albanese had years on him and won in straight sets.

World.title: Aussie beach volleyball stars have crafty plan for success in LA
World.content:
Australian beach volleyball player Taliqua Clancy sits up excitedly, a flicker of a plan flitting across her face and dancing behind her eyes.

The three-time Olympian is sitting beside the courts at the Sandstorm Beach Volleyball Club at Nathan, in Brisbane's south, the shadow of the Queensland Sports and Athletics Centre's skeletal eastern grandstand looming up on the hill to her left.

Her newest playing partner, 21-year-old Stefie Fejes, is sitting on her right.

For a moment, conversation has turned from volleyball and the success this fledgling partnership has enjoyed since they came together in May this year, to Fejes's side project, crocheting.

Stefie Fejes (right) has only played six tournaments with Olympic silver medallist Taliqua Clancy. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

"It started in high school actually with one of my design projects," Fejes explains to ABC Sport.

"I made an eco-friendly bikini out of cotton. I'm really invested in sustainable fashion and, I guess, everything that goes with it.

"I'm really not a huge fan of fast fashion and how much waste we're producing in the world, so that's kind of where the love started.

"And then I was like, this is a great way to pass time: It's very efficient. It's productive. I can make some money. And I love doing it.

"I started doing it on the plane, do it on the bus. I would say it's like a form of meditation, for sure.

Loading Instagram content

"Everyone probably knows, but I'm quite high functioning,

"I like to move around a lot, do a lot and not a lot stops, and this is like my time where I can actually just take a breath and I make myself sit down and still be productive, but I'm actually sitting down and resting."

Clancy chips in and tells Fejes to mention one of her main projects, the crocheted ball carrier.

"On my first international event away I started realising that we have to take our [volley]ball with us everywhere, especially if we don't have a big staff and coaching team with us, and the ball takes up so much space in your bag," Fejes says.

"So I was like, OK, I'm going to create a ball carrier that I can just clip onto the outside of my bag, and everyone was obsessed with it.

"I'm still making it four years later. And sales are going great.

"I think most of the Australian tour has one, which is actually really cool, and they're supporting my journey … It's really special actually, I'm like, 'I made that,' when I see one … it's very kind and I really appreciate that everyone's getting on board with it too. I think it's really cool to connect with the community like that."

Stefie Fejes's ball pouches have become a common sight on the circuit. (Supplied: Instagram/@cheekie_handmadecrochet)

There is something in this crafting contemplation that strikes a gleeful parallel with British diver Tom Daley, whose habit of knitting in the stands during the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo sent the five-time Olympic medal winner viral at those Games and the subsequent Paris Olympics.

It has sent Tokyo silver medallist Clancy's mind working into overdrive, too.

"You need to pick an athlete that you want to gift it to," Clancy says to Fejes.

"And you've got to find them in the village.

"Snoop Dogg! He always comes out to the event. Oh my God, make him something."

Fejes laughs and agrees to cook something up. She has time to plan what to make, at least.

Snoop Dogg appears likely to be receptive to a crocheted bit of kit. (Getty Images: Joe Scarnici)

As the pair speak to ABC Sport they are each, almost absent-mindedly, turning a gold medal around in their hands, spoils from the Asian Championships in Shangluo, China, earlier this month.

Indeed, on the table to Clancy's right sits the voluminous silver trophy, with a novelty-cheque-sized banner with "QUALIFIED" emblazoned across it — the ticket to the LA28 Olympic Games.

A change to the qualification process for the LA Olympics had meant Australia has already qualified a quota spot just under two years out from the Games.

Fellow Paris Olympians Mark Nicolaidis and Izac Carracher also secured Australia a quota spot by winning the men's competition, edging out fellow countrymen Tom Hodges and Ben Hood in an epic final 21-17, 17-21, 15-12.

In Clancy's almost two-decade elite career, Olympic qualifying has never been completed this far out from a Games.

"They kind of changed the whole Olympic cycle," Clancy says.

"It was really last minute that we, and all the other countries, found out that if you win your continental champs you also secure a ticket to LA, so it was an odd one because you're kind of making a short plan within the really big, long-term plan of getting to the Games."

Taliqua Clancy, Stefie Fejes, Mark Nicolaidis and Izac Carracher have secured a quota spot for Australia at the LA Games. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

Offering crocheted gifts to US rappers isn't something that should preoccupy Fejes and Clancy's mind too much yet. Earning a quota spot does not mean that Australia will send this particular pairing to the Games; only that there is a spot there for an Australian team.

But despite only playing six tournaments together so far, the signs are looking promising that this team could make it all the way.

Prior to their Asian Championships victory — Clancy's sixth continental championship win — the pair came fifth at the World Volleyball Beach Pro Tour Elite16 event in Hamburg.

Their subsequent success in China came despite Fejes being so sick she was bedridden in the lead-up and Clancy breaking a toe. She also required treatment for a knee injury that was "a bit more severe than we anticipated" during the off-season, which limited their playing time.

Clancy noted that securing qualification so early was just "one part of the job" as far as their development as a pairing was concerned and that there was still a lot of work to do in order to improve their seeding for the Games and to work on the nuances of what they needed to do together on the court.

She has, of course, been in this position before.

Mariafe Artacho del Solar and Taliqua Clancy claimed silver in Tokyo. (AP: Petros Giannakouris)

For the past two Olympic cycles she has worked with Mariafe Artacho del Solar, a partnership that produced an Olympic silver medal, back-to-back Commonwealth Games silvers, world championship bronze and eight world tour titles.

But it is looking back to her first Games cycle where Clancy has found parallels with her new partner.

In 2016 Indigenous beach volleyballer heads to Rio alongside Louise Bawden, with whom she was partnered for five years and more than 60 tournaments.

Bawden was already a two-time Olympian in two different disciplines at that stage. Now the tables have turned and Clancy is the one with the experience in the partnership.

Taliqua Clancy (left) made her Olympic bow in Rio with Louise Bawden. (Getty Images: Paul Gilham)

"Actually it's so funny because it's kind of the complete flip," Clancy, who is now 34, says.

"I'm pretty sure me and Lou actually had pretty much the same age gap as well [Clancy was 24 during the Games and Bowden was 35 in Rio].

"So it is pretty funny. Me and Lou are very close, so I have asked a few questions. I was like, shit, OK, what do I do?

"But she's always been a great support. I still lean on her quite a lot."

Taliqua Clancy has now won six Asian Beach Volleyball Championships gold medals. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

As for Fejes, she's far from overawed from playing with a multiple global medallist.

"It's definitely not intimidating," she says.

"I've watched Taliqua's career basically my whole life and I always wanted to play with her, so it's pretty cool that this could finally happen.

"But I think the biggest thing I've learned is like coming into the space with T, the actions are 100 per cent the best. It doesn't matter how she's feeling, the consistency and the level of mastery is not something I've really experienced with the players that I've played with before.

"Maybe because of that experience, but also just the level of dedication T has shown over the past 17 years is just incredible.

"I think it was more inspiring for me than intimidating and like, yeah, this is where I want to be and I'm super excited to continue the journey."

Stefie Fejes and Taliqua Clancy are developing a strong partnership. (Supplied: Volleyball World)

That journey will have to include more trips from her home in Sydney's Northern Beaches to Brisbane, mostly for training, but also to deliver a crocheted masterclass to Clancy's nephews.

"Every time I'm with them and call them and anything, they always ask, 'Is Stefanie coming over?' 'Is she going to come crochet?'" Clancy says.

"So they're actually waiting."

Fejes seems OK with that.

"We're going to have a little crochet session together for sure. Absolutely," she says.

Perhaps they can workshop things to make for a certain US Olympic super fan while they're there, too.

World.title: At 35, there is still no end in sight for Dane Gagai
World.content:
He might be 35 and in his 16th year of NRL football, but Dane Gagai is not old.

Is he older than other players? Yes, definitely. Gagai has been around long enough that he's faced footballers involved in the Super League war.

He's the last Newcastle Knight to have played alongside Danny Buderus and when he moves to Brisbane next season he'll join Ben Hunt as the last Broncos to have played with Darren Lockyer.

Penrith legend Craig Gower, who made his first-grade debut 30 years ago, is another former teammate and Gagai is the only player in the entire league who has played in a preliminary final for the Knights courtesy of their run through the 2013 finals.

Dane Gagai is one of the NRL's longest-serving players. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Cody Hopwood, a teammate for Friday night's sudden-death semi-final against South Sydney, watched those games under a Knights blanket at his grandmother's house because he was just seven years old at the time.

Gagai is the fourth most-capped player in Knights history with 238 appearances and has already played the most first-grade games of any outside back in the history of the sport in Australia with 336 and counting.

But that doesn't mean he's old, not by a long shot, because in rugby league to be old is to be done and Gagai is far from done.

Dane Gagai will return to Brisbane next year after leaving almost 16 years ago. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

"If you call me old and I'm out on that field and I'm leaving you behind, whether it's fitness games, conditioning or in the weight room, you better back it up," Gagai said.

"I've signed another contract for next year and I don't plan on finishing up after that but whether that's the end or not, you only have a limited time in this game.

"I don't want to leave it and think, 'If only I'd put in a bit more here or there.'

"Like a lot of players say, you're a long time retired so you might as well enjoy it while you're here.

"It's that competitive side of me [that gets going] when people tell me I'm getting old. It gives me a point to prove."

Gagai has been proving that point for many years now as part of a long goodbye with no end in sight.

Dane Gagai has played some of his best football in recent years. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

It's a different world from the old days of "Origin Gagai", when he shrugged off indifferent club form to become a Queensland superhero.

For many years Gagai has worked hard to make the most of every moment and he still pushes himself to new limits at an age when other players are slowing down.

This year Gagai had the eighth-most tackle busts of any player in the league and was second only to Herbie Farnworth among centres.

He set a new career high for linebreaks in a season two years ago and recorded his career high for average metres per game the year before that.

Some of his best days have come when Newcastle have had little else to go on. Along with Jacob Saifiti, Gagai is one of just two players remaining at the club since its interminable one-win wooden spoon season in 2016.

Hard times like that have made him stronger.

Dane Gagai has given his all for the Knights, in good times and bad. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Case in point was last year, when the Knights again slumped to last amid a horror campaign beset by misery and blighted by attacking struggles.

On a team that couldn't attack to save itself, Gagai had the second-most tackle busts of any player in the league as he gave fine service for a hopeless cause right to the end.

This year, where the Knights have surged back into the finals despite another torrid injury toll, is both a reward and a vindication of his approach, a reminder that while winning is nice the fighting is the point.

Because of those injuries, a lot of Gagai's younger teammates have had to grow up quickly. Many of them will be making their finals debuts on Friday night and Gagai will offer advice if required, but to him most of them won't need it.

Crook elbows and big dreams propel unheralded Knights for finals Newcastle forward Francis Manuleleua might be less than two weeks off dislocating his right elbow but at the end of an interview he'll still shake your hand and shake it hard.

"I don't think I need to say much. I've been so impressed with how these young boys have stepped up," Gagai said.

"I'm sure the nerves are through the roof but nerves aren't always a bad thing. It's just about making sure you prepare well, that's what I'd say to the boys.

"Not only on the field but away from the field, be it sleep, diet, just doing everything you need to do to make sure, come Friday night, you have no doubt in your mind.

"You'll never be able to control nerves, they'll always be there. I still get them. Trust your ability, because these guys have shown what they're capable of and that doesn't change Friday night."

Sixteen years and 336 games is a long time to carry nerves around and they might be warranted this week given Gagai will be marking up on Latrell Mitchell, the apex predator of South Sydney's lethal left edge.

But Gagai learned how to turn those nerves into steel many years ago and he'll take a sense of certainty into his battle with Mitchell, where his physicality and decision-making will prove crucial to Newcastle's hopes of pulling off the upset.

"The nerves, for me, show that you care and you're worried about what could happen," Gagai said.

"But then you need to find out how to control what you can control. We know what Latrell is capable of, we know what Cody [Walker] is capable of, but I can't control what they do.

"I can only control what I do, how I go about things, what my actions are. That's one way to control those nerves, even if they'll always be there."

Dane Gagai still has plenty of mates at South Sydney. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

It'd be easy for Gagai to give into nostalgia this week of all weeks. He still has plenty of mates at South Sydney from his Rabbitoh days who he speaks with all the time. Gagai was shaking hands and slapping backs with a fair few of them at Jai Arrow's 100th NRL game last week.

He thinks Alex Johnston's record-breaking try this year was one of rugby league's best moments of the season and was proud to play a part in a few of them.

Gagai loves that he and his old teammates can fight like demons and have a laugh about it once the dust settles and the blood dries up, like he did after his memorable running battle with Cameron Munster in a match against the Storm earlier this year.

Perhaps he will swap jerseys with someone, as he has many times this year, building a collection he can one day see hanging on the walls and in which he can lose himself in memories.

But not yet. Gagai will not surrender himself to thinking of days past and the recollection of old friends and foes alike. There are still great things to come, he is sure of it.

Why Alex Johnston's record try was pure humanity After all the speculation, the fans stormed the field in the aftermath of Alex Johnston's record-breaking try and the result was an outpouring of emotion celebrating a once-in-a-lifetime achievement.

Gagai insists he has never given a single thought to retirement, or to how Friday could be his last game as a Knight, or to what awaits beyond his return to Brisbane, because to look back is to not be here and not being here is to be lost.

There is still plenty of fight in Gagai yet, especially if someone is going to call him old.

"It's that competitive side of me and I love that side, when people tell me something and I have a point to prove, not to anybody else, just to myself," Gagai said.

"Until I lose that passion, that motivation to compete and play our game, or if the body can't physically keep up, I'm not going to let anyone decide when I'm going to retire. That's my decision and my family's decision.

"I love playing rugby league, I love competing and I hate losing and I'm just glad I'm in this position where we can compete for a premiership."

Tech.title: Slack can now vibe-code interactive charts and reports inside chats
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new feature coming to Slack will allow you to build interactive reports, polls, dashboards, presentations, microsites, and other tools directly inside a chat. With Slackforce Surfaces, you can describe to Slackbot what you need, and it will use AI to gather information from relevant conversations and connected apps, like Google Drive or Salesforce, to create it.

Once Slackbot creates a Surface, you can share it with colleagues and pin it to channels, allowing other people to view it, interact with it, and leave comments. In one example shared by Slack, a user asks Slackbot for help creating an arcade-themed visualization of AI token usage. The AI assistant then generates an interactive dashboard showing token usage across different divisions, such as sales, design, and engineering.

“You’re not exporting your data to some other tool to make sense of it, you’re asking Slackbot to build the dashboard, the deck, the report right where the conversation already is, and your whole team can act on it together,” Ryan Gavin, Slack’s chief marketing officer, tells The Verge in an email.

This update comes just months after Slack overhauled Slackbot to make the tool more like an AI assistant, allowing it to summarize information across channels, sort through messages, and find time to schedule meetings. It also added collaborative vibe coding channels last month.

It seems like there are many other ways to use Surfaces, too, like building a live dashboard for a customer support queue that other workers can view, or creating a weather-themed financial forecast that pulls in data from connected apps. Slack notes that the feature will only pull information that you’ve given its AI tools permission to access.

Slackforce Surfaces is available to all customers — including those who use it for free — with Slackbot enabled in their workspace. You’ll be able to use it with live data starting in October.

Tech.title: Schools are catching on to Big Tech’s playbook
Tech.content:
It’s the hot new thing in tech, and it’s where all the jobs are. Students who don’t learn to use it fall behind. And to help them catch up in time, its creators are graciously providing the resources and curriculum for learning it, often pro bono.

That’s the narrative AI companies are pitching schools on right now, but according to New York Times education technology reporter Natasha Singer, it’s also how the tech industry has built its influence in classrooms for the past 15 years.

In a new book, Coding Kids, Singer details how tech companies took a central role in promoting computers and coding skills in education, promising computer science skills were the ticket to high-paying jobs. But by the time many of those students entered the workforce, new technologies had thrown that promise into question. Meanwhile, the companies got schools to help them create a new class of would-be workers, and trained students on using their products and software, making them likely future customers.

“I worry we have collective amnesia”

Now, the AI industry is pitching itself to schools with similar force. “I worry we have collective amnesia,” Singer told me on a recent episode of The Vergecast. “Have we learned any lessons from these past tech cycles in schools that are going to inform the rollout of AI, make sure that it benefits education, and put in the safeguards now — not a decade from now?” Fortunately, in some ways, she believes the answer is yes.

Singer’s book recounts how more than a decade ago, the country’s largest tech companies embedded themselves directly into school curricula through courses for Advanced Placement Computer Science Principles classes. Apple and Microsoft each created their own curricula, featuring their own tools like Apple’s Swift or Microsoft’s Minecraft. “What’s striking about this is you can imagine that parents would not want, say, Pfizer AP Biology, or Northrop Grumman AP Physics, or ExxonMobil Environmental Science AP,” Singer says. She found that those in the medical field would likely understand why — medical students who are trained by a company on how to implant their proprietary device, one expert told her as an example, rarely choose to try another.

Google has also made itself a dominant force in education through its distribution of low-cost laptops called Chromebooks. Singer tracked their ubiquitous adoption across schools through the 2010s, which she says was accelerated even further during the school shutdowns of the covid-19 pandemic. Google also introduced its Classroom app to help teachers communicate things like assignments and grades. By the time generative AI took off, Singer writes, Google was already a key platform provider for many schools, and well-positioned to promote it.

Even when companies weren’t directly involved in education, they backed nonprofit groups like Code.org. Code.org kicked off its viral education campaign with a splashy celebrity-laden video that included tech moguls like Microsoft founder Bill Gates and then-Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, urging kids to learn to code. Code.org founder Hadi Partovi took a startup-style approach to promoting computer science education, and had little planned for how to capitalize on the attention of the video once it took off, Singer writes. He ultimately funneled that attention into a similarly splashy “Hour of Code” campaign across the country, urging schools to engage in entertaining hour-long courses introducing kids to coding building blocks.

At the time, there wasn’t much pushback, Singer found — though there were some attempts at alternatives. One group of academics engaged in a more traditional, methodological approach to testing and rolling out their own computer science curriculum. It had the express goal of diversifying the kinds of students enrolled in such courses, and taught students to think about big questions around the internet and technology, and scrutinize builders’ motivations.

Eventually, backlash arrived. Some recent graduates say they feel let down that they were told to code their whole lives, just to find such entry-level jobs to be diminishing, Singer told me. Some schools are getting rid of ubiquitous Google Chromebooks, and research around the world is finding that adding technology to the classroom often doesn’t have a significant impact on actual learning.

“Most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech”

“I’m not arguing against tech education or tech in schools,” Singer says. “But what I am saying is most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech. They want kids to learn how to be informed citizens in a democracy, and they want kids to figure out what their passions are and who they are and what their beliefs are… And so if we let the tech industry dictate or even heavily influence what happens in schools, then the question we’re asking is, how can we get AI into schools faster? Which is a product question, and not, ‘What are the most important things we want kids to learn?’”

While the AI industry of the 2020s may be pulling from the 2010s playbook, there already appears to be one distinct difference: Parents and school districts are pushing back. Just last week, the nation’s largest school system, New York City, banned elementary and middle schools from letting students use AI in the classroom for the coming school year. A day later, Los Angeles announced an even broader restriction that included high schoolers. And unlike the few-and-far-between critiques Singer documented in the early days of tech’s coding push, there appears to be a vibrant grassroots movement fighting the screen- and AI-ification of the classroom among parents and teachers alike.

“I think schools are beginning to figure it out,” says Singer, who’s “optimistic” that teachers and students are looking for a broader kind of tech education. That curriculum could teach kids “to ask deep questions about how companies are steering us with their technology, how software and AI are designed to affect our choices, and what role students have to use the tools productively. But also to push back if they like, and to not feel like they’re in a world where AI is driving them.”

Tech.title: Amazon’s Fire TV Stick 4K is over half off at under $20
Tech.content: Looking to take full advantage of your 4K television, but your current streaming stick doesn’t have the right features? Through September 13th, you can grab an Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K from Woot for just $16.09 when you use the coupon code FIRE30 at checkout.
